Allegedly from Proto-Albanian *batsā, from a root *bʰaḱ- shared with Ancient Greek φακός (phakós, “lentil”). See there for further connections.

From Proto-Albanian *bẹ(ð)ə < *baidā-, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰoydʰ-eh₂ < *bʰeydʰ- (“to persuade”). Compare Old English bād (“pledge, expectation”), Proto-Slavic *bě̄dà, Ancient Greek πείθω (peíthō), Latin foedus.

From Proto-Albanian *balbā + -ët, from Proto-Indo-European *balb-, *balbal- (“barbaric speech”), of onomatopoeic origin. Cognate to Ancient Greek βαβάζω (babázō, “chats, talks indistinctly”), Latin balbūtiō (“to stammer, stutter”), Lithuanian blebénti (“babble”). Cf. also Romanian bâlbâi.
From Proto-Albanian *bōr-, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰōrs-, from root *bʰers- (“point, tip bolt”). Cognate to Old Irish barr (“point”).
From Proto-Albanian *bardz(i)ka, from *bardza > bardhë (“white”). Similar sense development as in barmë.
From Proto-Albanian *barwa, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰorwos. Compare English barrow (“castrated boar”), Serbo-Croatian brâv (“male sheep or goat”).
From Proto-Albanian *bibā, from Proto-Indo-European *PiP(P)- (“to chirp, to peep”). Cognate to Serbo-Croatian bìba (“turkey-hen”). Probably a formation of onomatopoeic origin.
From dialectal bjej, bjer, from Proto-Albanian *bera, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerH- (“to strike”) (compare Old English berian, Latin ferīre).
From *bier, from Proto-Albanian *berja, from *bʰér-io-, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰer- (cf. English bear).

From Proto-Albanian *būnja, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰuH- (“to grow”) (compare Ancient Greek φύω (phúō), Old Armenian բուսանիմ (busanim, “to plant, germinate”), Sanskrit भुवन (bhúvana, “existence”).
From archaic and dialectal bilë, from Proto-Albanian *bir(i)lā, derivative of *bira. More at bir. Phonetically and semantically close to Messapic *bilia (“daughter”) and Messapic *biles (“son”).
From Proto-Albanian *būlānjā, from *būla and feminizing suffix *-ānjā, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰolH- (compare Greek φύλλο (fýllo, “leaf”), English blossom).
Archaic and dialectal form of bijë, from Proto-Albanian *bir(i)lā, derivative of *bira. More at bir. Phonetically and semantically close to Messapic *bilia (“daughter”) and Messapic *biles (“son”).
From Proto-Albanian *būmā, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰuH- (“to grow”) (compare Ancient Greek φῦμα (phûma), German Baum (“tree”)).

From Proto-Albanian *bind-, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeydʰ- (“to persuade, encourage; constrain”). Cognate to Ancient Greek πείθω (peíthō, “to persuade, convince”), Illyrian *Bindus (“Illyrian Neptune”) and Thracian Bithus (“theonym”). Doublet with be

From Proto-Albanian *bira, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰer- (compare Old English byre, Gothic 𐌱𐌰𐌿𐍂 (baur, “son”)). Phonetically and semantically close to Messapic *bilia (“daughter”) and *biles (“son”), Matzinger reconstructs two different stems: pre-Albanian *bʰi-ro- and pre-Messapic *bʰi-lo-, both
From Proto-Albanian *birjā, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerH- (“to bore, dig”) (compare English bore, Latin forāre). Probably a metathesized form *briə, from brij.

From Proto-Albanian *būšta, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰuH- (“to grow”) (compare English bush, Greek φύση (fýsi, “nature”), Armenian բույս (buys, “plant”)). Others, however, argue for a borrowing from a pre-Indo-European substratum, drawing parallels to Basque buztan and Romanian buștean.
From Proto-Albanian *bitška, from Proto-Slavic *bičьkъ, derived from *bičь (“whip”).
From Proto-Albanian *dišbera, from *diš- (“away”) + *bera (“to carry”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰéreti (“to be carrying”).
From Proto-Albanian *blaid-ura, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰleyd- (“pale”). Compare Proto-Slavic *blědъ (“pale”), Proto-West Germanic *blait (“pale”).

From Proto-Albanian *blöra-, from Pre-Proto-Albanian *blōra-, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰleh₁-r-ós, from the root *bʰleh₁- (“blue, green, yellow”). Cognate to Latin flōrus (“golden yellow, reddish-yellow”) and Proto-Germanic *blēwaz (“blue, dark”). Possibly borrowed from Proto-Celtic *blaros (“gray

From Proto-Albanian *mletə, from Pre-Proto-Albanian *m(e)lítā- / *mlaytā- "belonging to honey" from Proto-Indo-European *mélit (“honey”). Cognate to Greek μέλισσα (mélissa, “bee”). In view of the -bl- cluster one might also consider as alternative Proto-Indo-European *mlīto (“sweet”), in Gothic blei
From Proto-Albanian *bliga, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰelǵ-. Cognate to Ancient Greek φάλαγξ (phálanx, “stem”), Old Norse bialki (“log”).
From Proto-Albanian *blin-estā, based on bli (“linden”).
From Proto-Albanian *blāukā, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰl̥h₁wós, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰel- (“light, bright”).
From Proto-Albanian *blāgrā, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰlHg-ro- (compare Latin flagrum (“whip”)).
From Proto-Albanian *blezd-eH2, from Proto-Indo-European *melH (“to grind, crush”).

Metaphoric use of boj (“to drive”) (see dëboj), from Proto-Albanian *bāgnja, related to Lithuanian běgti (“to run”), Latvian bêgt (“id.”), Old Prussian begeyte (“id.”) and Greek φέβομαι (févomai, “to be put to flight, flee”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰegʷ-. Usually attested in the passi

From Proto-Albanian *bālnai, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰl̥-no-. Compare Ancient Greek φαλλός (phallós, “penis”), Latin follis (“bellows”), Old Irish ball (“limb, member, part, body part”), Old High German ballo, balla (“buttocks”). Occurs exclusively in the plural form.

parole.significato: any of various nonvenomous snakes of the families Colubridae or Boidae
parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *bālwā, close to Latin bēlua (“beast”) (cf. Italian belva and Romanian balaur. According to Price, they might have be of Dacian origin. It could also be of Pre-indo-European origins alongside Greek πελώριον (pelórion).

With apheresis from dialectal dëborë, dborë, dvorë, which is the original. This is corroborated by the form dorë, which is likewise an aphetic form of the metathesized variant bëdorë, bdorë, vdorë. These point to a Proto-Albanian *diš-bērā or -bārā, prefixed derivative of the verb *bera, whence bie
From Proto-Albanian *bāsta, akin to Proto-Germanic *bōsta (cf. Old High German buost (“rope made of bast”)), *bastaz (“bast”)), Latin fascis.
From Proto-Albanian *bwātā, from *bʰúH-tis, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰuH-. Cognate to Sanskrit भू (bhū́-, “earth, world”) and भूमि (bhū́mi-, “earth, ground, soil”).
From Proto-Albanian *bredza, from earlier *breda, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰrédʰ-e-ti (“to wade”), from *bʰredʰ- (compare Slovene brédem (“I wade”), Lithuanian breñda (“he wades”)).
From Proto-Albanian *brainja, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰreyH- (“to cut, spoil”) (compare English brine, Serbo-Croatian brȉjati (“to shave”), Latin friāre (“to rub, crumble”)).
From Proto-Albanian *(en) per en ta, from Proto-Indo-European *én per én tód, a sequence of particles.
From Proto-Albanian *brainikā, derivative of *brainja (modern brej).
From Proto-Albanian *braištā, denasalized from *brainštā, deverbative of *brainja (modern brej (“to gnaw”)).
Singularized plural of *brash, from Proto-Albanian *brauša, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰrews-. Compare Dutch broos (“brittle”), Latin frustum (“shard”).

To be split as brê (“belt, girdle”) + -zë (“diminutive suffix”). The base continues Common Albanian *brê, from Proto-Albanian *brêna-, which may go back to an Early-Proto-Albanian *brœna-, from Pre-Proto-Albanian *brōna-, or directly from Pre-Proto-Albanian *brena-. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-Europe
From Proto-Albanian *brin(i), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰreyH- (“to rub, scratch”). Cognate to Proto-Slavic *briti (“to shave”) and Thracian βρίλων (brílōn, “barber”).
From Proto-Albanian *brima, a derivative in -më of Proto-Indo-European *bʰerH- (“to bore, dig”).
From Proto-Albanian *breg(i)štā, from a disused verb, a derivative of Proto-Indo-European *bʰreg- (“to break”). Compare Latin fragilis (“id”), English break, German bersten, Manx brish, Irish briste.
From Proto-Albanian *britška, from Proto-Slavic *bričьkъ, diminutive of *bričь (“id”).

Gheg word. From Proto-Albanian *breita, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰreyH- (“to pierce, cut with something sharp”). Cognate to Lithuanian bárti (“to scold, chide”), Old Irish briathar (“argument”), Old Church Slavonic брати (brati, “fight”), Welsh brwydr (“fight, struggle”).

From Proto-Albanian *bruma, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰréwmn̥, from the root *bʰrew(h₁)- (compare Old English burme (“leaven”), Latin fermentum (“leaven, yeast”)), from *bʰrewh₁- (“to boil, seethe”) (compare English brew). The term is based on a Proto-Albanian *-bru- (“to knead"”), seen also in mbr

From Proto-Albanian *brustula, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰrust- (compare Old Saxon brustian (“to sprout”), Russian брость (brostʹ, “buds (of a shrub)”), from the root *bʰrews- (“to swell, grow”). Ylli and Topalli have argued for a borrowing from Serbo-Croatian bljȗšt (“black bryony”), dialectal blj
From Proto-Albanian *brudja, from Proto-Indo-European *bhrou-dh-. Cognate with Proto-Slavic *brudъ (“dirt”) and Thracian βρουτος (broutos, “barley beer”).

parole.significato: tender, soft, delicate, ripe (to the touch)
parole.testo: From brydh + -t, from Proto-Albanian *brūdza, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰruHg- (compare English brook, Serbo-Croatian brusiti (“to whet”)).

Formally identical with Thracian βóλινθος (bólinthos, “bull”), from a Proto-Albanian *bōlna. Phonetically, a borrowing from Byzantine Greek βούβαλος (boúbalos); (compare Latin būbalus, both from Ancient Greek βούβαλος (boúbalos)), is also possible.

parole.significato: to lodge, provide room and board
parole.testo: From *bunj, from Proto-Albanian *budnja, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰudʰ-ne/o, from *bʰewdʰ- (“to be wake, keep watch”) (compare Proto-Slavic *buditi (“to wake, to rouse”), Lithuanian budė́ti). According to Georgiev, from Thracian βουνον (bounon)

From Proto-Albanian *buliā, from Proto-Indo-European *bh(e)ū̆- (“swell, puff”). Cognate to Ancient Greek φῷδες (phōîdes, “blisters”), Old Irish bolach (“swelling, blister”), Latin bucca (“cheek”) and Old English bȳle (“swelling, blister”).

From Proto-Albanian *bukura, derivative of *buk- (“lush, lusty”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰoHu- (“to grow, swell”), close to Proto-Germanic *būkaz (“belly, body”), compare Icelandic búkur (“torso”), English bouk, German Bauch, Old Czech buj (“mad, foolish”)). Similar sense development as with kol
From Proto-Albanian *bukā, from Latin bucca (“mouth, mouthful”), with a semantic development to 'food' through a Balkan source.

From Proto-Albanian *buklā, derivative of *buk- (“lush, lusty”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰoHu- (“to grow, swell”). More at bukur (“beautiful”). For sense development, compare Latin lascivia (“mink”), from lascivus (“wanton”).
Related to ulpëti and ulzë, from Proto-Albanian *ul-, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁élem (“mountain elm”). Compare Latin ulmus, Welsh llwyf and English elm.
From bull + -ungë, the former element from Proto-Albanian *bulna, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰel- (“to swell”).

parole.significato: cheek, soft part of the face
parole.testo: Suffixed form of *bulë, from Proto-Albanian *bulā, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰelǵʰ-. Compare Irish bolg (“bubble; sack, bag, belly, husk, trouser”), Old Norse bolginn (“swollen”), bylgja (“wave”).

parole.significato: hut (of mountain shepherds), chalet, fenced area (for cattle)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Albanian *bhunā. Compare Illyrian *bounon. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰewdʰ- (“to be wake, keep watch”).

From Proto-Albanian *bunga, of uncertain origin: * Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₂ǵnos, nasalized variant of *bʰeh₂ǵos (“beech”); * earlier Proto-Albanian *bunka, from *bʰeu-n-ik-o-, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰew(H)- (“to grow”); * Proto-Indo-European *bʰn̥ǵʰ- (“to swell, be thick”) with a shift in mean
From Proto-Albanian *burništā, derivative of buron. Compare Old High German burjan (“to push up, raise”), Old English byrian (“to come up, occur”).

From Proto-Albanian *burmā, from Proto-Indo-European *bher-2 (“to boil, swell; to get high”). Cognate to Latin fretum (“a strait, sound, estuary, firth, channel”), Low German Bärme, and Middle Dutch berm, barm (“barm”).
From Proto-Albanian *buroniā, derivative of buron. Compare Old High German burjan (“to push up, raise”), Old English byrian (“to come up, occur”).

Continuing a Proto-Albanian *bur-na-, with a semantic change from "highly raised, elevated, exaulted" to "strong, sublime, great", from Proto-Indo-European *bʰer- (“to carry, bring, bear”), sharing origins with bie (“to bring, bear”), and related to the verb mburr (“to praise, extol, glorify”). Poss
From Proto-Albanian *bukta, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰewgʰ- (“to bend, bow”) (compare English bow, Irish bog (“soft”), Lithuanian bukùs).

From archaic and now chiefly dialectal (Arbëresh) budhë + -zë (collective suffix), from Proto-Albanian *budzā, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰudʰmḗn (“bottom”); compare Lithuanian budė̃ (“tree-fungus”), bùdė (“whetstone”), Sanskrit बुध्न (budhna), Ancient Greek πυθμήν (puthmḗn, “bottom”), Latin fundus
From Proto-Albanian *būtsia, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰew- (“to swell, bend, curve”).
From Proto-Albanian *būra, from Proto-Indo-European *bhū (“to grow”), probably a denominative based on an unattested abstract noun *bhūrom > *būra.

From Proto-Albanian *būtsā, or Proto-Albanian *būðā, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰudʰmḗn (“bottom”), possibly from *dʰewb- (“deep”). Cognate to Sanskrit बुध्न (budhna, “bottom”), Ancient Greek πυθμήν (puthmḗn, “bottom”), and Old English botm (English bottom).

From archaic and dialectal bënj (“to make appear; do, make”), from Proto-Albanian *banja, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰh₂-n-yé-ti, from *bʰeh₂- (“shine”) (compare Greek φαίνομαι (faínomai, “to seem, appear”).

From Proto-Albanian *bōrei ulnā, compound of *bōrei (“bow”) and *ulnā (“forearm”). More at ber and llërë. For sense development, compare English elbow, compound of ell (“ell”), originally ‘forearm’, and bow. See also ylber (“rainbow”), a mirror formation.
From Proto-Albanian *eburusa, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ebʰros. Compare Proto-Celtic *eburos (“yew”), German Eberesche (“rowan”). Possibly borrowed from Proto-Celtic *eburos

parole.significato: pomace, lees, dregs, residual mash (after pressing olives or grapes)
parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *britśiā, closely related to Latin brisa (“husks of grapes”). The further origin is uncertain; perhaps also cognate to Ancient Greek βρύτεα (brútea). According to Pokorny (1:144), Latin brisa (“husks of wine”) is an Illyrian loanword. Conversely, Orel considers it a borrowing fro

Metathetic reduced form of dialectal britas (preserved in Gheg), extension in -as of brit- (stem for optative, admirative, participle, etc.); compare klith > këlthas, thirr > thërras, fol > flas, etc. From Proto-Albanian *breita, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰreyH- (“to cut, pierce”); cognate with Old
From Proto-Albanian *tserka related to ther (“to slaughter”).

From Proto-Albanian *tˢermā, related to Lithuanian šarmà (“frost”), Latvian saŕma (“id”). Same as thermë and thermit, with the usual c:th alteration in Albanian, connected to an older form of ther, *cer.

From Proto-Albanian *tsitsā, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱik- (compare Serbo-Croatian sisa (“teat, tit”), Irish cíoch (“breast”)). Related to thith. Compare Macedonian цица (cica), Italian zizza, German Zitze. Akin to sisë and thithë.

Used mostly by Arbëreshë of Sicily, in passive voice citem (“to get full”). From Proto-Albanian *tˢeita, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷeiətos. Cognate to Proto-Slavic *čitъ (“whole”), Lithuanian ki̇́etas (“hard”). Alternative rejected proposed origins include the affiliation with σιτεύω (sitévo, “to f
From cit (“to make full, to stuff”), from Proto-Albanian *tˢeita, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷeiətos. Cognate to Proto-Slavic *čitъ (“whole”), Lithuanian ki̇́etas (“hard”).
From sup, from Proto-Albanian *tˢupa, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱuh₁-po- (compare Sanskrit शोफ (śópha, “swelling”)), from *ḱuh₁- (“to swell up”).

From Proto-Albanian *tšūtja, from *kju-t-jo, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱey- (“to set in motion”) (compare Ancient Greek σεύω (seúō, “to chase (away), rush, incite”), Latin cieō). Doublets include qoj and ndërsej.
Related to cërij (“to sauté, fry”), from Proto-Albanian *tˢira, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱerh₂- (“to mix”).

Inherited from Proto-Albanian *danja, transformed from earlier Proto-Albanian *daja under the influence of other verbs ending in -nj, from Proto-Indo-European *déh₂-ye-tor, from *deh₂- (“to share, divide”) (compare Ancient Greek δαίομαι (daíomai), Sanskrit दयते (dáyate)).
From Proto-Albanian *dauka, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰew-, further related to Lithuanian dvékti (“to breathe”), dvākas (“breath”). Related to dash.
From Proto-Albanian *dala, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰelh₁- (“to spring forth, flourish”). Compare Ancient Greek θάλλω (thállō, “to grow, bloom, thrive”), Welsh deillio (“to emanate, derive”).
From Proto-Albanian *daulnānja, deadjectival of *daulna, from Proto-Indo-European *delh₁- (“to cut”) (compare Latvian dalīt (“to divide”), Latin dolāre (“to hew”), Old Norse telgja (“to carve”)).

parole.significato: outgoing, extended, protruding (features, personality, clothing, etc.)
parole.testo: Participle of Albanian dal (“I exit, go out”). From Proto-Albanian *dala. See Albanian dal (“I exit, go out”) for more.
From Proto-Albanian *dangā. Cognate to Lithuanian dangà (“table cloth, cover”), Latvian dañga (“puddle, marshland”).
From Proto-Albanian *dardā, deverbative of *darda (“to spill, pour”) whence modern derdh, compare Proto-Slavic *kruša (“pear”) for such semantic development.

Inherited from Proto-Albanian *darkā, from Proto-Indo-European *dorkʷ-o-. Cognate to Ancient Greek δόρπον (dórpon, “supper, dinner; evening”). Has entered the declension of the feminine ā-stems. According to Alexander Lubotsky and Michiel de Vaan, considering the distribution of the term, both Greek
From Proto-Albanian *dartśei-, from Proto-Indo-European *dorkʷ- (“meal”). Cognate with Ancient Greek δόρπον (dórpon, “supper, dinner; evening”).
From Proto-Albanian *daknā, from Proto-Indo-European *denḱ- (“to bite”). Cognate to Ancient Greek δάκνω (dáknō, “to bite”) and Old High German zanga (“tongs”).
Potentially from Early Proto-Albanian *dauša, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰows-o-s (compare English deer, Lithuanian daũsos (“upper air; heaven”)).
Goes back to Proto-Albanian *dartšimā, originally, "wedding feast", derived from darkë.
From Proto-Albanian *duai-au, from Proto-Indo-European *duo-, from the root *du (“two”). Cognate to Old High German zweio (“by, in two, in pairs”). A frozen locative dual form.

From Proto-Albanian *deni̯ō, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁(y)- (“to suck, drink”). Cognate to Sanskrit धयति (dháyati, “to suck”) and Latvian det (“to suck”). Present deh, dej arose secondarily under the influence of the non-active paradigm. Possibly the origin of the Paeonian Dyalos, cognate to An

From Proto-Albanian *den(i)-, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰew- (“to run, flow”). Cognate to Sanskrit धन्वन् (dhánvan-, “desert, arid land, steppe”), Ancient Greek θέω (théō, “run”, verb) and Old English dēaw (“dew”).
From Proto-Albanian *dailjā, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁-l-. Compare Old English delu (“teat”). More at djalë. Possibly the source of the Illyrian tribe name Dalmatae.
Inherited from Proto-Albanian *daislā, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰiH-slo (compare Latin fīlum, Lithuanian gýsla, Serbo-Croatian žȉla).

From Proto-Albanian *dailjā, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁-l-. Compare Old English delu (“teat”). More at djalë. Possibly the source of the Illyrian tribe name Dalmatae. Hyllested noted that Delme is only a metathesis away from Proto-Germanic *tamila-, as Proto-Albanian *dalma a derivative of Prot
From Proto-Albanian *dama, from Proto-Indo-European *dm̥h₂ós (“bull”) (compare Irish damh, Ancient Greek δάμαλος (dámalos, “calf”)), from *demh₂- (“to tame”) (compare Latin domō, English tame).

parole.significato: a sack crammed with things, pile (of objects)
parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *dʰingʷ-u, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeygʷ- (“to stick, fix”).

From Proto-Albanian *derdza, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰorǵʰ-éye-ti, causative-iterative of the root *dʰerǵʰ- (“turn”) (compare Old Armenian դարձաւ (darjaw, “he turned (around)”)). For the semantic shift, compare French verser (“pour (out)”) from Latin versāre (“to turn, twist”).

parole.significato: to be bedridden, (be lying) ill, pine (away)
parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *dargei-, from Proto-Indo-European *derHgʰ-. Cognate to Lithuanian di̇̀rgti (“to feel faint, faint”), Proto-Slavic *dьrgati (“to pluck, to pull”), and Proto-Germanic *targijaną (“to tear”). Present dergjem with umlaut of the root vowel, as usual in the Albanian non-active paradig

A reduced form of older ndjeri, possibly from Proto-Albanian *en-terōd, ablative formation from Proto-Indo-European *h₁énteros (“inside, within”); compare Sanskrit अन्तर (ántara), Ancient Greek ἔντερον (énteron).

From Proto-Albanian *darja (“pig”), from *ǵʰóryos (“pig”) (compare Greek χοίρος (choíros, “id”)), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰḗr (“hedgehog”), from *ǵʰer- (“to be excited, bristly”) (compare Latin horrere (“to bristle, tremble”)). Perhaps the source of the name of the Illyrian tribe Deuri.
From archaic and dialectal derk, from Proto-Albanian *darika, diminutive of *darja (“pig”) (modern derr). More at derr.
From Proto-Albanian *dœrə < *dwōrā, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰwṓr (“door”). Compare Proto-Slavic *dvьrь, Sanskrit द्वारा (dvārā), Latin foris, English door.
Tosk; from Proto-Albanian *deuna, from Proto-Indo-European *dew- (“lack, fail”) (compare Icelandic tjón (“loss”), Ancient Greek δῠ́η (dŭ́ē, “misery”)).

From Proto-Albanian *dzalā, from earlier *dzalakta, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵlákt (gen. *ǵlaktós). Compare Old Armenian կաթն (katʻn), Ancient Greek γάλα (gála, “milk”), Hittite 𒂵𒆷𒀝𒋻 (galaktar, “balm, resin”), Latin lac (“milk, milky juice”), Waigali zōr (“milk”) and the irregular Romanian zară.

From Proto-Albanian *dʰh₁-teh₂, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁-, *dʰh₁- (“to place, put”). Cognate to Ancient Greek τίθημι (títhēmi, “to place”), Latin faciō (“to do, make”), Lithuanian dėti (“to put”), Sanskrit दधाति (dádhāti), Old English dōn (“to do”).

parole.significato: and (used to connect two similar words, phrases, et cetera)
parole.testo: * Conjunction e (“and, also”): according to Orel from Proto-Albanian *ō(d), from Proto-Indo-European *ēd ~ *ōd (ablative sg. stem of Proto-Indo-European *ē- ~ *ō-). See edhe.

From Proto-Albanian *dzō, from Pre-Proto-Albanian *dᶻȫs < *dᶻ́ȫs < *dᶻ́ö́s < *dᶻ́ṓs, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰǵʰōm (“earth”). Compare Ancient Greek χθών (khthṓn), Latin humus, Old Church Slavonic землꙗ (zemlja). By some identified as the source of Ancient Greek δῆ (dê, “earth”).
From Proto-Albanian *dzemba, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵembʰ- (“to bite”). Compare Sanskrit जम्भति (jambhati, “to snap at”) and Lithuanian žembiù (“to cut”).
From Proto-Albanian *dzōmjā, from *dzō (“ground, dirt”). More at dhe.
Plurale tantum; from the Gheg variant dhênd, from Proto-Albanian *dzenti, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵénh₁tis, from *ǵenh₁- (“to produce, to beget, to give birth”). Compare Latin gens, English kin.
From Proto-Albanian *və-dez with the prefix v(ë)-, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰegʷʰ- (“to burn”).

From Proto-Albanian *aidzijā, cognate to Ancient Greek αἴξ (aíx) and Old Armenian այծ (ayc, “goat”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eyǵ- (“goat”). The word may also be an ancient adjective like Ancient Greek αἴγειος (aígeios), similar to shtërpi (“reptile”).

From Proto-Albanian *dzelmā, related to dhallë (“buttermilk”) as per Orel. On the other hand, Demiraj derives it from Proto-Albanian *δem(-) as cognate to Ancient Greek δημός (dēmós, “fat”) and Romanian zeamă (“juice; sauce”), though Orel refutes this on the basis that, if related to the Greek term,
From *djeth + -të, from Proto-Albanian *detsa, from Proto-Indo-European *déḱm̥. Initial dh- from decimal compounds like tridhjetë (“thirty”).
From Proto-Albanian *dhu̯onti, from Proto-Indo-European *deh₃- (“to give”).

First attested in 1555 by Buzuku as dhunë. From Proto-Albanian *eðunā, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ed-ún-eh₂ (“pain”), from the root *h₁ed- (“to eat”). Cognate to Ancient Greek ὀδύνη (odúnē, “pain”), Old Armenian երկն (erkn, “birth pangs”), and Old Irish idu (“pains, birth pangs”). The variant dhurë
From Proto-Albanian *ðámba-, from Pre-Proto-Albanian *j́amba-, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵómbʰos (“tooth, peg”) (compare English comb, Greek γομφίος (gomfíos, “molar”), Serbo-Croatian zȗb (“tooth”)).

Multiple reconstructions: 1) Demiraj derives it from Proto-Albanian *ĝāmtḗr- 2) Orel from Proto-Albanian *dzanra 3) Matzinger from Proto-Albanian *ðándura-, from Pre-Proto-Albanian *j́ándura All ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵem- (“to marry”). Cognate to Latin gener, Ancient Greek γαμβρός (ga
From Proto-Albanian *dī̆ya (as well as in Pre-Proto-Albanian), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰ(e)yHe/o- (“to consider, think”) or Proto-Indo-European *diHyé/ó- (“to consider, think”).
The 3rd person singular din. From Proto-Albanian *dine, denominative of Proto-Indo-European *dey-no- (“day”). See din for more.

Disputed. Possibilities include: * From Proto-Albanian *delwa, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰelh₃u̯o-, from the root *ǵʰelh₃- (“gleam, yellow”), a tabooistic substitute for the original *sóh₂wl̥. Cognate with Lithuanian žel̃vas, Latin helvus, Sanskrit हरि (hari). * From Proto-Indo-European *sh₂wélyos
From Proto-Albanian *dīkā, Cognate to Lithuanian dykas (“idle, empty”), Proto-Slavic *dikъ (“wild”).

From late Proto-Albanian *dimənə, from *ðimənə, from earlier *j́īmanʉh, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰéy-mō < *ǵʰey- (“winter”). Orel reconstructs Proto-Albanian *deimena. Cognate with Ancient Greek χειμών (kheimṓn, “winter”) and the like.
From Proto-Albanian *deina (“day”), from Proto-Indo-European *dey-no-, ultimately from *dyew- (“to shine”). Cognate with Proto-Slavic *dьnь, Latvian diena, Lithuanian dėina, Old Prussian dēinā.
From Proto-Albanian *dī́tan, from Proto-Indo-European *dih₂-t- (“the shining”). See Sanskrit दीप् (dīp, “to blaze, glow”) for more. Reinforcement by Latin diēs is possible.
From an earlier djāll, from Proto-Albanian *diaβəł, borrowed from Latin diabolus (“devil”), ultimately derived from Ancient Greek διάβολος (diábolos, “slanderer”).

From Proto-Albanian *dela, from *dʰeh₁-l-os, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁-l- (compare Latvian dêls (“son”), Latin filius (“son”), Old English delu (“teat”), Old Armenian դալ (dal)), from *dʰeh₁(y)- (“to suck”). Originally a neuter noun, as it appears in Buzuku's Meshari.

From Old Albanian djathëtë, derivative of djathë (“right side”), from Proto-Albanian *detsa, from pre-Albanian *deḱsi̯o, from Proto-Indo-European *deḱs- (compare Ancient Greek δεξιός (dexiós),Old High German zeso, Middle Dutch tesuwe, Irish deas).
From Proto-Albanian *dedi, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰédʰh₁i (“milk”). Compare Old Prussian dadan, Sanskrit दधि (dádhi, “sour milk”).
From Proto-Albanian *de, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰǵʰyés.
From Proto-Albanian *dega, Proto-Indo-European *dʰégʷʰeti.

Attested historically with various genders and definite forms, most notably djep and djebë. These allow for a reconstruction of Common Albanian *dʲeb(i), older *dʰʲebi, which was inherited from Proto-Albanian *dᶻ́ʰʲebi-, from Pre-Proto-Albanian *j́ʰébi-, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰebʰ(y)i- (“contai

parole.significato: to be lying ill, to fall (down)
parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *derga/i-, from Pre-Proto-Albanian *dergamay, from Proto-Indo-European *derHgʰ-. Cognate to Lithuanian di̇̀rgti (“to feel faint, faint”).
Inherited from Proto-Albanian *dāsrā, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰésōr, from *ǵʰes- + *-ōr.
From Proto-Albanian *dā(i)tjā, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁(y)- (“to suckle”).

The dialectal forms of dra-t (Mat), drā-t (Tropojë), Arbëreshë drā, and Arvanitika dra-të, which are also neuter, point to a common neuter root *drā-. The long vowel indicates a vowel contraction due to the loss of an intervocalic segment, including Proto-Albanian *y, *w, *h, and *β. The likeliest s
From Proto-Albanian *dragɔ̄n, borrowed from Vulgar Latin *dragōnis, from Latin dracō, dracōnem, from Ancient Greek δράκων (drákōn).
From Proto-Albanian *dranga. Cognate with Old Norse drangr (“stone pillar”), Lithuanian dránga (“perch, pole”), Proto-Slavic *drǫgъ.

From Proto-Albanian *drani, identical to Hesychian ἀρανίς (aranís) (misspelling of δρανίς (dranís, “deer”)), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰreh₁n- (“drone, buzz”). Compare English drone, Ancient Greek θρήνος (thrḗnos, “lament”)).

From Proto-Albanian *dredza, rebuilt from earlier *dridza (preserved in ndrizë), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰregʰ- (“to run, drag”). Cognate with Old Armenian դարձ (darj, “return; change”), English draw.
From Proto-Albanian *drigā, close to Proto-Germanic *targijaną (“to pull, to stir”), Proto-Slavic *dьrgati (“to pull, to tug”), Lithuanian di̇̀rginti (“to move, to irritate”).
From Proto-Albanian *drikā, from Proto-Indo-European *dr̥kʷ-eh₂, from *dorkʷ-o-. Cognate to Ancient Greek δόρπον (dórpon, “supper, dinner; evening”).
Originally “doe”, from Proto-Albanian *dranjā, feminine of *drani (“deer, stag”), whence modern dre.
From Proto-Albanian *dreδ-, from Proto-Indo-European *d(h)r- (“to tremble, quake, rock”). Cognate to Lithuanian drebù (“to tremble, quake”).
From Proto-Albanian *drūnjā, from Proto-Indo-European *druh₂o (“tree”).

Inherited from Proto-Albanian *dritsa, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰr̥sdom-, *ǵʰr̥sdʰi-, null-grade of the root *ǵʰresdʰ- (“(kind of) cereals; barley”). Cognate with Ancient Greek κριθή (krithḗ), Old Armenian գարի (gari), and German Gerste. Probably an old Wanderwort.

* From Proto-Albanian *driktā, from Proto-Indo-European *dŕ̥ḱtis (“sight, vision; appearance”) + *-éh₂ (thematic feminine ending), from the root *derḱ- (“to see”). Cognate with Sanskrit दृष्टि (dṛ́ṣṭi, “sight, vision, aspect”) and Avestan 𐬛𐬀𐬭𐬱𐬙𐬌𐬯 (darštis, “sight”); further compare Old English torht
From Proto-Albanian *drāwā. Related to Latvian druvas (“fear”), Lithuanian draudžiù (“to forbid, to deter, to scare off”), from Proto-Indo-European [Term?].

From Proto-Albanian *drābnā, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰrew- (“to crumble, grind”), with diminutive suffix -icë, shaped similarly to grimcë (“crumb, particle”). Compare Old Church Slavonic дробити (drobiti, “crush, break, rupture, grind”), Gothic 𐌲𐌰𐌳𐍂𐌰𐌱𐌰𐌽 (gadraban, “cut out”).
From Proto-Albanian *drāusā, from Proto-Indo-European *drewh₂- (“steady, firm”), extension of *dóru. Cf. drënjë.
Inherited from Proto-Albanian *druwa, from Proto-Indo-European *druh₂-ó-m, from *dóru. Compare Ancient Greek δρῦς (drûs) and others.
From Proto-Albanian *drāunja, a derivative of droe.
From Proto-Albanian *drustā, from the same root of dru. More at dru.
From Proto-Albanian *drūdza, with a secondary suffix -ët, close to Proto-Slavic *dryzgati, *druzgati (“to squeeze, to crush”).

From Proto-Albanian *draunjā, from Proto-Indo-European *drew- (“tree; hard, strong, firm”). Compare Latin dūrus (“hard, rough”), Old English trum (“strong, firm”), Old Armenian տրամ (tram, “firm, solid”), and Ancient Greek δροόν (droón, “strong, mighty”).
From Proto-Albanian *dēma, from Proto-Indo-European *déh₁mn̥, from the root *deh₁- (“band”). Cognate to Ancient Greek -δημα (-dēma, “band”) and Sanskrit दमान् (dā́man-, “band”).
From Proto-Albanian *dānja, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₂nyós, compare Sanskrit धान्य (dhānyá, “grain”).

From *dum-dum, root doubling of Proto-Albanian *dubna, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewbʰ- (“to whisk, smoke, darken, obscure”). Close to Old Norse dumbr (“dumb”), German dumm (“dumb, stupid”), Greek τυφλός (tyflós, “blind”).

From Proto-Albanian *dupsa, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewh₂- (“blow, smoke; dark, gray, deep”). Compare Old English dofian (“rage”), Middle High German top (“senseless, brainless, crazy”), Ancient Greek τῦφος (tûphos, “smoke, steam, dense smoke; wooziness, folly, silly pride”), Latin suffio (“to fu

From Proto-Albanian *duk-, from Proto-Indo-European *dewk- (“to draw”). An etymological connection to ancient Greek δοκέω and Gothic þugkjan (to think, to appear) is phonetically impossible. The use of third-person singular present of δοκέω, δοκεῖ ("it seems" [to me]) in ancient Greek probably influ
From Proto-Albanian *duwō masc, *duwai fem, from Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁. Matzinger reconstructs *duu̯a.
From Proto-Albanian *j́ūla, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰuslom < *ǵʰew- (“to pour”). Compare Ancient Greek χυλός (khulós, “juice”)).

From Proto-Albanian *dūnda, cognate to Old Norse duna (“thunderous noise”), Ancient Greek θύνω (thúnō, “to rush, to dart along”), Sanskrit ध्वनति (dhvánati, “to sound”). Possibly related to tund or onomatopoeic.
From Proto-Albanian *dwis, as per Orel, and thus a doublet of s-. However, perhaps instead a contraction of dyfish; the noun and adjective seem to have related uncontracted forms too.

According to Orel, from dialectal dëllënjë, from Proto-Albanian *daislanjā, from *daislā (“tendon, sinew”) (modern dell). According to Çabej (corroborated by Demiraj), a derivative of dyllë (“wax, sap”) > *dyɫinjə with the -inj plural suffix. According to Topalli, the root could have been inherited
Inherited from Proto-Albanian *danga, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰengʰ- (“to cover”). Compare English dung.
Enlargement of Proto-Albanian *danga.
* Conjunction e (“and, also”): according to Orel from Proto-Albanian *ō(d), from Proto-Indo-European *ēd ~ *ōd (ablative sg. stem of Proto-Indo-European *ē- ~ *ō-).
From *etës (compare dialectal ecëj), from Proto-Albanian *aitatja, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁éyti, present of *h₁ey-. Compare Serbo-Croatian ìći, Lithuanian ei̇̃ti. See heci.
From Proto-Albanian *ayð(iy)a-, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eyǵ- (compare Ancient Greek αἴξ (aíx), Armenian այծ (ayc), Lithuanian ožỹs).

From Proto-Albanian *a-salwa, a compound equivalent to a privative e- (from *a-, from Proto-Indo-European *n̥-) + gjellë, literally "without food". Modern reinterpretation as simply e- + gjëlle (“starving”).
From Proto-Albanian *akˢka, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱ- (“sharp”).
From Proto-Albanian *albi-, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂élbʰit (compare Ancient Greek ἄλφι (álphi, “barley meal”), Pashto [script needed] (ōrbaše)).

Rhotacism from emën, preserved in Gheg. From Proto-Albanian *é(n)minad, from Pre-Proto-Albanian *é(n)mina, earlier *ánmina < *ánmena, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ń̥h₃menh₂ (“names”), collective of *h₁nómn̥ (“name”).
From Proto-Albanian *agni, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁n̥gʷnís (“fire”).
From Proto-Albanian *antis/t, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂n̥t-jes/t (“to plait, weave”).

parole.significato: to gallivant (about a place), gad about, to wander
parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *ende-, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁endʰ- (“way, to go”). Cognate to Ancient Greek ἐνθεῖν (entheîn, “to come”) and Sanskrit अध्वन् (ádhvan-, “way”). Possibly related to ἄνδινος περίπατος (andinos perípatos), a phrase attested in Greek, possibly of Illyrian origin. One might also

From Proto-Albanian *and-, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éndʰos (“sprout, germ”). Cognate to Ancient Greek ἄνθος (ánthos, “sprout, flower”) and Vedic Sanskrit अन्धस् (ándhas, “Soma, grass, herb”). A formation with umlaut of the root vowel from plural *andī̆.
From Proto-Albanian *anga, related to Lithuanian angùs (“sluggish, lazy, idle”), éngti (“to strangle”), Latvian îgt (“to wear off, to languish”), and Gothic 𐌰𐌲𐌲𐍅𐌿𐍃 (aggwus, “narrow”).
Proto-Albanian *agni, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁n̥gʷnis (“fire”).
From Proto-Albanian *aignjā, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eyǵ- (“oak”). Compare Sardinian eni. Cognates From Proto-Indo-European: Old High German eih, Old Norse eik.
From Proto-Albanian *agnjā, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂egʷnós.
Plurale tantum; diminutive plural of archaic arg, from Proto-Albanian *arga, from Proto-Indo-European *Horgʰi. Cognate with Armenian ոջիլ (oǰil, “louse”).

According to Orel, Proto-Albanian *ausra (“twilight”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ews- (“dawn”) (compare English Easter, Latin aurōra, Lithuanian aušrà). Another theory links it to Proto-Indo-European *h₁régʷos, but the phonological development required seems implausible.

parole.significato: period of time, span, space, stretch, lapse
parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *aiwesyā (Jokl L.-k. U. 34), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂óyu (“vital energy, vitality”). Cognate to Ancient Greek αἰές (aiés, “always”), Latin aevus (“eternity, age, time”) and Gothic 𐌰𐌹𐍅𐍃 (aiws, “time, eternity, world”).

From Proto-Albanian *a-tšilna or *a-čila-, a compound equivalent to a privative e- (from *a-, from Proto-Indo-European *n̥-) + sillë (“breakfast”). Interpretible as e- + sille (“breakfast”) A similar formation to egjëll.

From Proto-Albanian *aida(s), from Proto-Indo-European *h2eidh-o- (“burning fire”). Cognate to Ancient Greek αἶθος (aîthos, “burning, fire”), Old English ád (“funeral pile”), Old Saxon ēd (“firebrand”).

parole.significato: to sate (with food or drink), gorge, stuff
parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *spanja, related to Proto-Germanic *spannjan (“to tighten”), with a secondary expressive gemination, to be compared with Old Norse spenna (“to tighten”).

From Proto-Albanian *farā-, from *pʰarā-, from EPA *pharā-, (via metathesis) from Pre-Proto-Albanian *hparā-, from *sparā-, from Proto-Indo-European *sporéh₂ < *sper- (“to spread out”). Compare Ancient Greek σπόρος (spóros, “seed”).

From Proto-Albanian *spesla, metathesized form of *spelsa, from Proto-Indo-European *pels- (“rock, boulder”), variant of *spel- (“to cleave, break”). Compare Latin hydronym Pelso, Latin Palatium, Pashto پرښه (parša, “rock, rocky ledge”), Ancient Greek πέλλα (pélla, “stone”), German Felsen (“boulder,
From Proto-Albanian *spernā, from Proto-Indo-European *sper (“spear, stick”), close to Latin sparus (“short spear”), Proto-Germanic *speru (whence Old Norse spjǫr).
From an unattested *fij, from Proto-Albanian *spija, cognate with Sanskrit स्फायते (spháyate, “to become fat”), Proto-Slavic *spěti (“to ripen”).

From Proto-Albanian *speika, related to Lithuanian pei̇̃kti (“to despise, to scold”), pykti (“to be angry”), Latvian peĩkt (“to be spoilt”). Possible cognates in Germanic are Swedish spink (“lean man”) and Norwegian spiken (“dry”).
From Proto-Albanian *spinā, semantically identical to Thracian [script needed] (pinos, “kind of stone which burns when water is poured on it”), possibly derived from it.

From Proto-Albanian *spinga, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)pingos (“chaffinch”), identical with Greek σπίγγος (spíngos, “id”), English spink, Old Norse spiki (“kind of bird”). One might also consider a borrowing from Proto-Germanic *finkiz, *finkōn (“finch”), possibly Balkan Gothic.
From Proto-Albanian *spūška, cognate with Lithuanian pùškas (“blister, fin, pimple”), Latvian pusks (“tuft”).

From Proto-Albanian *v-mel-neH2, from Proto-Indo-European *melh₂- (“to grind, crush”). Compare English millet and various other cognates with various different meanings. Ultimately a doublet of bluaj, mjell, and miell.
Unclear. Might be related to Proto-Hellenic *āwḗr (“morning mist”) as Proto-Albanian *awuòr, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂weh₁- (“to blow”). See Ancient Greek ᾱ̓ήρ (āḗr) for more.

parole.significato: to throw, hurl, toss, fling off
parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *awa-laka, from Proto-Indo-European *lek- (“to jump, scuttle”) (compare Norwegian lakka (“to hop, patter about”), Latvian lèkt (“to spring, jump”), Ancient Greek ληκάω (lēkáō, “to dance to music”)).

From Proto-Albanian *śp(e)latśi-, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)pel- (“to say aloud, recite”); compare English spell, Ancient Greek ἀπειλή (apeilḗ, “threat”). Related to fjalë (“word”), folje (“utterance, speaking”).

From Proto-Albanian *plakska, from Proto-Indo-European *plek-. Cognate to Lithuanian plókščias (“flat”), Proto-Slavic *ploskъ (“id”), *ploxъ (“flat, bad, evil, poor”), Old High German flasca (“flask”), English flask.

Apheresis of Old Albanian ënfle, with th > f (cf. uthull, ufull (“vinegar”)) from *ënthle, from Proto-Albanian *en-tsleja- (“to lie down (for sleep)”), prefixed from Proto-Indo-European *ḱloy-éye/o-, from the root *ḱley- (“to lean”); cp. Tocharian A klis- ~ Tocharian B klänts- (“to sleep”).

Related to fregull (“door-leaf”) which Orel derives from metathesis of flegër (“wing of the nose, wooden plate”), Proto-Albanian *awa-laga, from Proto-Indo-European *legh; however, this etymology is disputed.
From Proto-Albanian *awa-lekta, from *awa-laka (modern flak). More at flak.

From Proto-Albanian *spleida, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)plei- (“to split, splice”). Compare Latin spolium (“stripped hide”), Lithuanian spaliai (“flax shives”), Ancient Greek ασπαλον (aspalon, “skin, hide”), σπολάς (spolás, “flayed skin”). Orel derives it from Vulgar Latin firigilīnum. Gheg flî.
From *fllusë + -kë (enlargement suffix), from Proto-Albanian *(s)blèwsa, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰleh₁- (“to blow”).
From Proto-Albanian *awa-luga, possibly continuing Proto-Indo-European *lewg- (“to break”) or *lewgʰ- (“to lie”). Compare Gothic 𐌻𐌹𐌿𐌲𐌰𐌽 (liugan) and Old Church Slavonic лъгати (lŭgati).
From Proto-Albanian *śpl(e)u-g(h)ā / Proto-Albanian *awa-luga, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)pel-eu-,*s-bhel-eu- (“to split”).Compare English splinter.
From Proto-Albanian *spālai, from Proto-Indo-European *spel (“to cleave, break”). Related to fyell and fell. Compare Greek φωλιά (foliá, “nest”), from Ancient Greek φωλεά (phōleá).
From *frak, from Proto-Albanian *awa-raka. Close to Latvian rakt (“to dig”), Lithuanian rakù, ràkti (“to peck open, to lance”). Variant of older form thrak.

From Proto-Albanian *frikā, possibly from Ancient Greek φρίκη (phríkē, “shivering, shuddering”) but the semantic area is more uncommon for Ancient Greek loans in Albanian. Assumption of a loan from Byzantine Greek φρίκη (phríkē) seems implausible, because velar followed by front vowel would be palat
From an earlier fëruor, from Proto-Albanian *fəβruor, borrowed from Latin Februārius.

* According to Orel, from Proto-Albanian *sprūgnja, etymologically connected to Lithuanian sprūgstu, sprūgti (“to escape, get out”) and Proto-Slavic *prygati (“to spring, jump”). * Earlier form might have been *fnyj, from *pnyj, from Proto-Albanian *pnewa, hence from Proto-Indo-European *pnew-. Comp
From an earlier *pnyjma, from Proto-Albanian *pnew-ma, hence from Proto-Indo-European *pnéwmn̥, from *pnew-. Compare Ancient Greek πνεῦμα (pneûma, “id”). Related to fryj.
From Proto-Albanian *pušanja, cognate with Lithuanian pùškinti (“to puff”), puškénti (“to splash”), Proto-Slavic *puxati (“to blow, to puff”).

From dialectal Tosk pshij, pëshinj, from Proto-Albanian *bʰs-in-je/o-, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰes- (“rub”) (compare Old High German besamo (“broom”), Ancient Greek ψάω (psáō, “to rub”), English berry).

From Proto-Albanian *tpē-, rebuilt analogically after the original inchoatives, from Proto-Indo-European *tep- (“to be warm”). Cognate to Latin tepeo (“to be lukewarm, tepid”). From a metathesized pre-form ptoh.
From Proto-Albanian *sputja, from Proto-Indo-European *pHu-tó- (compare Serbo-Croatian pítati (“to ask”), Tocharian B putk- (“to divide, share”), Latin putāre (“to prune”)).

From *föł, from Proto-Albanian *pʰȫla (“thin piece of wood, thin rod”), from Pre-Proto-Albanian *spōla, from Proto-Indo-European *spōlH-ó- (“the split/torn off”), from *(s)pelH- (“to split, tear off”), with a semantic change from "to split off, torn off" > "thin piece of wood, thin rod" > "flute". A
From the same source of fyl, from Proto-Albanian *fylbē.
Inherited from Proto-Albanian *spūta, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)pytew- (“to spit”). Compare Latin spuere, Greek πτύω (ptýo), Lithuanian spjáuti.
From Proto-Albanian *spHul, from Proto-Indo-European *puH- (“rotten, foul”). Cognate to English foul, Latin puter (“rotten”), Lithuanian pṹliai (“pus”), and others. Doublet of puçërr.

From dialectal gabë + -onjë (feminine), related to shkabë, with the same stem but different prefix. The source is Proto-Albanian *gabā, from Proto-Indo-European *kobuǵos (compare English hawk, Latin capys (“bird of prey”), Russian ко́бчик (kóbčik, “red-footed falcon”)).
From Proto-Albanian *gartsā, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰor-, *gʷʰer- (“to be hot”).
Inherited from Proto-Albanian *gauka, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷṓws (“ox, cow”) (compare English cow, Latvian govs, Ancient Greek βοῦς (boûs)). Also see ka.
From *gald, from Proto-Albanian *galda, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰl̥-néh₂-ti, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʰel- (“to shout”). Compare Proto-Slavic *galiti, Proto-Germanic *galdraz.
Singularized plural of *gamulë, from Proto-Albanian *gamula, close to Lithuanian gãmulas (“bale, lump”), Proto-Slavic *gomola (“id”). See also magulë.

Competing etymologies. Possibly: # from Proto-Albanian *ganda, close to Lithuanian gañdas (“rumor”), gañdinti (“to frighten”), Latvian gañdêt (“to spoil”), # identical with ganë, participle of gas, ngas.
From Proto-Albanian *gangula, suffixed form of *ganga, close to Lithuanian gangá (“movement”), gángytis (“to move”).

parole.significato: flowerpot; pot or jug with a broken neck
parole.testo: Singularized plural from variant garbë, from Proto-Albanian *gar-ibā, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰer- (“to burn”). Cognate to Proto-Slavic *gъrnъ (“oven, pot”).

parole.significato: pot with a broken opening used for planting flowers
parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *garbā, from Proto-Indo-European *gr̥bʰ- (compare Old Prussian garbis (“hill”), Serbo-Croatian gȑba (“hump”), Irish gearb (“scab, mange”)).

From Proto-Albanian *garẟ-, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰórdʰos, from *gʰerdʰ- (“to enclose, to encircle”) (compare English yard or garden, Latin hortus, Lithuanian gar̃das). A potential loanword from Gothic 𐌲𐌰𐍂𐌳𐍃 (gards) is also supported.

parole.significato: up to the brim, full to the brim, brimful
parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *gargula; akin to Lithuanian gar̃galas (“knot, knotted thread”), gargõlas (“lump, clump”).
From Proto-Albanian *galstā, a suffixal derivative related to Lithuanian gãlas (“end”), and Latvian gals (“id”).
Originally ‘leaf’, from Proto-Albanian *gazda, from *gʷozdo, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷésdos (compare Dutch kwast (“tassel”), Czech hvozd (“dense forest”)).

From Proto-Albanian *gat-, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷem- (“to go”). Cognate to Sanskrit गति (gáti-, “going, course”), Proto-Slavic *gatь (cf. Russian гать (gatʹ, “road of brushwood, weir”)), Romanian gata (“ready”). For sense development compare Germanic *funsaz "ready, willing", from Proto-Indo-E
From Proto-Albanian *gatā, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰh₂éns.
From Proto-Albanian *ga-wara, a prefixal derivative of varr. Cf. also Aromanian gavrã, Romanian gaură.
From Proto-Albanian *ga-daina, deadjectival from Proto-Indo-European *dh₂ey-nos, from *deh₂y- (“to divide”) (Albanian daj). More at daj.
From g(ë)- + Old Albanian dhend (Bogdani), from Proto-Albanian *denta, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰen- (“to beat, push”). Compare Old Norse detta (“to fall, drop”).
From Proto-Albanian *ka-deinja, from Proto-Indo-European *d(e)i-n- (“day”). More at di.
From the participle stem Proto-Albanian *(gV-)dīm-, from gdhin.
From Proto-Albanian *gaura. Compare Lithuanian gauras (“hair, down, tuft of hair”), Latvian gauri (“pubic hair”) and Middle Irish gúaire (“hair”).

From *gicë, from Proto-Albanian *geidza, from Proto-Indo-European *geid- (“to tickle, stick”). Identical with Old High German kizzilōn, kuzzilōn, Old Saxon kitilōn, Old Armenian կիտակ (kitak, “prick, sting, point”).

From older and dialectal glisht, from Proto-Albanian *glista, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷelH- (“to sting”) (compare German Kiel (“quill”), Lithuanian gãlas (“end, tip”), Greek βελόνα (velóna, “needle”)).

Multiple theories: #From Proto-Albanian *jaga, from Proto-Indo-European *yeǵʰo- (compare German jagen (“to hunt”), Tocharian A yoke (“desire”), Sanskrit यहु (yahú, “restless”)). Related to gjuaj. # From Proto-Albanian *źakʰa-, from Pre-Proto-Albanian *źahka, from Proto-Indo-European *sh₁-s-ko-, orig
From Proto-Albanian *ga-lab-nja, a denominative verb based on *lab- etymologically identical with Lithuanian lãbas (“good”), Latvian labs (“good”).

From Proto-Albanian *ǵákə, from earlier Proto-Albanian *źaka, from Proto-Indo-European *sokʷos (“sap, resin”). Compare Lithuanian sakai̇̃ (“resin”), Ancient Greek ὀπός (opós, “sap”), Proto-Slavic *sokъ (“juice”). For the sense development from "sap, juice" > "blood", note the unrelated Tagalog dugo
From Proto-Albanian *salpna; cognate with Lithuanian iš-selpinė́ti (“to be divided”) and Ukrainian солόпити (solόpyty, “to stick one’s tongue out”).
From Proto-Albanian *selpa, from Proto-Indo-European *sélp-os, from *selp- (“fat, oil”) + *-os.

Singulare tantum; originally a Gheg form, from Proto-Albanian *jausna, from Proto-Indo-European *yéwHs (“broth”) (compare Serbo-Croatian juha, Lithuanian jū́šė (“fish soup”), Latin iūs). Doublet of gjër.
From Proto-Albanian *serpena, from Proto-Indo-European *serp-en-o-s, from the root *serp- (“to crawl”). Compare with Latin serpens, Ancient Greek ἑρπετόν (herpetón) and Sanskrit सर्प (sarpá).
From dialectal and archaic glatë, from Proto-Albanian *dlata, from pre-Albanian *dl̥h₁gʰto, from Proto-Indo-European *dl̥h₁gʰós and suffix *-to.
Inherited from Proto-Albanian *sedjā, from Proto-Indo-European *sed-yeh₂, from *sed- (“to sit, be settled”). Cognate to Proto-Slavic *sadь (“garden, grove”).

From Proto-Albanian *sada or *seda, deverbative of Proto-Indo-European *sed- (“to sit”) (compare English sit, Greek έδραι (édrai, “seat”), Romanian ședea). Çabej connects it to Proto-Indo-European *gʷṓws (“cattle”).

From *gjegjë, from Proto-Albanian *glaglā, root doubling of Proto-Indo-European *gʰel- (“to call, cry”). Compare Old Church Slavonic глаголъ (glagolŭ, “word”), глаголати (glagolati, “speak”), Ancient Greek γλάζω (glázō, “lets a song resound”), Welsh galw (“call”).

From dialectal Tosk gjenj, from Old Albanian gjãnj (Bogdani), from Proto-Albanian *gadnja, from *gʰédnje/o, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰed- (compare English get, Greek κτήση (ktísi, “possession”), Slovene gádati (“to guess”)). First attested in Buzuku's work Meshari as E ju të më lypëni e të mos më

Tosk form of Old Gheg glemb (Buzuku), from Proto-Albanian *glamba, from Proto-Indo-European *glembʰ- (compare Old Church Slavonic глѫбъ (glǫbŭ, “trunk, stump”), Ancient Greek γλάφω (gláphō, “I scrape up”)). Compare also Romanian ghimpe.

Variant of dialectal glep, from Proto-Albanian *glēpa, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷl̥H-bʰo-, derivative of *gʷelH- (“to prick, stick”) (compare Lithuanian geluoni̇̀s (“sting”), Greek βελόνα (velóna, “needle”)).
From Proto-Albanian *serba, from Proto-Indo-European *srebʰ-, cognate to Latin sorbeō, Proto-Slavic *sьrbati.
From Proto-Albanian *saina, from Proto-Indo-European *sh₁i-nos, from the root *seh₁- (“long, lasting”). Compare Gothic 𐍃𐌴𐌹𐌸𐌿𐍃 (seiþus, “late”), Old Irish sír (“long, lasting”).
From Proto-Albanian *(V)iōś-, from Proto-Indo-European *yeh₃s- (“to gird”). Cognate to Ancient Greek ζώννυμι (zṓnnumi, “to gird”) and Old Church Slavonic по-ꙗсати (po-jasati, “to gird”).
Singularized plural, from Proto-Albanian *gadh-ška (cf. bashkë), from gjethe.
From Proto-Albanian *ɟeθ (definite *ɟeði̯a) < *gẹð < *gadih < *gu̯azdih, from Proto-Indo-European *gwosdis. Compare Proto-Slavic *gvozdъ (“nail”), especially Czech hvozd (“forest”).
From (pre-)Proto-Albanian *źinu (“bosom”), from Proto-Indo-European *s(e)i-nu (“curved body part”). Similar development to Latin sinus (“breast; curve”).

A singularized plural of Gheg gjê (“stable, pen”), from Proto-Albanian *saina, identical with the Baltic word for 'wall', from Proto-Indo-European *sēi (“to bind”). Cognate to Lithuanian si̇́ena, Latvian siêna.

From dialectal gjidhë, from Proto-Albanian *semdza, from Proto-Indo-European *sem-ǵʰo- (compare Old Armenian եզ (ez), Latin singulus). The dialectal gji, with the same meaning, derives from simple Proto-Indo-European *sem-.
From Proto-Albanian *jāgnja, a derivative of gjuaj. Compare Old High German jagon (“to hunt”). More at gjuaj.
From Proto-Albanian *śālā, from Proto-Indo-European *sḗh₂l (“salt”). Cognate to Latin sal (“salt”).

Uncertain; perhaps from Proto-Albanian: * *jāgnja, from *jaga (whence gjah (“a hunt, chase”)) + *-nja, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁yoǵʰ-ó-s, from metathesized *h₁eyǵʰ- (“to desire, long for”) + *-ós; * *sāgnja, from *sāgna (whence gjah (“a hunt, chase”)) + *-ja, from Proto-Indo-European *seh₂g-no-s,

From Proto-Albanian *supna, from Proto-Indo-European *súpnos (compare Latin somnus, Lithuanian sãpnas, Ancient Greek ὕπνος (húpnos), Proto-Slavic *sъnъ). Also reconstructed as Proto-Albanian *źupnʉh. modërn -ë descends from Proto-Indo-European *-ós as Proto-Albanian *-ʉh.
From Proto-Albanian *surma, from Proto-Indo-European *sor-m-eh₂ (compare Ancient Greek ὁρμή (hormḗ, “onset, onrush”), Sanskrit सर्म (sárma, “flow, streaming”)), from *ser- (“to flow”).
From gjysh + -e (feminine noun suffix). From Proto-Albanian *źýśe(i̯)a-, from older *sū́sii̯a-, from Proto-Indo-European *súHsii̯o- (“progenitor”).
From Proto-Albanian *sana, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁sónts (active participle of *h₁es- (“to be”)) (compare Old English sōþ (“true”), Old Lithuanian santi, Ancient Greek ἐών (eṓn, “being”)).
From Proto-Albanian *gladā. Cognate to Old High German glat (“shining, even, smooth”), Latin glaber (“smooth”), Lithuanian glodùs (“smooth”), Proto-Slavic *gladiti (“to caress”).
Contracted from dialectal gëluq, from Proto-Albanian *ka-lāukja, from *lāuka (“testicles”). More at loqe.
From *gobë, reflecting Proto-Albanian *gāub-elā, related to Lithuanian gaũbti (“to cover, to wrap”), Proto-Slavic *gъnǫti (“to bend”). Compare Romanian gobellă.

Possibly from Proto-Albanian *gā̆gā̆-(ti-), from Proto-Indo-European *gheh₂-(gheh₂-) (“to yawn, gape”). Cognate to Ancient Greek χάσκω (kháskō, “to yawn, gape”) and Lithuanian gagù (“to cackle”). An onomatopoeic root from gogës-, as a verbal basis for further Albanian verbal formations. The adjectiv
From Proto-Albanian *gāgul, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷelh₂-gʷl̥h₂ by reduplication, from *gʷelh₂- (“oak, acorn”). Cognate to Lithuanian gi̇̀lė (“acorn”).

From Proto-Albanian *gā̆gā̆-(ti-), from Proto-Indo-European *gheh₂-(gheh₂-) (“to yawn, gape”). Cognate to Ancient Greek χάσκω (kháskō, “to yawn, gape”) and Lithuanian gagù (“to cackle”). An onomatopoeic root from gogës-, as a verbal basis for further Albanian verbal formations.
From Proto-Albanian *goll, from Ancient Greek γωλεός (gōleós)
From Proto-Albanian *galwom-, from Proto-Indo-European *gelH- (“naked, bald”), compare Proto-Slavic *golъ (“naked”). The sense "bat" is a synonym of lakuriq nate (“bat, lit. nocturnal naked”).
From Proto-Albanian *gāupā, from Proto-Indo-European *gewpeh₂ (compare English cove, obsolete Polish żupa (“mine”), Ancient Greek γῡ́πη (gū́pē, “cave”)).
From Proto-Albanian *gātjā, close to Proto-Slavic *gatь (“dam, pool”), Sanskrit गातु (gātú, “passage, way”).
From Proto-Albanian *graska or *grah, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷr̥H-sḱé-ti, from *gʷerH- (“to raise a cry”). Frequently ngrah with the intensive prefix n-.

In view of its meaning and the variant greth "flax-combings", likely from a diminutive *grabth of Proto-Albanian *graba, an o-grade noun related to kreh. Alternatively, with voicing of initial, from krath (“leaf bud, sprout on a tree”), variant of kranth ~ krëndth, diminutive of krand ~ krënd (“brus
From Proto-Albanian *gravā, close to Lithuanian griovà, Latvian grava (“ravine, precipitous valley”), Old Prussian grauwus (“side”). Probably related to grabë.
Suggested to be from Proto-Albanian *gritlā, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷr̥h₃-tló-m, from *gʷerh₃- (“to swallow, eat”), however this is semantically dubious.
From Proto-Albanian *graisnā, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱr̥h₂s-Hon- (compare Dutch horzel, Lithuanian širšė, Slovene sršen).
From Proto-Albanian *greiska, cognate with Greek χρίω (chrío, “to rub, to anoint, to prick”), Lithuanian griejù (“to scoop (cream), to take hold of”).
From Proto-Albanian *grinja, nasal present of Proto-Indo-European *gʷerh₃- (“to swallow”).

From Proto-Albanian *griś-, from Proto-Indo-European *gwer-s- (“to raise one’s voice, lift up a cry; set up a clamour”), from *gʷerH-. Cognate to Lithuanian gar̃sas (“call, sound”). Also compare Old English grētan, grœ̄tan (“assail, greet”), Old High German gruozen (“weeping, cry”).
From Proto-Albanian *grāwā, from the Proto-Indo-European root *ǵerh₂- (“old”). Compare Ancient Greek γραῦς (graûs, “old woman”).

A -ull lengthening of grumb, from Proto-Albanian *grumba, from Proto-Indo-European *gru(m)bʰ, derivative of Proto-Indo-European *grewb- (“to crumple, bend, crawl”). Identical with Latvian grumbulains (“uneven, rough”), and close to Old Church Slavonic grǫbь (grǫbĭ, “ignorant, uneducated”), Old Norse

From Proto-Albanian *grunā, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵr̥h₂nóm. Cognate to Proto-Balto-Slavic *źírˀnan (Latvian žìrnis (“pea”), Old Church Slavonic зрьно (zrĭno)), Proto-Celtic *grānom (Old Irish grán, Breton greun), Proto-Germanic *kurną (Gothic 𐌺𐌰𐌿𐍂𐌽 (kaurn), English corn), Proto-Italic *grānom (L

From Proto-Albanian *grykā-, from Pre-Proto-Albanian *grūkā-, from Proto-Indo-European *gruHkeh₂, from older *gruHkó- (“turning, curving”). Orel claims from Proto-Albanian *grīwīkā, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷriHwéh₂, from *gʷerh₃- (“to swallow”). While *-iwi- to -y- is possible, there is no explan
From Proto-Albanian *gāla or *gōl(w)a, from Proto-Indo-European *golH-weh₂, from *gelH- (“naked; head”); compare Serbo-Croatian gláva (“head”), Lithuanian galvà (“head”).
From Proto-Albanian *gula, from Proto-Indo-European *gelH-; cognate with English callow, Serbo-Croatian gol, Latvian gāle (“sheet of ice, black ice”). Possibly related to ngul.
From archaic *gumonj, from Proto-Albanian *guònmi, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰw-, zero grade of *ǵʰew-.

From Proto-Albanian *gungā, from Proto-Indo-European *geng-, *gong- (“lump”). Identical with Lithuanian gùnga (“hump, hunchback, ball, clump”), gùnginti (“go slowly, from a humped going person”), and cognate with Latin gingiva (“gum”).

Inherited from Proto-Albanian *gūr < *gurə < PPA *guri- /*gurV-, from o-grade of Proto-Indo-European *gʷr̥H- (“mountain”), from *gʷerH-. Compare Lithuanian gùras (“promontory”), Serbo-Croatian gòra, Ancient Greek δεῖρος (deîros).

From Proto-Albanian *gur-gur, root-doubling of Proto-Indo-European *h₂ger- (“to put together”). Identical with Lithuanian gurgulỹs (“coagulation, thickening”), gùrguolė (“bulk, mass, lump”), and cognate to Ancient Greek ἀγείρω (ageírō, “gather; assemble”), Latvian gùrste (“bundle of flax”).
From Proto-Albanian *gunša, close to Lithuanian gùžas (“knag”), Old Norse kjuka (“ankle”) and Old Church Slavonic gustъ (gustŭ, “thick, dense”).

From Proto-Albanian *gal-ānja, cognate to Old High German quellan (“to well up, pour out, stream from”) and Sanskrit गलति (gálati, “to drip, to drop, to ooze”). Ultimately from Latin jānua (“door, entrance”).
From Proto-Albanian *gradīnja, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰrendʰ- (compare English grind, Lithuanian gréndžiu (“to scrape, scratch”)).
Singularized plural of *gërgallë, from Proto-Albanian *gargalā; akin to Lithuanian gar̃galas (“knot, knotted thread”), gargõlas (“lump, clump”).
From Proto-Albanian *g(a)ratjā, from Proto-Indo-European *gred- (compare English scratch, German kratzen).

parole.significato: garden scissors; claw, nipper (of a scorpion)
parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *ga-tsap-. Related to thep.

From Proto-Albanian *griδ-(ati-), from Proto-Indo-European *gwr-edh- (“to cry, shout”). Enlarged formation with the suffix -as/t. Cognate to Lithuanian ger̃das (“clamor”), gar̃sas (“clangor”), Old Prussian gerdaut (“say”).

Plurale tantum; contracted form of gërthije, plural of variant gërthël, from Proto-Albanian *kartˢila, from Proto-Indo-European *kh₂er- (“hard”) (compare Welsh crach (“crust”), Sanskrit कर्कर (karkara, “hard”)).
From Proto-Albanian *śtal-, from Proto-Indo-European *stel- (“set/put (up)”). Cognate to Ancient Greek στολίζω (stolízō, “to get ready”).
From Proto-Albanian *skalbā, from Proto-Indo-European *skel- (“to split”). Close to Latvian skalbs (“sharp, shrill”).
From Proto-Albanian *skalā, from Proto-Indo-European *skoléh₂ (compare English shale, Lithuanian skalà (“splinter”)), from the root *skel(H)- (“to split”).

From Proto-Albanian *ksandā, from pre-Albanian *skandneh₂, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kand- (“to shine”) (compare Welsh can (“white”), Latin candeō (“to shine, gleam”), Sanskrit चन्द्र (candrá, “shining; moon”)). One might also consider a connection to Ancient Greek ἕνος (hénos, “old”) and Latin a
From Proto-Albanian *(s)karba, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kerb- (“rough, sharp”). Cognate with Latin acerbus (“tart, bitter”), Latvian skârbs (“sharp, rough”), Old English sċearp.

parole.significato: vine-branch, grape-vine, shot of a vine
parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *harδ, the etymology is unknown.

From *hardhë, from Proto-Albanian *skardā (“digger”), from Proto-Indo-European *skord- (compare Ancient Greek σκορδύλος (skordúlos, “newt”), Lithuanian skardùs (“deep”), Latvian skārdît (“to divide”)), from *sker- (“to cut”). More at harr.

From *hardhë, from Proto-Albanian *skardā (“digger”), from Proto-Indo-European *skord- (compare Ancient Greek σκορδύλος (skordúlos, “newt”), Lithuanian skardùs (“deep”), Latvian skārdît (“to divide”)), from *sker- (“to cut”). More at harr.
From Proto-Albanian *skarima, from Proto-Indo-European *sker- (“to cut”).
From Proto-Albanian *skarna, from *skera. Cognate with Gothic 𐌿𐍃𐍃𐌺𐌰𐍂𐌾𐌰𐌽 (usskarjan, “to tear out”), Lithuanian ski̇̀rti. More at shqerr.
From *harr, from Proto-Albanian *skara, from Proto-Indo-European *sker- (compare Lithuanian skėrỹs (“ram”), Russian скоро (skoro, “quickly”), Ancient Greek σκαίρω (skaírō, “to hop, dance”)).

From *etës (compare dialectal ecëj), from Proto-Albanian *aitatja, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁éyti, present of *h₁ey-. Perhaps the laryngeal is preserved. Compare Serbo-Croatian ìći, Lithuanian ei̇̃ti. See eci.

From Proto-Albanian *skeuda, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kewd- Compare Proto-Germanic *skeutaną (whence German schießen (“to shoot”), English shoot), Sanskrit चोदति (códati, “to incite”), Russian кида́ть (kidátʹ, “id”), Lithuanian skudrùs (“id”).
From Proto-Albanian *skaljā, cognate to Lithuanian at-skala (“supply, stock”), skalà (“stick of firewood”).
From Proto-Albanian *skakā, cognate to Lithuanian šòkti (“to jump, to dance”), Old Irish scén (“horror”), Proto-Slavic *skokь.
From Proto-Albanian *skōla, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kol- (“stake”); compare Lithuanian kuõlas, Polish kół, Ancient Greek σκύλος (skúlos).

Uncertain, possibly a formation in -më. Several hypotheses have been proposed: # Akin to Old High German scalmo (“plague”) (German Schelm). # Connection with Ancient Greek χάλιμα (khálima) can only be justified as a borrowing from it. # Akin to Sanskrit आल (āla, “poison”). # Akin to Ancient Greek σκ
From Proto-Albanian *skapa, related to hap.

From dialectal and archaic helq, though the further etymology is uncertain. * It may derive from Proto-Albanian *(w)alkja, from *h₂wolké-ye-ti, causative of Proto-Indo-European *h₂welk- (“to pull”) (compare Lithuanian velkù, Bulgarian влека́ (vleká, “to drag”), Greek αυλάκι (avláki, “furrow”)). * Pe

parole.significato: Heksat/Heqsat (Heq = Remove + suffix -at denoting occupation, prular)
parole.testo: From dialectal and archaic helq, from Proto-Albanian *(w)alkja, from *h₂wolkéye-, causative of Proto-Indo-European *h₂welk- (“to pull”) + -im (suffix denoting an act).
From Proto-Albanian *ardzai, from pre-Albanian *h₁órǵʰiya, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁órǵʰis (compare Ancient Greek ὄρχις (órkhis), Old Armenian որձիք (orjikʻ)).

Singularized plural of *hardh, from Proto-Albanian *skarda, from pre-Albanian *skordʰos, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kerdʰ- (“herd”) (compare Slovene črẹ́da, English herd, Ancient Greek κόρθυς (kórthus, “heap”)).
From Proto-Albanian *skarna, from Proto-Indo-European *sker- (“to cut”). Related to harr.
Tosk form of Gheg hî (pl. hin), from Proto-Albanian *skina, from *skines, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱenHis (compare Latin cinis (“dust; cinder”), Ancient Greek κόνις (kónis, “ashes; dust”)).
From Proto-Albanian *eikrā, an -r derivative of iki (“to go”). For semantic development compare German gerinnen (“to coagulate”) from rinnen (“to run”).
From Proto-Albanian *skeidma, from Proto-Indo-European *skeid-men-. Cognate to Gothic 𐍃𐌺𐌰𐌹𐌳𐌰𐌽 (skaidan, “to divide”), Lithuanian skiemuo (“opening used to insert the shuttle”).
From Proto-Albanian *skūpa, from Proto-Indo-European *skewbʰ- (“to push”). Compare German schieben (“to push”), English shove, Lithuanian skùbti (“to hurry”).

Possibly from Proto-Albanian *skīra, from a Proto-Indo-European *sḱeyr-o- (“shine, reflex”), whence German schier (“pure, clear”), Polish szczery (“sincere, earnest”), Ancient Greek σκίρον (skíron, “parasol”).

Uncertain: * Perhaps from Proto-Albanian *haula, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eu-l-om (“a hollow, channel, tube”), with the laryngeal unusually preserved. If so, cognate to Ancient Greek αὐλός (aulós, “hollow tube, flute, haulm”) and Old Norse (huann-)jóli (“hollow stalk, stem”). The original sense w

From Proto-Albanian *skuna < *skuja + *-na, from Proto-Indo-European *skuy-os < *skwey-. Compare Norwegian/Faroese skon (“snout”), from Proto-Indo-European *skewd-. More at hedh. For the 4th meaning, compare also Proto-Slavic *xȗjь.

Inherited from Proto-Albanian *ksōn(w)ja. Akin to Ancient Greek ξένος (xénos, “foreign”), which according to Beekes could be Pre-Greek, although the existence of an Avestan cognate (Avestan 𐬑𐬱𐬥𐬀𐬎 (xšnau)) questions this.

Two possible etymologies: * from Proto-Albanian *xāljā, from earlier *ksān and suffix -jā, from pre-Albanian *s-keh₂n, metathesis of Proto-Indo-European *kh₂en, oblique of *kóh₂r̥ (“wax”) (compare Greek κηρός (kirós), Lithuanian korỹs (“id”)). The change of *n to l is irregular. * from Proto-Albania
Metathesis of archaic and dialectal hurdhë, from Proto-Albanian *skurdā, from a Mediterranean substrate word *skʰor(o)d- (compare Greek σκόρδο (skórdo), Armenian սխտոր (sxtor)).

Originally ‘snout’, from Proto-Albanian *skuntā, from *skuna (“take, pole”) (modern hu), close to or derived from Proto-Germanic *skuna, *skunō (compare Faroese skon, Norwegian skut (“projection, overhang”)). More at hu.
From Proto-Albanian *skurbā, cognate to Lithuanian skerbiù (“to cut deep”), Latvian šķirba (“fissure, slot”).

Plurale tantum; with prothetic h- from dialectal urdhe, plural of dialectal urdhë, from Proto-Albanian *wurdā, from Proto-Indo-European *wr̥dʰo (“sweetbriar”) (compare Old English word (“thorn-bush”), dialectal Norwegian erre, orr (“bush”), Latin rubus (“bramble”)). From dialectal urdhë, from Proto-Albanian *urdā, from Proto-Indo-European *weh₁r- (“water”). Cognate to Sanskrit वार् (vā́r-, “water”), Old Prussian wurs (“pond, pool”).
From Proto-Albanian *hut, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ewt- (“downwards”). Cognate with Ancient Greek αὔτως (aútōs, “in vain”), Gothic 𐌰𐌿𐌸𐌴𐌹𐍃 (auþeis).

parole.significato: to enter, to go in, to get in
parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *ūnja, from *h₂u-nye/o, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ew (“away (from)”).

parole.significato: precedes and reinforces an expression of emotion
parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *skainai. Compare Gothic 𐍃𐌺𐌴𐌹𐌽𐌰𐌽 (skeinan), Old High German skinan (“to shine”), with a similar sense development to that of English 'in a twinkling'.

From Proto-Albanian *kʰandnā, from earlier *skond-nah₂, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kand- (“to shine”) (compare Welsh can (“white”), Latin candeō (“to shine, gleam”), Sanskrit चन्द्र (candrá, “shining; moon”)). Possibly borrowed from Proto-Celtic *kando-

From Proto-Albanian *skeuda, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kewd- Compare Proto-Germanic *skeutaną (whence German schießen (“to shoot”), English shoot), Sanskrit चोदति (códati, “to incite”), Russian кида́ть (kidátʹ, “id”), Lithuanian skudrùs (“id”).
From dialectal ik, from Proto-Albanian *eika, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ey- (“to go”) (compare Latin ire, Lithuanian ei̇̃k (“go!”), Serbo-Croatian ići).

parole.significato: my, of mine (possessive pronoun in nominative form, adjectival aspect)
parole.testo: Demonstrative pronoun Proto-Albanian *is + (unstressed) 1st sg. pronoun Proto-Albanian *me, from Proto-Indo-European *ís and Proto-Indo-European *me.
From Proto-Albanian *īs-mos, cognate with Sanskrit ईषत् (īṣat, “a little, slightly”), Latvian īss, from Proto-Indo-European *is (“a little”).

From Proto-Albanian *its, from Proto-Indo-European *eǵʰs (“from, out of”). Related to Lithuanian i̇̀š, Latvian iz and Old Prussian is.
