Inherited from Proto-Albanian *esmi, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ésmi (“to be, exist”). The forms in qe- may derive from Proto-Indo-European *kʷel- (“to turn, revolve”), whence also Ancient Greek πέλω (pélō, “to be”).

Variant of dialectal ap, from Proto-Albanian *apa, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁op-eio/e-, from *h₁ep- (“to take”). The verb is suppletive with past dhashë and participle dhënë from Proto-Indo-European *deh₃-.
From Proto-Albanian *ergā, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃erǵʰ-. Close to Old Norse argr (“bad, evil, coward”), Lithuanian aržùz (“lusty”), Avar ərəzant (“bad”).

From Proto-Albanian *e(k)šta, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁eǵʰs-tos (compare Ancient Greek ἐκτός (ektós, “outside”)), suffixed form of *h₁eǵʰs, whence Latin ex (compare also extra, exter from *h₁eǵʰs-tro-, *h₁eǵʰs-ter), Ancient Greek ἐξ (ex), Old Church Slavonic из (iz). Compare the now ob

From older ep (Buzuku), with the initial j- coming from a reanalysis of "i ep" (roughly, i ep > ijep > i jep). Old Albanian ep further comes from *epi < Proto-Albanian *apijo, also reconstructed as *apīh, *apī(t), from Pre-Proto-Albanian *apii̯i/a-, inherited from Proto-Indo-European *h₁op-éi̯e/o-,

From Proto-Albanian *erma. Compare Lithuanian ermas (“monster”), Latvian erms (“wonderful apparition”), and also Old English gyrman, dialectal Danish jærme (“to lament, shriek”), dialectal Norwegian jerme (“to bleat”), dialectal Swedish jarma (“to lament, shriek”), Icelandic jarma (“to whine, compla

From Proto-Albanian *jétˢa-, from Pre-Proto-Albanian *jétja/i-, perhaps from a Proto-Indo-European *h₁⁄₂yeth₁ye/o- (“to stand firm”), albeit with no adduced cognates. Older theories including a connection to Proto-Indo-European *sed- (“to sit”) is phonetically untenable, while the relation to the fa

From Proto-Albanian *aidza + -ull, close to Ancient Greek αἴθαλος (aíthalos, “thick smoke, ashes, soot”). Phonetically possible also from Proto-Indo-European *eǵʰerom (“lake”), from the stem *eǵʰ- (“border”), cf. Proto-Balto-Slavic *éźeran, Lithuanian ẽžeras, Old Prussian assaran ([azaran], “lake”)
From Proto-Albanian *jāudsja, from Proto-Indo-European *Hyewdʰ- (compare Lithuanian jáudinti (“to excite, arouse”), Polish judzić (“to incite”), Latin jubere (“to order”)).
From Proto-Albanian *ju(s) identical with Lithuanian jūs id., Gothic jūs id., English you. Ultimately derived from Proto-Indo-European *yúHs.
From Proto-Albanian *ka-, from Proto-Indo-European *ko-
Either a formation in -sht, from an unattested *kap, from Proto-Albanian *kaba (cf. Lithuanian kabeti (“to hang”), kabà (“crooked tree”)), or a ka- prefixed form of bisht.

parole.significato: pruning knife, billhook with long handle
parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *kadā, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kend-. Cognate to Greek σκεδάννυμι (skedánnymi), Sanskrit स्खदते (skhadate, “to split”). Related to Albanian kij (“I prune, I trim”).
From Proto-Albanian *kala, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷelh₁- (“to turn, twist”).
From Proto-Albanian *ka-laisa, a derivative of lesh.

parole.significato: to stick (on, into), put (up), thrust, instigate
parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *kalei-, from Proto-Indo-European *kelH- (“to prick, jab (into); thrust (into)”). Cognate to Lithuanian kálti (“to strike, forge”) and Russian коло́ть (kolótʹ, “to prick, jab, hoe, hack”).
From Proto-Albanian *kapna, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷh₂wep- (“smoke, seethe”).

Suppletive. The present, imperfect, and subjunctive are from Proto-Albanian *kapmi, from Proto-Indo-European *kap- (“to seize, to grasp”), cognate with Latin capiō (“take, seize”) and Proto-Germanic *habjaną (“to have, to hold”) (whence English have, German haben (“to have”), Gothic 𐌷𐌰𐌱𐌰𐌽 (haban, “t

From Proto-Albanian *kapa, from Proto-Indo-European *kap-. Cognate to (Baltic) Latvian kàmpju, kàmpt; Proto-Celtic *kawnos (Old Irish cúan, Irish cuan, Scottish Gaelic cuan); Proto-Germanic *habnō, Proto-Germanic *habjaną (“to have, lift”); Proto-Hellenic *kapt͏̌ō (Ancient Greek κάπτω (káptō)), Prot

From kap (“I grab, catch, grip”) + -th (diminutive suffix); the former from Proto-Albanian *kapa, from Proto-Indo-European *kap-. Cognate with Lithuanian kāpas (“grave”), kopà (“dune”), Latvian kãpa (“dune”).
From Proto-Albanian *kapā, cognate with Proto-Slavic *kopa (“mow, shock, stack”), Greek κάπη (kápi, “manger, crib”).
From Proto-Albanian *kar(i)bā, related to Lithuanian kárti (“to hang”), kaběti (“id”), Proto-Slavic *kobьcь (“vulture”).

parole.significato: rocky bank or bluff overlooking a body of water
parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *karpnā, from *karpā (modern karpë). More at karpë.

From Proto-Albanian *karpā, from Proto-Indo-European *kerpéh₂, from Proto-Indo-European *kerp- (“to pluck”). Compare Lithuanian kar̃pas (“hack, notch”), Swedish harv (“harrow”), Ancient Greek καρπός (karpós, “fruit”). See also the name of the Carpathians.
From Proto-Albanian *kar-usa, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to cut”), semantically similar to karpë.
From Proto-Albanian *karā, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to cut”), identical with Proto-Slavic *kora (“bark”), Lithuanian kerù and kérti (“to become separated”).
From Proto-Albanian *kalstā, from *kalsa (“ear or spike of grain”) (modern kalli). More at kalli. Compare Sardinian càstia.
From Proto-Albanian *kalsarā, from *kalsa (“awn, ear of grain”) (modern kalli). More at kalli.

From Proto-Albanian *katsa, cognate with Hittite [Term?] (/⁠kattu⁠/, “spiteful”), Old Irish cath (“id”), Tocharian A kat (“destruction”), Old Norse hǫðr (“war, slaughter”). The sense development went from 'infection, disease' to 'protuberance'.

From Proto-Albanian *kátur, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷtur- ~ *kʷétur- (compare Lithuanian keturi̇̀, Serbo-Croatian četiri, and possibly Latin quattuor), oblique of *kʷetwóres. Probably borrowed from Latin quattuor.
From Proto-Albanian *ka-štšala, a derivative of çalë.
From Proto-Albanian *kapna, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷh₂wep- (“smoke, seethe”) (compare Ancient Greek καπνός (kapnós, “smoke”), Polish kopeć (“soot”)).
Inherited from Proto-Albanian *kapja, from Proto-Indo-European *kop(H)- (compare Lithuanian kàpti, Ancient Greek κόπτω (kóptō)).

* From Proto-Albanian *kakja, from Proto-Indo-European *kak- (compare Ancient Greek κακός (kakós, “bad”), if not *kn̥ko- related to Lithuanian keñkti (“to do harm”). * From Proto-Albanian *kakija / *kakijā, same origin.
From Proto-Albanian *kahā (“plaited hair”), related to Proto-Slavic *kosa (“plait”), Old Norse haddr (“woman's hair”).

* According to Çabej and Orel, from *këinj < Proto-Albanian *kadinja, denominative verb from *kadā (whence kadhë). Source of kizë (“pruning-hook”). * From Proto-Albanian *kī̆-, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)keh₂y-, *(s)keyh₂- (“to beat, cuff, poke”). Cognate to Latin caiō (“to cut, hew”).

Dialectal; from Proto-Albanian *kūlā, from Proto-Indo-European *kh₂u-l-eh₂ (compare Old Norse haull (“hernia”), Serbo-Croatian kȉla (“hernia; outgrowth (on plants)”), dialectal Lithuanian kū́la(s) (“lump, hernia”)).
From Proto-Albanian *ka-jā, based on a pronominal element *ka and a demonstrative (see ajo).
From Proto-Albanian *ka-lapā, a derivative of llap.
Uncertain. Possibly from Proto-Albanian * ̊kapneti̯ā, from Proto-Indo-European *kop(H)-, or a contracted derivative of kamë (cf. shkel > shklesë) (possibly a singularized plural). See also shkmes.
A variant of an unattested *kodh (cf. kec ~ kedh), from Proto-Albanian *kādzā, related to kedh. A possible relation with Old English codd (“cod”), Proto-Germanic *kuddaz is uncertain.

Inherited from Proto-Albanian *kēsā, from *kēs-(ḱ)eh₂, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷeh₁s- (compare Old Prussian kīsman (“time”), Proto-Slavic *časъ (“time”)). Orel reconstructs Proto-Albanian *kāxā instead.
From Proto-Albanian *kāslā, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷeh₂s- (“cough”) (compare English wheeze, Lithuanian kosulỹs, Serbo-Croatian kašalj).
From Proto-Albanian *kālima, a suffixal derivative of Proto-Indo-European *kal- (“healthy; handsome”). Compare Sanskrit कल्य (kalyá, “healthy”), Ancient Greek καλός (kalós, “beautiful”).

From Proto-Albanian *kāsra, from Proto-Indo-European *kars (“to scratch, rub”). Compare Lithuanian kar̃šti (“comb, curry”), Latvian kā̀ršu (“wool comb”), Latin cardus (“thistle”), Middle High German harsten (“become hard, rough”).
From Proto-Albanian *kāra, from earlier *kasra, from Proto-Indo-European *kes- (compare Lithuanian kàsti (“to dig, scrape”), Latin raccogliere (“to harvest, reap”), Serbo-Croatian kòsa (“scythe”)).

Theoretically from Proto-Albanian *kākta, of uncertain origin; potentially akin to Lithuanian koktùs (“disgusting”) via Proto-Indo-European. An older hypothesis connects it to Ancient Greek κότος (kótos, “rancor, grudge”).

From Proto-Albanian *kāta, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kHtos (“shade, shadow, darkness”). Compare Old Irish scáth (“shadow”), Ancient Greek σκότος (skótos, “darkness”), Sanskrit छत्त्र (chattra, “umbrella”), English shadow.

From Proto-Albanian *krok-sko, a -k enlargement of krah, from Proto-Indo-European *kr(o)k-sko (“arm”). Compare Lithuanian kárka (“pig's foot”), kirkãlis (“shinbone”), Bulgarian крак (krak, “leg, foot”), Serbo-Croatian krôk (“footstep”).
From Proto-Albanian *krapa, from Proto-Indo-European *kreh₁p- (“strong”) (compare Welsh craff, Serbo-Croatian krȉjep).

parole.significato: to plunge, immerse; steep, smother, bespatter
parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *krōda, Identical with Proto-Slavic *krasti (“to steal”), as shown by the related krydh. Further relation to similar Slavic verbs or to Latvian krâju, krât (“to gather, to collect”) are uncertain.
From variant greh, from Proto-Albanian *grebska, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰrebʰ- (compare German graben (“to dig”), Lithuanian grebti (“to rake”)).
From Proto-Albanian *krebnja, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰrebʰ. Related to kreh.
From Proto-Albanian *krepa, from Proto-Indo-European *krepos (“body”), from *krep-. Compare Old English hrif (“belly”), Latin corpus, Welsh praff (“burly”).
From Proto-Albanian *ka-rand-iskā, a derivative of krënd.
From Proto-Albanian *ka-rand-iskā, a derivative of krënd.
Singulare tantum; from Proto-Albanian *kriwi, from dialectal Proto-Indo-European *kʷŕ̥wis (“worm”) (compare Serbo-Croatian cȓv), dialectal variant of *kʷŕ̥mis. More at krimb.
From Proto-Albanian *krōda. See kredh for more.
From Proto-Albanian *krūda, from the same root of kridhem and kredh.
Back-formation from variant krife (plurale tantum), from Proto-Albanian *kripsijā, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱripes- (“headhair”) (compare Latin crinis (“mane”)). More at krip.

PIE word  *kʷŕ̥mis From Proto-Albanian *krima, earlier *krimi, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷŕ̥mis, with the -b suffix. Cognate with Lithuanian kirmi̇̀s, Serbo-Croatian cȓv, Persian کرم (kerm), Sanskrit कृमि (kṛ́mi).
From Proto-Albanian *kripa, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱripo- (“headhair”). Compare Avestan 𐬯𐬭𐬌𐬟𐬁 (srifā, “plume”), Sanskrit शिप्रा (śíprā, “mustache and beard”).
Inherited from Proto-Albanian *krūpā, from Proto-Indo-European *kroup- (“rough”). Compare Dutch roof (“scabby”), Lithuanian kraupis (“scab”), Serbo-Croatian krúpa (“hail”).
From Proto-Albanian *krādā. Possibly cognate to Gothic 𐌷𐍂𐍉𐍄 (hrōt, “roof”), Old High German rāza (“honeycomb”), and Proto-Slavic *krada (“heap, pile”), *korda (“pile of logs”).
From Proto-Albanian *krāðā, from Proto-Indo-European *kar- (“hard”). Compare Gaulish crōdios (“hard”), Old Norse harðr (“hard”) and Latin carina (“nutshell”).
From Proto-Albanian *krōⁿ, from *kron, from Pre-Proto-Albanian *krāna, from Proto-Indo-European *kres-. Compare Ancient Greek κρήνη (krḗnē, “spring, fount”), Old English hærn (“wave”).
From Proto-Albanian *krupa, related to Lithuanian kraupùs (“easily scared”), krupùs, krúpti (“to scare”).
From Proto-Albanian *krũba, cognate to Greek κρύπτω (krýpto, “to hide”), Lithuanian kráuti (“to pile up”), Proto-Slavic *kryti (“to cover, to hide”).
From Proto-Albanian *krūda, semantically identical with Proto-Slavic *krasti (“to steal”), as shown by the related kredh, although further connections are uncertain.

From Common Albanian *krœ̄n, with lengthening of vowel before the final *-n, from *krœn, with an apocoped ending from an earlier Common Albanian *krœni. This was inherited from Proto-Albanian *kroni, with i-umlaut, from an older *krā̊niyə. This follows Pre-Proto-Albanian *krā́niyàd < *krāniyan < *kr

parole.significato: tender thin branches cut up with leaves used for fodder for domestic animals
parole.testo: Tosk variant of Gheg krand, from Proto-Albanian *ka-randa, from Proto-Indo-European *rendʰ- (“to tear”). Compare English rend, Sanskrit रन्ध्र (rándhra, “fissure, split”).

To be analyzed as k- + thjell, with the k- prefix inherited from Proto-Albanian *k-, from Proto-Albanian *kə-, from Proto-Indo-European *ko(m)- (“together, with”), and the base -thjell inherited from Proto-Albanian *tˢ́ʲéla/i-, from Pre-Proto-Albanian *ćʲéla/i-, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱléh₃u- or

parole.significato: where (asking about a place, where or towards which direction)
parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *ku, from Proto-Indo-European *kú (“where?”). Cognate to Proto-Baltic *kur (“where”), Lithuanian kur̃ (“where”) & kur (“where”), Latvian kur, Proto-Slavic *kъde (“where”), Old Church Slavonic къде (kŭde, “where”), Russian где (gde) and Sanskrit कुह (kúha, “where”), Sanskrit कू (k
From Proto-Albanian *kuka, from Proto-Indo-European [Term?].
From Proto-Albanian * ̊kull-, from Proto-Indo-European *kwel- (“to revolve, twist”). Occurs almost exclusively in prefixed form with për-. Probably related to ul.

parole.significato: traveller's joy, old man's beard, virgin's bower (Clematis vitalba)
parole.testo: Dialectal; from Proto-Albanian *kulpa; some derive it from Proto-Indo-European *kʷel (“to turn”).
From Proto-Albanian *kum to(m); accusative singular of *ku and a pronominal stem *to-.
From Proto-Albanian *kur, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷur; cognate to Lithuanian kur̃ (“where”), Old Armenian ուր (ur, “id”), etc. See also Albanian ku (“where”). Less likely from Latin quā hōrā.
From Proto-Albanian *kurpna, from Proto-Indo-European *krep-. Compare Latin corpus (“body”), Proto-Germanic *hrefaz (“body”).

From *kurr and suffix -iz, from Proto-Albanian *kurna, from Proto-Indo-European *k(ʷ)or(H)- (compare Latvian cȩrs (“stump, knotty root”), Serbo-Croatian kȍrijen (“root”)). By analogy of a root (taproot) with the spine.
From Proto-Albanian *kʉśśə, from Pre-Proto-Albanian *kʉs-sa, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷos + *sos, meaning "who (is) this". (compare Tocharian B kᵤse (“who”)).
From an earlier kūt, from Proto-Albanian *kuβət, borrowed via Vulgar Latin from Latin cubitum (“elbow, cubit”). Compare also Aromanian, Romanian cot.
From Proto-Albanian *ka-ei, based on a pronominal element *ka and a demonstrative (see ai).

From Proto-Albanian *ku ̊, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷu- (“who, where”), derived from *kʷ-. Cognate to Gothic pronominal element for the formation of indefinite pronouns -hun. A deictic particle of remote distance. It only occurs in the pronominal system as the first member of a compound.
From Proto-Albanian *kaN, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷo- (“who”). Cognate to Latin quom.
From Proto-Albanian *kalbatiā, a derivative of kalb, + feminine -zë suffix. For sense development, compare shkëlbazë. Compare Romanian gălbează.

parole.significato: animal young, baby animal (of a quadruped mammal)
parole.testo: From *kul + -ysh diminutive suffix, from Proto-Albanian *kull-, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷl̥-io-, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kʷel- (“to cry, shriek; roar, howl”) (compare Lithuanian skali̇̀kas (“hound”), Greek σκύλα (skýla, “female dog”)).
From Proto-Albanian *kambjɔnit (> third person singular këmben), borrowed from Vulgar Latin *cambiō, from Late Latin cambīre, from Latin cambium, from Gaulish cambion.

From Proto-Albanian *kam(b)ā, from Proto-Indo-European *kh₂em-p (“to bend”). Close to Ancient Greek κάμπτω (kámptō, “curve, bend”), Sanskrit कम्पते (kampate, “trembles”), Latin campus (“field”), Lithuanian kam̃pas (“point, edge, angle”), Old High German hamf (“lame”). Related to Latin gamba. Orel (2

parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *kan tan, sequence of two pronouns (Proto-Albanian *kan + *tan). Proto-Albanian *kan from Proto-Indo-European *kʷo-, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷ-. The second element Proto-Albanian *tan from Proto-Indo-European *to-. Continuing in accusative form of kush as kë (Gheg Albanian kâ,
From Proto-Albanian *ka-antā, a derivative of *antā (modern ëndë) with the nominal prefix *ka.
From Proto-Albanian *karputja, a derivative verb from këputë (“sole”).
From Proto-Albanian *kri-būsta, a compound of kër + bisht. See kërci for the former element.
From Proto-Albanian *karbā, related to Latin corbis (“basket”), Lithuanian karbas (“basket”), Latvian karba (“birch bark vessel”).

parole.significato: shank, shin, lower leg (shin and calf); shinbone
parole.testo: Metathesized form of *kri-tsi, from Proto-Albanian *krū ̊, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱruh₂-s (“limb”). Cognate to Latin crūs (“shank, leg, limb”).
From Proto-Albanian *kar-laisa, a derivative of lesh.
From Proto-Albanian *krim-īla, derived from krimb.
Metathesis of variant këpurdhë, from Proto-Albanian *kapur, from Proto-Indo-European *kep- (compare Lithuanian kepùrė (“cap”), Latvian cȩpure (“id”), Serbo-Croatian čèpac (“bonnet”)).
A suffixal derivative of an unattested Proto-Albanian *kara, further related to karthi. According to Meyer, a derivation of grep.
From Proto-Albanian *karilā, cognate to Old Norse hǫrr (“snivel”), Old High German horo (“excrement”) and Ancient Greek κόρυζα (kóruza, “snivel”).

parole.significato: to bend (one's back), bend over, bend down, hunch over, stoop
parole.testo: Denominative verb from *kurr and suffix -us, from Proto-Albanian *kurna, whence kurriz; see there for more.
A prefixal derivative of an unattested *tyl reflecting Proto-Albanian *tūla. The latter is related to Lithuanian tṹlás (“many”) and Greek τύλος (týlos, “corn”).
From Proto-Albanian *kar-wesja, a derivative of vesh (“to wear”).
From Proto-Albanian *kantšenja. Cognate with Old Norse há (“to torment”) and Lithuanian kenkiù, keñkti (“to damage, to harm”).
Compound kë- (“this”) + Proto-Albanian *este, cognate to Latin iste (“that”).
From Proto-Albanian *ϑōp-, * ̊tśap-, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱeh3-(i-) (“to sharpen”). (Indirect) cognate to Latin cippus (“pale, peak, point”). A formation with the prefix kë-.
From Proto-Albanian *ka tu, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷo- (“relative pronoun”) + a component *tu possibly related to Sanskrit तु (tú, “now, but”). By surface analysis, kë- + tu.

From Proto-Albanian *lag-, from Proto-Indo-European *legʰ- (“to lay, lie (down)”). Cognate with Ancient Greek λόχος (lókhos, “ambush, ambuscade, armed band”), Gothic 𐌻𐌰𐌲𐌾𐌰𐌽 (lagjan, “to lay”). Singular form of lagje.

parole.significato: neighbourhood, ward, quarter, particularly (politics, historical) as a former administrative division of Albanian cities
parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *lag- with -je suffix, from Proto-Indo-European *legʰ- (“to lay, lie (down)”). Cognate to Ancient Greek λόχος (lókhos, “ambush, ambuscade, armed band”). Plural form of lag.
From Proto-Albanian *lau-, or *launja, from Proto-Indo-European *lewh₃- (“to wash”). Cognate to Latin lavō, Ancient Greek λούω (loúō), with the same meaning. Related to lag.

parole.significato: to pay off a debt, pay up
parole.testo: From older and dialectal lanj, from Proto-Albanian *launja, from Proto-Indo-European *leuh₃- (“release”) (compare English lose, Latin luere (“to release from debt”), Ancient Greek λύω (lúō, “to untie, set free; dissolve”)).
From Proto-Albanian *laka (“bend, curve”). Cognate to Latin lax (“bait, lure, noose, slip”), laqueus (“cord, rope (as noose, slip)”).
(Adj., verb, adverb & noun) suffixed form of dialectal lakur, from Proto-Albanian *laukura, from Proto-Indo-European *lewk- (“light, shine”). Related to loqe, gloq.
Uncertain. Maybe a diminutive in -th of Proto-Albanian *lagmo, related to log.
From Proto-Albanian *lapitja, close to Greek λαπαρός (laparós, “weak”), λαπάζω (lapázo, “to weaken”).
From Proto-Albanian *laubitja, from Proto-Indo-European *lewbʰ-, related to Sanskrit लुभ्यति (lúbhyati, “to wish”), Proto-Slavic *l'ubiti (“to love”). Ultimately a doublet of lyp.
From Proto-Albanian *lapā-. Cognate to Ancient Greek λοπός (lopós, “peel, cortex, skin”).
From Proto-Albanian *laudra, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁lewdʰ- (“to grow”).

parole.significato: white spot; something which is spotted, dappled, motley, variegated, multi-colored, particolored
parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *laurā, based on laj.

parole.significato: early, anciently, long ago, once (time; era in the past)
parole.testo: From (lashë (le(f)t behind) + -të) Proto-Albanian *lauša. According to Jokl (& Slavia Praha) from Proto-Indo-European *h₁lewdʰ- (“to grow; people”). A similar developement can be seen in Proto-Germanic *aldaz (“old”) (release → let grow → grow old). Related to Gothic 𐌻𐌰𐌿𐍃 (laus, “loosen, set free, e
From Proto-Albanian *laptā, from Proto-Indo-European *leh₂p- (“to be flat, even; shovel”). Cognate to Lithuanian lopetà (“shovel”) and Old Prussian lopto (“spade”).

Jussive particle le (“let”) corresponds with 2nd person/singular Aorist form of Albanian lë (“to let/leave (go/behind)”); le (“you let/left (go/behind)”). From Proto-Albanian *laide (“let”). Identical to Baltic permissive and optative particles Latvian lai (“to let”), Lithuanian lai̇̃, Old Prussian
From Proto-Albanian *laida, an ostensibly o-grade thematic present from the root *leyd- (“to let go, release”).

From Proto-Albanian *laida, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂leyH- (“to smear, slip”). Cognate with Old Prussian laydis (“loam, clay”), layso (“earth, clay”), English loam, and Ancient Greek λεῖος (leîos, “smooth, sleek”).

From Proto-Albanian *leð/dᶻ́-a- or *lœ̄ð/dᶻ́-a-, from a Pre-Proto-Albanian *lai̯d/j́a- or *lōd/j́a-, from an Proto-Indo-European *lói̯ǵ-o-, connected to lidh (“to bind”), with the meaning going from "the (bound) one" > "(dry) stone wall, boundary wall" > "raised boundar, raised edge (of a surface)".
From Proto-Albanian *laidza, possibly a variant of lëndoj, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *lento- (“bendsome, resilient”).
From Proto-Albanian *lexta, from pre-Albanian *h₁legʷʰ-to, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁lengʷʰ- (“not heavy, light”). Compare Lithuanian lengvas, Sanskrit लघु (laghú), German leicht.
From Proto-Albanian *laurā, from Proto-Indo-European *leu, etymologically identical with Lithuanian laure (“dirty person”).

From Proto-Albanian *laurā, a rebuilt form after the stem in -eh₂, from Proto-Indo-European *leh₁w- (“stone”). Cognate to Ancient Greek λᾶας (lâas, “stone”) and Old Irish lie (“stone”), and perhaps Old Armenian լեառն (leaṙn).
From Proto-Albanian *lē(i)tja, and adjective in *-no-, from Proto-Indo-European *lēi (“to pour”).
From Proto-Albanian *līdza, from Proto-Indo-European *leyǵ-. Compare Dutch lijk (“boltrope”), Latin ligare, Ukrainian нали́гати (nalýhaty, “to bridle, fetter”).
Inherited from Proto-Albanian *liga, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃ligos (“indigent, needy, ill”). Cognate to Lithuanian ligà (“illness”), Old Irish líach (“wretched”).
A variant of lëngatë, from lig (“ill, bad”) + -atë, from Proto-Albanian *ligatā.
From Proto-Albanian *leilā. Cognate to Lithuanian leilas (“thin, supple, flexible”).
Related in root to lej (“to give birth; to be born”). From a Proto-Albanian *lindi/a-, from Proto-Indo-European *leyd- (“to let go”).
From Proto-Albanian *linga, from Proto-Indo-European *leig-. Compare English lark (“to frolic”), Lithuanian láigyti (“to run around wildly”), Ancient Greek ἐλελίζω (elelízō, “to whirl around”).
From Proto-Albanian *lingā, close to Latvian liñga (“loop”), Lithuanian li̇̀nge (“flexible pole; bend”).

Singularized plural of *lik from Proto-Albanian *lika, from Proto-Indo-European *leykʷ- (“to leave, to remain”). Cognate to Sanskrit रिणक्ति (riṇákti, “to leave”), Latin linquō, and Old High German lihhan.

First attested in 1555 by Buzuku as liqē, as well as by other Old Albanian authors, who also used lëqē. Both forms lead to a Common Albanian form *licẽ́n, with lengthening from *licến, inherited from Proto-Albanian *li/ekến(iy)a-, which was borrowed from Ancient Greek λεκάνιον (lekánion), a derivati

From Proto-Albanian *leitšja, from Proto-Indo-European *ley- (“to pour”). Cognate with Latin libare (“to pour, to libate”), Old Church Slavonic лити (liti, “to pour”), Gothic 𐌻𐌴𐌹𐌸𐌿 (leiþu, “fruit wine”).

parole.significato: slate, fragile earth, stony field, clay
parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *litšimā, a derivative of liq and lisë.
From Proto-Albanian *litšā, from Proto-Indo-European *leykʷyeh₂, derivative of *leykʷ- (“to leave, to remain”); related to liq.
From Proto-Albanian *lubiç, a derivative of lubi.
From Proto-Albanian *lukā, from Proto-Indo-European *leu-(ə) (“dirt”).

parole.significato: to sip, lap, swallow, eat greedily
parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *ɫop, from Proto-Indo-European *leh2p- (“to lick, lap”).
From Proto-Albanian *lur(i)bā. Cognate to Lithuanian lãuré (“dirty person”).
From Proto-Albanian *slinjā, cognate to Latvian sliẽnas (“saliva, mucus, slime”), Proto-Slavic *slina (“saliva”).

From Proto-Albanian *alanā, compare Latin ulna (“forearm”), Ancient Greek ὠλένη (ōlénē). According to Huld, it's a borrowing from an Ancient Greek dialect from the Argead Kingdom labeled as Ancient Macedonian *ὠlénā (*ōlénā).
From Proto-Albanian *lātjā, from the same root as lot (“teardrop”).
From Proto-Albanian *lēda, from *leh₁d-o-, from Proto-Indo-European *leh₁d-. Compare Ancient Greek ληδεῖν (lēdeîn, “to be tired”), English late, Latin lassus (“weary”).

From Old Albanian lodrë, from Proto-Albanian *lādrā, from Proto-Indo-European *leh₁d-. More at lodh. Alternatiely from Proto-Indo-European *leyd- (“to play”), whence Latin lūdō (“to play”), Ancient Greek λίζω (lízō, “id.”).
From Proto-Albanian *lāpā, from Proto-Indo-European *leh₂p- (compare Latvian lùops (“cattle”), Old Irish lóeg (“calf”)).
Singularized plural of *lok, from Proto-Albanian *lāuka, from Proto-Indo-European *lewk- (“light, shine”). Related to gloq, lakuriq.
From Proto-Albanian *lā(i)ta, and adjective in *-to-, from Proto-Indo-European *lēy- (“to pour”).
From Proto-Albanian *lādja, etymologically close to Proto-Slavic *ladъ (“order, peace”), *laditi (“to make order, make peace”).
From Proto-Albanian *lādnja, related to loz. Compare Latin ludere.

From Proto-Albanian *lug(ā), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)leuK- (“to gulp/drink (down), swallow”). Cognate to Lithuanian liũgas (“morass”), Old Norse slok (“trough, spillway”), Middle High German slūch (“gulf, abyss”).

Singularised plural of *lulë, from Proto-Albanian *lulā. For Orel, an ancient Balkan loanword from an oriental source. From the substrate source responsible for Persian لاله, Latin līlia, Ancient Greek λείριον (leírion), ultimately from Egyptian ḥrrt (“flower”).
From Proto-Albanian *lubn-, from Proto-Indo-European *lewbʰ- (“to love”). Cognate to Latin lubens (“willing, (be) fond of something”), and ultimately a doublet of lyp, lubi, lugat, and laps.

From Proto-Albanian *lubnaka, from Proto-Indo-European *leubh (“to peel, to skin”). Cognate to Lithuanian lubà (“board (of a ceiling)”), Latvian luba (“bark, board”), Old Prussian lubbo (“board”) and Proto-Slavic *lьbь (“forehead, skull”).
From Proto-Albanian *lumā, from Proto-Indo-European *lew(ə) (“dirt”). Etymologically identical with Ancient Greek λῦμα (lûma, “dirt”) (Greek λύμα (lýma)).

From Proto-Albanian *lunkā, from Proto-Indo-European *lewk- (“to bend”) with a nasal infix, similar to that of Old Prussian lunkis (“angle”), Lithuanian luñkanas (“supple”), Latvian llùnks (“supple”).

From Proto-Albanian *lup-esja, from llup (“to gulp down, swallow”) (Proto-Albanian *lupa), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *lupa. Compare Sanskrit लुम्पति (lumpáti, “to break down, injure”), Lithuanian lùpti (“to peel”), Latvian lupt (“to peel; eat”), Proto-Slavic *lupiti (“to peel”).
From Proto-Albanian *lušā. Compare Sanskrit लष् (laṣ, “desire”), Old English lust (“lust, pleasure, longing”). Possibly related to këlysh.

parole.significato: scale (flake of keratin on an animal)
parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *lup-t-ya, from Proto-Indo-European *lep (“to peel, flay”). Akin to Greek λέπος (lépos, “id.”).

The -ye- (present stem), -e- (aorist stem) point towards a Proto-Albanian *lœ-, from Pre-Proto-Albanian *(s)lōi̯e/a-, or *(s)lōCe/a- (with C = *b, *d, *u̯, *i̯ , or *s), from Proto-Indo-European *sléh₃d⁽ʰ⁾-e/o-, with a semantic change from "to smear" to "to oil, annoint". The theory by Orel which st
From Proto-Albanian *luPi-, from Proto-Indo-European *lubʰ-yé-ti, from *lewbʰ- (“to love”). Cognate to Latin lubens (“willing”), Old High German lupu, Old English lufu (“love”).

From *lan, from Proto-Albanian *ladna, from Proto-Indo-European *lh̥₁d-ne/o-, from *leh₁d- (“to be tired”); cf. (Germanic) Gothic 𐌻𐌴𐍄𐌰𐌽 (lētan, “to let”) (English let (“id”)) and (Baltic) Latvian laist (“to let”), ļaut (“id”), Lithuanian leisti (“id”).
from the transitive verb lë, or from Proto-Albanian *lV-.

Also lëngatë under the influence of lëng ~ lang. From Proto-Albanian *leugatā, related to Illyrian *Lougeon (Strabo 7.43), Lithuanian liūgas (“marsh”), Proto-Slavic *luža (“pool”). Analyzable as lag + -at(ë).

A lë- prefixed formation, from an unattested *kunda, from Proto-Albanian *kunda, related to Proto-Germanic *hutaną (“to swing”) (cf. Middle High German hutzen), and perhaps Lithuanian kuzdeti (“to tremble”), kùdulti (“to pull hair hair or beard”).

From Proto-Albanian * ̊kurā, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)keuh₁- (“to cover (over), wrap (up)”). Cognate to Ancient Greek σκύλος (skúlos, “fell, pell, rind”), Latin corium (“leather, skin”). Related to lakur (“skin”) (now dialectal). See also lakuriq.

parole.significato: expanse of rubble, stones-lide, pile of stones
parole.testo: Singularized plural of *lëmak, a derivative of lëmë, from Proto-Albanian *lamā, cognate to Old High German lam (“lame”), Proto-Slavic *lomь (“breaking; crow-bar; broken branches”).

From Proto-Albanian *lemesja, from Proto-Indo-European *lemesi-o-, a derivative of Proto-Indo-European *lem- (“to break”). Cognate to Lithuanian lemesis (“sharp edge of the plough”), Proto-Slavic *lemešь (“ploughshare”). Orel claims the transition of '*broken lump of earth' > 'globe of earth' to be

From Proto-Albanian *(a)lōu-m- (“(threshing-, malting-)floor”), with enlargement in -mo- or -mn/men-. Cognate to Ancient Greek ἅλως (hálōs, “(threshing-)floor”), Old Norse lófi (“(threshing-)floor”), Old High German lam (“lame”).

From an unattested *lënd < Proto-Albanian *lenta (cf. lëndë), from Proto-Indo-European *lento- (“bendsome, resilient”). Akin to Lithuanian leñtas (“still, quite”), Latin lentus (“supple”), English lithe (“supple”), German lind (“mild”). Possibly a nasal variant of ledh (“to caress, stroke”).

From Proto-Albanian *lentā, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *lenteh₂, from a tentative root *lent-, or a wanderword. Compare Old High German linta (“linden”), Lithuanian lentà (“board”), Proto-Slavic *lǫtъ (“bast”). Possibly connected with lëndinë (“heath, pasture”).
From Proto-Albanian *(u)la-n-g-, from Proto-Indo-European *welg- (“wet, moist”), with metathesis. Cognate to Russian воло́га (vológa, “liquid”).
A nasalized variant of ligatë, from lig (“ill, bad”), from Proto-Albanian *ligatā. See lig for more. Orel claims the appearance of inlaut -ën- to be the result of influence from lëngoj.

parole.significato: small plot of arable land on the hillside, delimited by a wall
parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *lengā, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *h₁lengʷʰ- (“light, not heavy”). For sense development, compare Old Irish laigiu (“smaller”), Welsh llai (“smaller”), Ancient Greek ἐλαχύς (elakhús, “small, little”), all from the same root.
From Proto-Albanian *lanna-.
From Proto-Albanian *lapā, a derivative of lapë. Cognate to Greek λοπός (lopós, “shell, husk, bark”), Lithuanian lãpas (“leaf”).
From Proto-Albanian *madza, from Proto-Indo-European *méǵh₂-.

parole.significato: porridge (of corn flour, prepared with boiling cream or cheese)
parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *maθ-, from Proto-Indo-European *mh₂sd- (“fat, feed, fodder”). Cognate to Old High German mast (“fodder, feeding, fattening”).
From Proto-Albanian *mazdnja, a deverbative based on Proto-Indo-European *mazd- (“feeding”), whence also German mästen (“to fatten”), Sanskrit मेदस् (médas, “fat, flesh”).
From Proto-Albanian *maljā. Close to Lithuanian malà (“land”), Latvian mala (“bank, shore”). Related to mal.

From Proto-Albanian *makā, which has entered the declension of the feminine -eh₂-stems, from Proto-Indo-European *mh₂ek- (“wet, moist”). Cognate to Serbo-Croatian mȍkar (“wet”), Lithuanian makõnė (“mud”).
From an unattested *mall, from Proto-Albanian *maldwa, related to Latin mollis (“soft”), Sanskrit मृदु (ṃrdú, “id”).
From Proto-Albanian *manta. Compare Ancient Greek βάτος (bátos, “bramble”), said by Beekes to be a Mediterranean wanderwort, and μαντία (mantía, “blackberry”) (Dacian loan).
from Proto-Albanian *mandja, from *mand- (“to feed (trans.), suckle”) (modern mënd). Close related to Messapic menza (“foal”). Lent Romanian mânz. More at mënd.
From Proto-Albanian *mardzā, from Proto-Indo-European *mórǵ-o-. Compare Proto-Slavic *morzъ and its descendants.

Cognate to Albanian marrë; both from Proto-Albanian *marsa (from Proto-Indo-European *mergʷ- (“to flicker; to darken; to be dark”); Proto-Indo-European *h₂mergʷ- (“dark”)). Cognate to Proto-Slavic *morkъ (“darkness”), *morxъ (“dusk, fog”), Proto-Slavic *mergъ (“brown”), Proto-Germanic *merkuz (“dark
Literally ‘dim, murky’, from Proto-Albanian *marsa; akin to Proto-Slavic *morxŭ (“dusk, fog”). Cognate to marrtë. See marrtë (“dim, murky, etc.”).
From Proto-Albanian *matja, from *mh̥₁ti̯-e-, from Proto-Indo-European *meh₁- (compare Old English mǣd, Latin mētior).

Gheg variant of Tosk pas (“behind, beyond, after”). From mbasi, mbas (“after”). A compound of më (“more, most”) + pas (“behind, after, beyond”) (pas from Proto-Albanian *pa ̊ (see pa), from Proto-Indo-European *pos(t) (“directly to, at, after”). Cognate to Ancient Greek πός (pós, “at, to, by”), Old
From Proto-Albanian *mata, from pre-Albanian *mn̥to, from Proto-Indo-European *men- (“to tower, stand out”) (compare Welsh mynydd, Latin mōns, Avestan 𐬨𐬀𐬙𐬌 (mati)).

From Proto-Albanian *madź(i)ā, from Proto-Indo-European *meh₂ǵ- (“to knead, stroke”). Cognate to Ancient Greek μαγίς (magís, “kneaded mass/substance”), Russian мазь (mazʹ, “salve, ointment”). Demiraj suggests a formation from mâj (“to fatten”) (standard majm).

From mbanj (Arbëreshë), from *ënbanj (compare Old Gheg ënbaj), the *m- being from Proto-Albanian *en- (intensive prefix). The identity of the root is disputed. * Orel posits Proto-Albanian *barnja, a causative formed to Proto-Indo-European *bʰer- (“to carry”). * Schumacher and DPEWA after him insist
From Proto-Albanian *en-bara, intensive of *bara (modern dialectal bar). More at mbart.

parole.significato: pregnant (of animals); with calf, in foal
parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *en-bartja, from *en-barta (“to carry, transport”) (modern mbart). More at mbart. Cognate to Illyrian *bardia (“id”).

Prefixed form of bart, from Proto-Albanian *bar-, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰor-eyō, further from *bʰer- (“to bear, to carry”). Compare Ancient Greek φορέω (phoréō). Cognate to Illyrian *bardia (“id”).

First attested in 1555 by Buzuku as ëmbarë. Various theories exist on the etymology: * From mbar (“to bring (back), return”) (from Proto-Albanian *en-bara; further related to Albanian mbart (“to bear, carry”), mbaroj (“to finish, complete, end, fulfill, comply”), mbaj (“to carry, hold”)). * Orel dis

To be dissected as (ë)mb-ath, and not as (ë)m-bath, which is shown in the Arbëresh word xath "to take off (shoes)", as well as the more common form dath (“to take off (shoes)”). Thus, *ath should be seen as the base, and is from Proto-Albanian *atˢ́, with final devoicing from earlier *að/dᶻ́, from P
From Proto-Albanian *amb(i)-etja, from jes (“to remain”), a denominative of jetë.
From Proto-Albanian *nepōtś(i)ā, from Proto-Indo-European *népōts.
From Proto-Albanian *ambi-etja, a denominative of jetë.

From Proto-Albanian *(V)(m)pi, perhaps from a compound of Proto-Indo-European *h₂en-h₁pi (“up, on, upon, (on-to, un-to)”), from *h₂én (“on”) + *h₁(é)pi, *h₁ópi (“by, near, at”); otherwise just the latter component and phonetically influenced by mbë. Compare Ancient Greek ἐπί (epí, “on, to, towards”)

Uncertain; from archaic and dialectal mblonj, possibly: * from n- + plonj, from Proto-Albanian *plānja, from *plā + *-nja (denominative suffix), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pleh₁- (“to fill”); * or borrowed from Latin impleō (“to fill up”), also from the same root.
From *ënbrenj, from Proto-Albanian *en-breunja, from *breuna (“belt, girdle”) (modern brez). More at brez.
From Proto-Albanian *brāu, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰrewh₁- (“to boil up, ferment”). Cognate to Latin ferveō (“to boil (up), bubble”) and Old English brēowan.

parole.significato: to cram, fill to the brim
parole.testo: Possibly a denominative verb, from Proto-Albanian *bruta, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰrewh₁- (“to boil up, ferment”) (cf. Latin ferveō (“to boil (up), bubble”), Thracian *brutos (“beer, a type of barley beer”)) or Proto-Indo-European *bʰrews- (“to swell”)(cf. Latin frustum, Old English brēost (Engli

From Proto-Albanian *en-prama, the second element of which is used throughout Gheg subdialects on its own, and is from Proto-Albanian *pramā-, from Proto-Indo-European *promeh₂- (“last, rear part of the day”). Related to Proto-Germanic *fram, Ancient Greek πρόμος (prómos), Umbrian promom, and Lithua

From mbi (“on, upon”) + ul (“to lower, put down”), from Proto-Albanian *ambi-wēla, from Proto-Indo-European *wel- (“to press together”), probably a secondary formation after mbyll (“close, shut down”). See mbyll and ul.

From Old Albanian ëmbush, from Proto-Albanian *en-busa, or *am-buśś-it, from Proto-Indo-European *bu-n-s-, nasalized weak stem of *beus- (“to blow up, puff out, swell”) (compare Ancient Greek βυνέω (bunéō, “to stuff”), Old High German pfoso (“bag”)).
From Proto-Albanian *ambi-wēla, from Proto-Indo-European *wel- (“to press together”). More at ul.

parole.significato: to strangle, suffocate, choke to death
parole.testo: From *(ë)m-byt, with the prefix identical to that in mbloj and inherited from Proto-Albanian *án(a)- (“on, upon”). The base *byt comes from *býti < Proto-Albanian *búti < *bútit < *búti̯it < *búti̯et < Pre-Proto-Albanian *búti̯ét < *bʰut-i̯é-ti, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰut-i̯é/ó- (“to strike”), f
From Proto-Albanian *ambi-stata, based on *stata, from Proto-Indo-European *sth₂tós (“standing”). Compare Sanskrit स्थित (sthitá), Greek στατός (statós, “standing”), Latin status (“standing”).
From Proto-Albanian *me(t). Cognate to Ancient Greek μετά (metá, “after, beyond; in the middle, between”), Gothic miþ (“with”), Old Norse með.
From Proto-Albanian *meuska, from Proto-Indo-European *mewH- (compare Latvian maût (“to submerge”), Serbo-Croatian mȉti (“to wash”)).

parole.significato: to fail, fade, wane, slowly run out
parole.testo: Reflective form of mej, from Proto-Albanian *mōja, cognate with Old High German muoan (“to work diligently”), Ancient Greek μῶλος (môlos, “toil of war”) and Proto-Slavic *majati (“to work slowly”).

First attested in 1618 by Budi. From Proto-Albanian *me(i̯)ə, from Pre-Proto-Albanian *mai̯-ii̯i/a-, from Proto-Indo-European *moi̯H-éi̯e/o- (“to make small”), from Proto-Indo-European *meyH- (“to become small, diminish”). Connected to me (“little, slightly”).
From Proto-Albanian *mē̆-, from Proto-Indo-European *me- (“me”).
From Proto-Albanian *mek-, from Proto-Indo-European *mek- (“to bleat”). Cognate to Lithuanian meknénti (“to bleat”). An onomatopoeic root.
From Proto-Albanian *maka, related to makë.
From Proto-Albanian *mazdnja, deverbative of Proto-Indo-European *mh₂sd-, from *meh₂d- (“wet”).

Singularized plural of Proto-Albanian *marā, from Proto-Indo-European *mor- (“feminine evil spirit”). Compare Polish zmora (“nightmare”), Czech mura (“nightmare, moth”) and Old English mare (“nightmare, monster”).

From Proto-Albanian *meTi, *meTśi-, from Proto-Indo-European *me-t/dhi (“with, middle”), ultimately from *medʰyo-. Cognate to Gothic 𐌼𐌹𐌸 (miþ, “with”). It might represent a devoiced variant of mez. A loan from Modern Greek μέσος (mésos, “in the middle”) is not excluded.
From Proto-Albanian *matšā, from Proto-Indo-European *mokʷi̯. Related to makë.
From Proto-Albanian *mūh-, from Proto-Indo-European *múHs (“mouse”).
From Proto-Albanian *melwa, from Proto-Indo-European *melh₂-wo-m, from *melh₂- (“to grind”), close to German Mehl (“id”), Greek μύλος (mýlos), Latin molere. Compare also Romanian mălai.
Possibly from Proto-Albanian *meila (“fastening (of a knife)”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *mey- (“to attach, fasten”).

From Proto-Albanian *mīrā, from older Proto-Albanian *meirā, from Proto-Indo-European *meih₁-ro- (“peace”). Compare Proto-Balto-Slavic *meiˀrás (“peace”), Proto-Slavic *milъ (“nice, gentle, mild”)), enlargement of *meih₁- (“soft, mild”) (compare Latin mītis (“soft (not chewy)”)).
From Proto-Albanian *mitja, related to Lithuanian mi̇̀klas (“supple”), mitrùs (“id”), Latvian mikls (“id”), mitrs, mikât (“to knead”).

From Proto-Albanian *miśśa < *meśśa, from Proto-Indo-European *memsa- (“meat”). Compare Armenian միս (mis), Serbo-Croatian meso, Russian мя́со (mjáso), Tocharian B mīsa, Old Prussian mensa, Gothic 𐌼𐌹𐌼𐌶 (mimz), Sanskrit मांस (māṃsá).
From Proto-Albanian *mit-ono, from Proto-Indo-European *meH1i (“mild, soft”). Compare Latin mitis.
From Proto-Albanian *meita. Compare Lithuanian miẽtas (“post, stake”), Old Norse meiðr (“beam”), Sanskrit मेथी (methí, “pillar, post”).
From Proto-Albanian *melitjā, from *melita (“honey”). More at mjaltë.
From Proto-Albanian *melita, from Proto-Indo-European *mélit (compare Greek μέλι (méli), Armenian մեղր (meġr), Gothic 𐌼𐌹𐌻𐌹𐌸 (miliþ)). Originally of neuter gender.
From older mjedvis, from Proto-Albanian *metwisa. By surface analysis, mjet (“between, among, amid”) + vis (“place, land, country”).

From the more conservative variant mjedhër, from Proto-Albanian *mesdrā, presumably cognate with Lithuanian mẽdis (“tree; wood”) and Latvian mežs (“wood”); however, these are in fact from Proto-Indo-European *médʰyos (“middle”). On both semantic and phonetic grounds, one might also consider a deriva
Apocope of dialectal mjegullë, from Proto-Albanian *meg(u)lā, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃migʰ-leh₂ (“mist”) (compare Lithuanian miglà, Polish mgła, Greek ομίχλη (omíchli)).
From an earlier mjēk, from Proto-Albanian *mʲeðək, borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin medicus (“doctor, physician, surgeon”).

Demiraj claims descent from Proto-Albanian *m(i)ier-, cognate to Ancient Greek μιερός (mierós), μιαρός (miarós, “polluted, defiled”). On the other hand, Orel claims a borrowing through Vulgar Latin from Latin miser, although this does not reflect the phonetics of Latin loanwords into Albanian.
From Proto-Albanian *met-, from Proto-Indo-European *me-t- (“with, in the midst/middle of, between”). Cognate to Ancient Greek μετά, μέτα (metá, méta, “in the midst/middle of, between, behind”).
From Proto-Albanian *mē, from Proto-Indo-European *méh₁ (prohibitive particle).
From Proto-Albanian *mādzula, from Proto-Indo-European *meh₂ǵʰ-ulo (“a small bean”). Compare also Romanian mazăre.
From Proto-Albanian *mādzā, feminine of Proto-Indo-European *meh₂ǵʰ-. Compare Lithuanian mãžas, mažùlis (“small”).
From Proto-Albanian *mākanā, from Doric Greek μᾱχανᾱ́ (mākhanā́, “machine, tool”). Doublet of makinë.

According to Oryol, from Proto-Albanian *mērwa, from Proto-Indo-European *mer- (“to die”). Oryol compares semantically Ancient Greek φθείρ (phtheír, “louse”) and φθείρω (phtheírō, “to destroy”), though the etymological connection of the Greek cognates is uncertain.
From archaic motshë, from Proto-Albanian *mātusā, from *māti (“time”) (modern mot). Possibly lent Romanian moș (“grandfather”) after the changes of *-t(u)š- to *-š-. More at mot.

From Proto-Albanian *māti (“time”), from Proto-Indo-European *méh₁tis (“measurement”), deverbative of *meh₁- (“to measure”); compare Old English mǣþ (“measure”), Lithuanian mẽtas (“time”), Ancient Greek μῆτις (mêtis, “plan”). Sense shift from ‘time’ to ‘weather, year, era’ influenced by Latin tempus

From muj, a Gheg variant of mund (attested in Meshari), from Proto-Albanian *magti-on with diphthongized a > ou before stops, from Proto-Indo-European *mag (“be able, have power”). Compare German Macht, English might.
From Proto-Albanian *en-pāginja, from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂ǵ-. Cognate with Ancient Greek πήγνυμι (pḗgnumi, “to make firm, to make stiff”), Latin pangō (“id”), Gothic fahan (“to catch”).
From Proto-Albanian *moN, from Proto-Indo-European *me- (“me”).

From Old Albanian muoj, from Late-PA *mōj, earlier *moj, from Proto-Albanian *moi̯i̯ə, from Early-PA *mā̊i̯i̯ad, from Pre-Proto-Albanian *mā́i̯i̯a- < *mā́hi̯a-, from Proto-Indo-European *mḗh₁n̥si̯o-, from *mḗh₁n̥s (“moon”). (compare English moon, Latin mensis, Tocharian A mañ, Lithuanian mėnuo, Russ
From Proto-Albanian *muska, from Proto-Indo-European *mewH- (“wet”). Cognate with Latvian maût (“to plunge”), Serbo-Croatian mȉti (“to wash”).
Inherited from Proto-Albanian *smuga, cognate to Old English smoca (“smoke”), Old Irish múch (“smoke”), Armenian մուխ (mux).
Inherited from Proto-Albanian *mugula; akin to Lithuanian muguliúoti (“to move”), mùginti (“to touch, move”). Compare also Romanian mugur (“bud”).

Gheg; from the adjective Proto-Albanian *melana (“black”), from Proto-Indo-European *melh₂-n-os (“dull black”), from *melh₂-. Compare Latvian męl̃ns (“black”), Serbo-Croatian malina (“raspberry”), Ancient Greek μέλαινα (mélaina, “black”). For sense development from ‘black’ to ‘heartache’, compare zi

From Proto-Albanian *murga, from *morHgʷo, from Proto-Indo-European *(h₂)merHgʷ- (compare Old English mierce (“darkness”), Lithuanian márgas (“multicolored”), Ancient Greek ἀμορβός (amorbós, “dark”)).
From zero-grade form of extended form Proto-Albanian *meus, from Proto-Indo-European *mew- (“wet; dirt; to wash”). Compare Old High German mos (“id”).

From Proto-Albanian *mūka, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)meug-, *mewk-. Close to Latvian mukls (“swampy”), Old Norse myki, mykr (“dung”), Ancient Greek μύξα (múxa, “mucus, lamp wick”) and μύκης (múkēs, “fungus”).
From Proto-Albanian *mũtja, from Proto-Indo-European *meuɘ (“wet, dirty, to wash”).
From Proto-Albanian *džija, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷii̯ā. Cognate to Sanskrit ज्या (jyā, “bow string”), Old Church Slavonic жила (žila, “vein, tendon”), Greek βιός (viós).

parole.significato: more, some more, (in negative sentences) any more
parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *məi̯es with secondary nasalization, from the comparative of Proto-Indo-European *méǵh₂s (“big”). Cognate with Gothic 𐌼𐌰𐌹𐍃 (mais, “more”), Oscan mais (“more”). Related to madh (“big”).

parole.significato: indicates position in space or time. in, at, to, on
parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *ambi, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂m̥bʰi. Cognate with Ancient Greek ἀμφί (amphí). The simplification of /mb/ to /m/ is expected in Gheg but not in the standard language, hence the alternative form mbë.
From Proto-Albanian *melanjā, from the feminine of the adjective *melana (“black”) (modern mëllë (“grief”)). More at mëllë.
From Proto-Albanian *ma(m)mā, from Proto-Indo-European *mā̆(m)mā, *meh₂-(m)meh₂ (“mother”). Cognate to Ancient Greek μάμμη (mámmē, “mother”) and Latin mamma (“mother”). A nursery word
From older and dialectal mbërshel, which contains a negating prefix Proto-Albanian *ana-pra-, attached to Proto-Indo-European *eǵʰs-sélǵ-e/o- (“to open”), which originally meant "to let go, release".

From Old Albanian mpson (Bogdani, Budi), ëmpson (Buzuku), from Proto-Albanian *imbitjɔnit, borrowed from Vulgar Latin *invitiō, *invitiāre, from *vitiō, from Latin vitium (“vice”). Compare Romanian învăța. Otherwise from pësoj, itself of Latin origin, developing in mpsoj, psoj, mbsoj, mbësoj and oth

Tosk form of Gheg mâz, from Old Albanian manz (Buzuku), from Proto-Albanian *mandja, from *mand- (“to feed (trans.), suckle”) (modern mënd). Close related to Messapic menza (“foal”). Lent Romanian mânz. More at mënd.
Inherited from Proto-Albanian *naktā, from Proto-Indo-European *nókʷts.
Antonym and prefixal form of dal (“to exit, go out”) (n- + dal), from Proto-Albanian *en-dala. See dal for more.
From Proto-Albanian *en-tenja, from Proto-Indo-European *ten- (“to hammer out, stretch (out)”). Cognate to Ancient Greek τείνω (teínō, “to stretch out”).

First attested in 1555 by Buzuku as ëndēr. Inherited from Common Albanian *əndér, which was part of a small group of consonant-ending feminine nouns, from Proto-Albanian *əndéri-, following i-umlaut from Pre-Proto-Albanian *andári-, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂(e)ntóri- (“front, face”), which would
From Proto-Albanian *en-das-ja, related to Greek δήω (dío, “to find”).
From Proto-Albanian *en-dadžja, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰegʷʰ- (“to burn”).
From Proto-Albanian *(a)n-di-e-, enlargement of di. More at di.

From Proto-Albanian *əndíhi/a-, further reconstructions disputed: # From Pre-Proto-Albanian *an-dikʰí/á-, from Proto-Indo-European *(h₂)ano-dih₁sḱé/ó- (“to hurry”). # From Pre-Proto-Albanian *an-tikʰí/á-, from Proto-Indo-European *(h₂)ano-tigʰsḱé/ó- (“to run”). In both cases, the meaning "to run, hu
From Proto-Albanian *en-teka, from Proto-Indo-European *tekʷ- (“to run”). Cognate to Lithuanian tekėti (“to run, flow”) and Sanskrit तक्ति (tákti, “to hasten”). A prefixed formation in (a)n-.

From Proto-Albanian *a/N(e)dri, from Proto-Indo-European *mé-ǵʰ(s)ri (locative) from *me (“with”). Cognate to Ancient Greek μέχρι (mékhri), Old Armenian մերձ (merj), and doublet of me as well related to dorë.

From Proto-Albanian *en-tādza, from Proto-Indo-European *teh₂g- (“to order, arrange”) (as implied by Baltic). Cognate to Ancient Greek τάσσω (tássō, “to arrange, to put in order”) (note the particularly close prefixed formation ἐντᾰ́σσω (entắssō, “to place”)), ταγή (tagḗ, “ordering, array”), Lithuan
From Proto-Albanian * ̊dē-(h), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰed- (“to shit”). See dhjes for more.
From Proto-Albanian *(a)n-draga, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰrā́ks (“dregs, sediment”), likely of non-Indo-European origin.

parole.significato: wool band to hold infants in a cradle
parole.testo: Analyzable as *n-dridh-zë, from Proto-Albanian *dridza (whence dredh), with n- prefix and -zë feminine suffix.

From Proto-Albanian * ̊truδ-, or *entrūda, from Proto-Indo-European *trewd- (“to squeeze, crush, press”). Cognate to Old Church Slavonic троудити (truditi, “to load, plague”), Latin trūdō (“to thrust, push”), Gothic 𐌿𐍃𐌸𐍂𐌹𐌿𐍄𐌰𐌽 (usþriutan, “to burden”).
From Proto-Albanian *en-drūna, derivative of dru, from *dóru.
From Proto-Albanian *en-truka, from Proto-Indo-European *trūk-, *trūg- (“to press, beat”). Close to Old High German drucken (“to press”), English thrutch.
From Proto-Albanian * ̥trud-io-, from Proto-Indo-European *trewd- (“to squeeze, crush, press”).

parole.significato: to pluck out, pull out, tear
parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *duk-, from Proto-Indo-European *deuk- (“to draw”). Cognate to Gothic tiuhan (“to draw”).
From Proto-Albanian *en-tulka, close to Lithuanian telkiù, telkti (“to gather, to bring together”), Proto-Slavic *telťi (“to beat, to pound”).

From Proto-Albanian *ən-dūja, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewh₂- (“smoke, mist, haze”). Cognate with Latvian dujs (“dirty”), Lithuanian dujà (“swamp; mist, drizzle”), English dusk and possibly Dacian Δουιανα (Douiana, “Duiana”), a toponym.
Attested by Buzuku as ëndër. From Proto-Albanian *enter, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁entér (“between”); or borrowed from Latin inter. See also ndë (“in”), ndën, nën (“under”).

parole.significato: to set on (to do), incite, instigate
parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *tśeu-, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱey- (“to put, set in motion; be on the move”). Cognate with Ancient Greek σεύω (seúō, “to actuate”) and Latin cieō (“to set in motion”). An intensive formation with the Albanian prefix ndër-. Doublets include cys and qoj.

The nominative-accusative is from accusative Proto-Albanian *nōs, stressed form of clitic Proto-Indo-European *nos, which is continued by the clitic na. Neve and nesh are innovated, but Gheg retains dative nahe (Old Albanian nae) from a genitive *nosōm.
An innovation stemming from Early Proto-Albanian *nōhōn. Cognate to Proto-Slavic *nasъ (“our”).
From Proto-Albanian *en-ka and related to the preposition ka (“from, out, out of, to”). Cognate with Old Church Slavonic къ (kŭ, “to”).

Inherited from Proto-Albanian *en-gaska, from *gʷm̥sḱéti, making it a cognate of Ancient Greek βάσκω (báskō). The variant ngaj from a slightly different root (see ngaj), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰeh₁- (“leave”). Compare English go, Ancient Greek κιχάνω (kikhánō, “to meet with, arrive at”), Sanskri
Variant of standard ngah, though from Proto-Albanian *en-gānja instead of *en-gaska.
From Proto-Albanian *en-gala, a denominative based on an unattested *gala, related to Lithuanian gãlas (“end”), Latvian gals (“end”), Old Prussian gallan (“death”).
From Proto-Albanian *en-gatja, causative of *en-gānja (modern ngaj). More at ngah.
Unknown. Comparison with Ancient Greek γαστήρ (gastḗr, “belly, appetite”) yields Proto-Albanian *en-gastanja.
From dialectal ngae, from Proto-Albanian *en-gadā, with the latter from Proto-Indo-European *gʰodʰ-o-s, from *gʰedʰ- (“to unite; join; suit”), cognate with Proto-Slavic *godъ (“time, year”).
From Proto-Albanian *gleinja, related to Lithuanian gliejù, gliēti (“to smear”), Old High German klēnan (“id”).
From Proto-Albanian *en-ga-lab-nja, a denominative verb based on *lab. Cognate to Lithuanian lãbas (“good”), Latvian labs (“id”).
From Proto-Albanian *śal(u)-, from Proto-Indo-European *solh₂- (“safe and sound, unhurt, whole”). Related to gjallë.

From Proto-Albanian * ̊śali(m)-, from Proto-Indo-European *sḗh₂l (“salt”). Cognate to Ancient Greek ἅλιμος (hálimos, “of the sea, sea”). Enlargement with the prefix (a)n-. The root vowel points to umlaut, caused by -i- of the following syllable.
From Proto-Albanian *en-salma, from Proto-Indo-European *sḗh₂l (“salt”). Related to ngjelmë with cognates including Ancient Greek ἅλς (háls), Latin sāl, Old Armenian աղ (ał) and the like.
Variant of ndjerë, from Proto-Albanian *(a)jeri, identical to Ancient Greek ἦρι (êri, “early”), further related to Gothic 𐌰𐌹𐍂 (air), Old Norse ár), and Avestan 𐬀𐬌𐬌𐬀𐬭 (aiiar, “day”).
From Proto-Albanian * ̊gneś-, from Proto-Indo-European *gen- (“to compress”). Cognate with Old Church Slavonic гнєсти (gnesti, “to press on”). Formed using the intensive prefix (a)n-.
From Proto-Albanian * ̊ker-, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)Ker-. Cognate to Latin crōciō (“to croak”).
From Proto-Albanian *en-gleitja, from Proto-Indo-European *gleyH- (“to smear; to stick”). Compare Proto-Germanic *klaiþą (“garment”), English cloth.
From gop (“greedy, gluttonous”). The latter continues Proto-Albanian *gāpā probably related to Indo-European.

parole.significato: to die (for animals and insects only, excluding bees), to stiffen, strangle, kill
parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *kār(i)da, from Proto-Indo-European *kēr dʰeh₁- (“to take root, to stiffen”), prefixed with n-. Original meaning 'to starve, die of hunger'.
Parallel formation of ngop, from Proto-Albanian *en-gāptja.
From Proto-Albanian *(-)greδ-, from Proto-Indo-European *gwr-edh- (“to cry, shout”). An Albanian intensive formation with the prefix n-. The raising of e > i is determined by the Albanian paradigm.
From Proto-Albanian *en-kreinja, a derivation in *en- of Proto-Indo-European *gwrH-i-. Cognate to Ancient Greek κρῡ́ον (krū́on).

From Proto-Albanian *engrāja, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰer- (“warm, hot”). Cognate to Old Church Slavonic грѣти (grěti, “to warm”). The form may have entered the class of Albanian inchoatives in -sk-. The anlaut points to a formation with the prefix *en-.
From Proto-Albanian *en-krūda, cognate to Lithuanian grúžiu, grústi (“to stamp, to punch”), Latvian grúst (“id”).
From Proto-Albanian *en-krūtja, further related to Lithuanian kráuju, kráuti (“to pile”), Proto-Slavic *kryti (“to cover”) and possibly Ancient Greek κρύπτω (krúptō, “to hide”).
From Proto-Albanian * ̊gull-, from Proto-Indo-European *gwelH- (“to prick”). Cognate to Lithuanian gélti (“to prick”), gi̇̀lti (“to get pained, ache”). A formation with the prefix (a)n-.
From Proto-Albanian *en-kuša, related to Lithuanian kùšti (“to strike”), Latvian kustinât (“to move, to touch”).
From Proto-Albanian *en-kutja, related to Lithuanian káuti (“to strike”), Latin cūdō (“to strike”), Old High German houwan (“to strike; to hew”) and Proto-Slavic *kovati (“to forge”).

parole.significato: to set on, threaten, unleash (especially the dog)
parole.testo: Probably from double prefixed form of suffixed lengthened root Proto-Albanian *men-yo, from Proto-Indo-European *men (“to protect”). Compare Latin minere (“to threaten”).
From Proto-Albanian *nū, from Proto-Indo-European *nū (“now”). Cognate to Sanskrit नू (nū, “now”). Often occurs in coordination with other particles, compare tani, nani, nime.

From Proto-Albanian *nepō, from Proto-Indo-European *népōts (“grandson, nephew”). Cognate to Latin nepos (“grandson”) and Sanskrit नपात् (nápat-, “grandson”). Reinforcement/influence or a borrowing from Latin is also possible.

From Proto-Albanian *neitša, from Proto-Indo-European *néykʷyeti, related to Lithuanian su-ni̇̀kti (“to set upon, to attack”), Proto-Slavic *niknǫti (“to rise, grow”), and, proposed by some, Ancient Greek νεῖκος (neîkos, “quarrel, struggle”). More likely borrowed from Latin initio.

From Proto-Albanian *nemska, from Proto-Indo-European *nem- (“to divide, to take, to arrange, to count”). Cognate to Greek νέμω (némo, “to divide”), Gothic niman (“to take”), Latin numerus (“member, element, number”), nummus (“coin, money”). More and more replaced by the loanword numëroj.
From Old Albanian njer, from Proto-Albanian *nera, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂nḗr.

parole.significato: to know; recognize; be familiar with
parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *gnāska, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵneh₃-sḱe/o-, from *ǵneh₃- (compare English know, Serbo-Croatian znati, Latin (g)nōscō).

parole.significato: to know; recognize; be familiar with
parole.testo: Perhaps from Proto-Albanian *gnāska, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵn̥h₃sḱéti, from *ǵneh₃- (compare English know, Serbo-Croatian znati, Latin (g)nōscō). According to Oryol, the full-grade was drawn from the aorist.
From archaic and dialectal ngjollë, from Proto-Albanian *en-sālā, from Proto-Indo-European *solH- (compare English sallow, Russian соло́вый (solóvyj, “cream-colored”), Latin salīva).
From dialectal ngjomë, nglomë, from Proto-Albanian *glāima, from Proto-Indo-European *gleh₁i-m- (compare English clammy, Lithuanian gléima (“slime”)), enlargement of *gleih₁- (“to stick, adhere”).

From Old Albanian nja, from Proto-Albanian *nyá-, from Pre-Proto-Albanian *myá-, from Proto-Indo-European *smiyo- (“a, an”), from Proto-Indo-European *s(e)mih₂ or Proto-Indo-European *smiyah₂. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sem- (“together, one”). According to Neri, the etymology connecting nj
Unknown. Maybe a diminutive in -c of earlier *nrronjë from Proto-Albanian *en-wradnjā (“to radicate, to cause roots”). Alternatively a diminutive in -c of earlier *ndër-rrënjë.
From Proto-Albanian *nu, from Proto-Indo-European *nu (“now”). Related to ni. Compare Ancient Greek νῦν (nûn), Old High German nu (“now”).
A Gheg word. From Proto-Albanian *snutja, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)neh₁- (“to turn, to spin”). Cognate to Sanskrit स्नावन् (snāvan, “band, sinew”).
From Proto-Albanian *en-džernja, related to ziej, zjarr.
From Proto-Albanian *džita, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷeyh₃- (“to live”). Cognate to Sanskrit जीवति (jīvati), Latin vīvō, Old English cwic (“alive, living”) (cf. English quick).
From Proto-Albanian *džeina, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰendʰe/o (compare English begin, Ancient Greek χανδάνω (khandánō, “to hold, contain”)).

From Proto-Albanian *ana, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂enō (“along a slanted surface, etc.”), from *h₂én (“on, upon, onto, up to”). Cognate to Ancient Greek ἀνά (aná, “on, upwards, along”), Gothic 𐌰𐌽𐌰 (ana, “on, in, against, because of, about”), English on, and Old Prussian no, na (“on (where), again

Nominative-accusative from accusative Proto-Albanian *nōs, stressed form of clitic Proto-Indo-European *nos, which is continued by the clitic na. Neve and nesh are innovated, but Gheg retains dative nahe (Old Albanian nae) from a genitive *nosōm.
From Proto-Albanian *namā, from Proto-Indo-European *nem- (“to apportion, sacrifice”) (compare German nehmen (“to take”), Ancient Greek νέμω (némō, “to distribute”), νέμεσις (némesis, “wrath”)).
From original nëndë but influenced by the -të in 6-8 and 10, further from Proto-Albanian *neunti-, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁néwn̥. Compare Old Norse niund, Old High German niun, Latin novem.

From Proto-Albanian *na(n)nā, from Proto-Indo-European *nan(n)-eh₂- (“mother”), possibly a Lallwort. Closely related to Messapic ana, cognate to Ancient Greek νάννη (nánnē, “aunt, mother”), Welsh nain (“grandmother”), Sanskrit नना (nanā́, “mother”), Persian ننه (nane, “mother, grandmother”), Ukraini

parole.significato: Traditional leather shoes worn by Albanians in Albania, Serbia, North Macedonia, Montenegro, Greece (by the Arvanites)…
parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *api + *ga, *api also giving rise to hap (“step”). Related to hap (“open”). According to Orel, from Proto-Slavic *ob(ъ)pьnъkъ (“sandal, shoe”), comparing Serbo-Croatian opanak, though differences between the Gheg and Tosk forms may suggest otherwise; as per Fortson, a Proto-Alban
From Proto-Albanian *apa, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂epó (“off, away”). Cognate to Messapic [script needed] (apa, “from, out of, by”), Ancient Greek ἀπό (apó, “away, off”), Sanskrit अप (apá).
From Proto-Albanian *pauja, from Proto-Indo-European *pew-. Compare Armenian հոգի (hogi, “breath”).
From Proto-Albanian *palei-, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)pel- (“to speak with a loud voice”). Cognate to Gothic 𐍃𐍀𐌹𐌻𐌻𐍉𐌽 (spillōn, “to proclaim”).
From Proto-Albanian *palā, from Proto-Indo-European *pel- (“to fold”). Cognate to Romanian pală and Gothic 𐍆𐌰𐌻𐌸𐌰𐌽 (falþan).
Back formation from përpara, from Proto-Albanian *pər-parə-a, from Proto-Indo-European *pr̥H-e/o-s (“before, in front”)
Singularized plural of Proto-Albanian *par continuing Proto-Albanian *para. See Lithuanian periù~perti.
From Proto-Albanian *para.
From Proto-Albanian *pa ̊, from Proto-Indo-European *pós (“directly to, at, after”). Cognate to Ancient Greek πός (pós, “at, to, by”), Old Church Slavonic по (po, “behind, after”).

From Proto-Albanian *pa ̊, from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂(y)- (“to herd, watch over”). Cognate to Sanskrit पति (pā́ti-, “to herd, watch (over)”). A suppletive verb, which occurs in the participle and the aorist and as in the tempora and modi derived from these stems.

From Proto-Albanian *patśiā, from Proto-Indo-European *poti-o- (“to be in possession of something”), which would appear related to *pótis (“lord, owner”), and thus partial cognate with English possess.
From Proto-Albanian *patā, related to petë.
From Proto-Albanian *paitsa, from Proto-Indo-European *peiḱ. Related to Old Norse feigr (“close to death”), Lithuanian pai̇̃kas (“stupid”).
From Proto-Albanian *petslā, a derivative in -l, related to Greek πέκω (péko, “to comb”), Lithuanian pèšti (“to pull, to pluck”), Latin pectem (“comb”).

parole.significato: to stir up water, make liquid turbid
parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *pelkja, from Proto-Indo-European *pelHk-. Compare Latin palūs (“marsh”), Latvian peļķe (“puddle”), and the like.

From Proto-Albanian *pöllə, from Pre-Proto-Albanian *pṓlya (or *pṓlnya), from Proto-Indo-European *pwólh₂o- (“young animal”) + *-(n)ih₂. A connection to Proto-Indo-European *pōlH- (“animal young”) is unlikely due to the singular ablaut relationship. It is also etymologically unrelated to pjell (“to

parole.significato: pair or team of draft animals yoked together
parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *pendā, from Proto-Indo-European *spen-d-. Compare Latvian spanda (“rope binding plow to yoke”), English span, Ossetian fsondz (“yoke”).

From Proto-Albanian *pait- (“gown, cloak”), a derivation with the suffix -kë. Cognate with Gothic 𐍀𐌰𐌹𐌳𐌰 (paida, “tunic, shirt”) and Ancient Greek βαίτη (baítē). A loanword from Gothic is also phonetically possible. Orel considers it a derivation from petë, reconstructing Proto-Albanian *patika.
From Proto-Albanian *pati, from Proto-Indo-European *peth₂- (“to stretch”). Cognate to Greek πετάννυμι (petánnymi, “id”), Latin pateō (“to stretch, to be spread”).

From Old Albanian pii, from Proto-Albanian *pīja, from Proto-Indo-European *pih₃-, *peh₃- probably via the reduplicated form *píph₃eti; compare Greek πίνω (píno), Serbo-Croatian pìti, Italian bere. Orel compares the similarity between Proto-Albanian *pīja and Proto-Slavic *pijǫ; Tomaschek compares T
From Proto-Albanian *pizda, from Proto-Indo-European *písdeh₂ (“vagina”). Cognate with Serbo-Croatian pizda, Old Prussian peisda (“ass”), Persian پیزی (pizi, “ass, anus”).
A form of pidh from Proto-Albanian *pizda, from Proto-Indo-European *písdeh₂ (“pudenda”). Cognate to Lithuanian pyzdà (“pudenda”) and Russian пизда (pizda, “pudenda”)
From Proto-Albanian *pinkā, related to Lithuanian pinklas (“wicker-work”), Latvian pinka (“tuft”), pinkât (“to tousle”).
From Proto-Albanian *pirā, a zero grade form related to Greek πείρω (peíro, “to bore”), Proto-Slavic *perjǫ.
From Proto-Albanian *pitšā, suggested to be from Proto-Indo-European *píts-ih₂ ~ *pits-yéh₂, from *pī́ts (“resin”) + *-ih₂, cognate with Ancient Greek πίσσα (píssa, “pitch, resin”).

A singularized plural of *pitë, from Proto-Albanian *pītu-, related to Lithuanian piẽtus (“noon meal, lunch”), Sanskrit पितु (pitú, “feeding, drink”), Old Irish ithid (“to eat”). Compare pitë (“pastry”).
From Proto-Albanian *pi(m)ita, related to Old Irish éim (“quick, fast”), Old Norse fimr (“id”).
From Proto-Albanian *pelm-, from Proto-Indo-European *pelh₂- (“to push”), the same root of pjell (“to beget, procreate”).

From Proto-Albanian *peka, from Proto-Indo-European *pékʷeti, from *pekʷ- (“to cook, become ripe”). Cognate with Latin coquō, Sanskrit पचति (pácati), Avestan 𐬞𐬀𐬗𐬀𐬌𐬙𐬌 (pacaⁱti), Ancient Greek πέσσω (péssō), Tocharian B päk-, Old Church Slavonic пекѫ (pekǫ), Russian печь (pečʹ).
From Proto-Albanian *peka with irregular development of IE -ḱ-. Cognate to Greek πέκω (péko, “to comb”), Lithuanian pešù, pèšti (“to pull, to pluck”).
From Proto-Albanian *pekā, from pjek, originally 'to comb'.

parole.significato: to bring forth young beasts, cub, whelp, calve, foal
parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *pelna, from Proto-Indo-European *pelh₂- (“to push”). Cognate to Latin pello (“to push”).
From Proto-Albanian *pelā (“child”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pelh₂- (“to drive”). Related to pjell and mbjell.
From Proto-Albanian *perda, from Proto-Indo-European *pérdetor. Cognate with Ancient Greek πέρδομαι (pérdomai), English fart.
From Proto-Albanian *pera, cognate to Lithuanian periù, perti (“to strike”), Proto-Slavic *pьrǫ (“to press”).

parole.significato: to be ruptured, to have hernia
parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *peta (“to be ruptured”), related to Greek πετάννυμι (petánnymi, “to widen”), Latin pateō (“to be open”).

From Proto-Albanian *plaska or Proto-Albanian *plaksa, metathesized from Proto-Indo-European *pel-sḱo-, from Proto-Indo-European *pel- (“covering, hide”) (compare Lithuanian palà (“linen kerchief”), Ancient Greek ἐρυσίπελας (erusípelas, “erysipelas”), German Fell (“fur, pelt”)).
From plak (“to make old”) (from Proto-Albanian *plaka-, from Proto-Indo-European *pl̥h₂-ko-, *pelh₂-) + -em (passive suffix).

Inherited from Proto-Albanian *platˢ̌a-, from Pre-Proto-Albanian *plača-, from Proto-Indo-European *pl̥Hḱyé-, with a semantic change from "to tear" to "to burst". Etymologically close to pëlcas (“to burst”). Cognate to Lithuanian plė́šti (“to burst, crack”), Latvian plêst (“to tear”) and perhaps Ger
From Proto-Albanian *platśiā, from Proto-Indo-European *pleh₁ḱ- (“to tear, rend”). More at plas.
From Proto-Albanian *pleustā, from Proto-Indo-European *plews-, a form of Proto-Indo-European *plus-. Cognate with Latin pūlex, Sanskrit प्लुषि (plúṣi), Armenian լու (lu), all also meaning 'flea'.
A deverbative in -i(m), based on an unattested verb *plyej, from Proto-Albanian *plānja (“to fill”), from Proto-Indo-European *plē (“full”).
From Proto-Albanian *p(i)litja, cognate to Old High German filz, Latin pellis, pilleus, Greek πῖλος (pílos), Proto-Slavic *pьlstь.

parole.significato: reed grass, common reed (Phragmites australis, syn. Phragmites communis)
parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *plūši, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰleus- (compare Lithuanian pl(i)ūši̇̀s, Slovene bljúšč (“black bryony”), Ancient Greek φλέως (phléōs)).
From an earlier *ploe, from Proto-Albanian *plāgā, from Proto-Indo-European *pleh₂k-, *pleh₂g-. Compare Ancient Greek πληγή (plēgḗ, “blow”), Latin plaga (“blow, slaughter”).

From Proto-Albanian *pēpli, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)pel- (“to sliver, split off, splinter off”), allegedly also the source of Old English *popel (“pebble”). Cognate to (Hes.) Ancient Greek πέλλα λίθος (pélla líthos) and Old High German Fels (“rock”). An Albanian formation with (broken) reduplic
From Proto-Albanian *pārdā, deverbative of *perda (“to fart”) (modern pjerdh). More at pjerdh.
From Proto-Albanian *pārā, cognate to Greek πρήσω (príso, “to burn, to set on fire”), Proto-Slavic *parь (“vapour, steam”).

parole.significato: to incline to, cling to, lean
parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *per(i)-anja.
From Proto-Albanian *prainja, from Proto-Indo-European *prāy-, *prēy- (“like, love”). Cognate to Sanskrit प्रिणति (prīṇāti, “to please”) and Gothic frijon (“to love”).
From Proto-Albanian *per apa, *pra apa, the second element being identical with pa.
A combination of two contiguous particles, from Proto-Albanian *pər apə. Compare Proto-Albanian *pər-parə-a > modern përpara (> para).
From Proto-Albanian *prōjena (“front”), from Proto-Indo-European *prō (“forward, in front of, before”). Cognate to Greek πρωΐ (proḯ, “early in the morning”), Old High German fruo (“id”).
From Proto-Albanian *prei, from Proto-Indo-European *prō (“forward, in front of, before”), close to Greek πρωΐ (proḯ, “early, in the morning”), and Old High German fruoi (“early”).
Inherited from Proto-Albanian *prek-, from Proto-Indo-European *prékʷ- (“to take, grasp”).

From Proto-Albanian *p(e)retja, from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“to strike, beat”) (compare Ancient Greek πρίω (príō, “to saw”), Lithuanian per̃ti (“to flog, beat with besom”), Avestan 𐬞𐬆𐬭𐬆𐬝 (pər^ət̰, “strife”)).
From Proto-Albanian *pratja, from Proto-Indo-European *prot- (compare Dutch vroed (“wise, clever”), Lithuanian pràsti (“to understand”)).

From Proto-Albanian *prasa, from Proto-Indo-European *pr̥so-, possibly of non-Indo-European origin. Cognate with Ancient Greek πράσον (práson), Latin porrum, or perhaps borrowed from Ancient Greek. Variants porr and purri are probably from Latin.

From Proto-Albanian *per(i)-era, a prefixal verb, cognate to Hittite [Term?] (/⁠arnumi⁠/, “to move, to shift”), Sanskrit ऋणुते (ṛṇóti, “to arise, to move”), Ancient Greek ὄρνυμι (órnumi, “to stir up”), Latin orior (“to rise”).
From Proto-Albanian *pratja, from Proto-Indo-European *prot- (compare Dutch vroed (“wise, clever”), Lithuanian pràsti (“to understand”)).
From për + ridh, from Proto-Albanian *reida. Compare Ancient Greek ἐρείδω (ereídō, “to push, to prop”).

* From *pron-, suppletive verb, occurring in aorist and (its) participle as well as in the tempora and modi built on those stems. * From Proto-Albanian *p(e)rē-(n-), from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“to bear, lead across”). Cognate to Ancient Greek περάω (peráō, “to penetrate, pierce”).
From Proto-Albanian *pruś-, from Proto-Indo-European *prews- (“to burn up”). Cognate to Latin pruna (“embers”).

A derivative in -kë of Proto-Albanian *priknjā, from Proto-Indo-European *perḱ- (“colored; motley”). Cognate to Sanskrit पृश्नि (pṛśni, “spotted, speckled”), Greek περκνός (perknós, “dark, spotted”), Welsh erch (“spotted”).

The current form is a participle of an obsolete form *pojë, which is a zero-grade suffixed derivation of *h₃ep- (“to work”). Relationship with Hittite [script needed] (ḫappinaḫḫ, “to become rich”) is unclear, even though there have been cases in which an older -i- has become a -u- (ahu (“beech”) is
From Proto-Albanian *pupā, from Proto-Indo-European *pu-p- (“to puff (out/up), swell”). Cognate to Latin puppa (“nipple, teat”) and Latvian pupa (“bean”).
From Proto-Albanian *pukja, from Proto-Indo-European *puḱ- (“press together”) (compare Ancient Greek πύκα (púka, “thickly, strongly”), Avestan 𐬞𐬎𐬯𐬁 (pusā, “headband, diadem”).
From Proto-Albanian *purwa with -th suffix, related to Latvian purvs (“swamp, marsh”), Lithuanian purvas (“filth, dirt”).

parole.significato: light hair, fluff, down, nap, pile
parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *puša, from *puksja, from Proto-Indo-European *pewk- (“covered with hair, bushy”). Related to Sanskrit पुच्छ (púccha, “tail”), Proto-Slavic *puxъ (“down”).

From Proto-Albanian *pútśa/i-, from Pre-Proto-Albanian *púća, from Proto-Indo-European *puḱ- (“press together”) (compare Ancient Greek πύκα (púka, “thickly, strongly”), Avestan 𐬞𐬎𐬯𐬁 (pusā, “headband, diadem”).
From Proto-Albanian *pūkta, from Proto-Indo-European *pūk- (“press together”) (compare Ancient Greek πύκα (púka, “thickly, strongly”), Avestan 𐬞𐬎𐬯𐬁 (pusā, “headband, diadem”).

From an expressive variant in -rr of Proto-Albanian *putso, from Proto-Indo-European *puH- (“rotten, foul”); compare Sanskrit पूयति (pūyati, “stinks, rots”), Latin pus (“discharge from a sore”), Ancient Greek πύθω (púthō, “to rot”). Doublet of fëlliq.
From earlier pëlqenj (third person singular pëlqen), from Proto-Albanian *plakjɔnit, borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin placeō. Compare Romanian plăcea, Italian piacere.

From a phonetic collapse of two Proto-Albanian terms, *per(i) and *pra, the former from Proto-Indo-European *péri (“leading (out) across or around”) and *pér (“through”) (compare Sanskrit परि (parí, “(a)round”)), the latter from Proto-Indo-European *pró (“towards, before”) (compare Ancient Greek πρό
From për + *dhos, from Proto-Albanian *dhātja, derivative of dhe. See përdhe (“underfoot, down(wards), under-/beneath”).
From Proto-Albanian *per-kula, a prefixal derivative of Proto-Indo-European *kʷel- (“to turn”) in zero-grade. Related to sjell. By surface analysis, për- + kul.
From Proto-Albanian *per-ambi. Reanalyzable as për + mbi.

From Proto-Albanian *per-ambi-uptja related to përmbi and ultimately to mbys. The second element *uptja is cognate with Greek ὑπὸ (hupò, “under”), Sanskrit उप (úpa, “towards, near to”) and Gothic uf (“under”).
Goes back to Proto-Albanian *per-medzra, derivative of Proto-Indo-European *h₃meiǵʰ- (“to urinate”).

Prefixed formation of *pël, from Proto-Albanian *pela, from Proto-Indo-European *pelem- (“to swing, shake”) or *pel(H) (“to push”). Compare Latin palpō (“touch, feel, caress, pat”), Ancient Greek πάλλω (pállō, “swing, shake, shake loose”), English feel.
From earlier pësonj (third person singular pëson), from Proto-Albanian *patjɔnit, borrowed from Vulgar Latin *patīre from Latin patī (“suffer”). Compare Romanian păți, Italian patire.

From variant qanj, from older klanj, from Proto-Albanian *klaunja, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱlew- (compare English loud, Czech slout (“to be called, have a reputation”), Greek κλαίω (klaío, “to weep, sob”)).
From Proto-Albanian *ki(i)al-, from Proto-Indo-European *kei-(h2)- (“to put, set in motion”). Possibly, an original nominal formation.
From Proto-Albanian *klapā, a nominal derivative of qep.

parole.significato: to approach, draw near, receive (at home), go away
parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *ki(i)atśi-, from Proto-Indo-European *kei-(h2-) (“to put, set in motion”). Cognate to Ancient Greek κίατο ἐκινεῖτο (kíato ekineîto), Lithuanian kečiù, kėsti (“to stretch”).
From Proto-Albanian *kenja (“new skin”), from Proto-Indo-European *ken- (“new”) (compare Latin recens, Ancient Greek καινός (kainós)).

From Proto-Albanian *kaka or *keka. Related to Lithuanian kankù, kákti (“to seize, reach”), Latvian kacèt (“to grasp”) and Proto-Slavic *čekati (“to expect, to wait”). Alternatively a variant of cek (“to touch”).
From Proto-Albanian *kalba, from Proto-Indo-European *gṷol-bh. Compare Armenian կեղ (keġ, “tumor”). Related to kalb.
From Proto-Albanian *kela, from Proto-Indo-European *kel- (compare English hold, Ancient Greek κέλλω (kéllō, “to drive on”)).

parole.significato: first-person plural simple perfect indicative of jam
parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *klema/e, from *kʷl-e-mé, thematic aorist of Proto-Indo-European *kʷelh₁- (“turn, become”) (compare Ancient Greek ἔπλετο (épleto, “(s)he became”), Old Armenian եղեւ (ełew, “he became”), Tocharian B klutk- (“turns, becomes”)).
From Proto-Albanian *kenagā, from Proto-Indo-European *kn̥h₂ónks. Cognate with Ancient Greek κνηκός (knēkós, “pale yellow”), Latin canicae (“bran”), English honey.

Oryol derives the term from Proto-Albanian *klepa, which itself has various proposed etymologies: * It has been connected to Proto-Slavic *klepati * It may relate to Ancient Greek κάπτω (káptō) and Latin capiō. * Another theory suggests a relationship to Proto-Indo-European *skep- (“to cover”).
From Proto-Albanian *kerktja, related to Proto-Slavic *kьrčь (“stubbed plot”), Latvian kùrkt (“to become empty (of a turnip)”), Old Prussian Churche (“the last sheaf in which the deity hides”).

First attested in 1555 by Buzuku as qesh, as is also seen in all Old Albanian authors, both Gheg and Tosk. From a Common Albanian *qeshë, from Proto-Albanian *kʲeśśi < *kéśśi (i-umlaut) < *káśśi, inherited from Pre-Proto-Albanian *kánśi < *kánsii̯i, from Proto-Indo-European *kn̥Hsei̯éti (“to be plea

parole.significato: first-person singular simple perfect indicative of jam
parole.testo: from Proto-Albanian *kl-esa from Proto-Indo-European *kʷel-
From Proto-Albanian *kaiδa, from Proto-Indo-European *kh₂eyd-. Cognate to Latin caedō (“to cut, hew, lop, fell”).

parole.significato: second-person plural simple perfect indicative of jam
parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *kletā, from *kʷle-té, thematic aorist of Proto-Indo-European *kʷelh₁- (“turn, become”) (compare Ancient Greek ἔπλετο (épleto, “(s)he became”), Old Armenian եղեւ (ełew, “he became”), Tocharian B klutk- (“turns, becomes”)).
From Proto-Albanian *klaitā, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱleytéh₂ (compare Welsh clud (“heap”), Lithuanian šlai̇̃tas (“slope”)), from *ḱlei- (“to slant, lean”). More at qye.
Singularized plural of *qekël, from Proto-Albanian *kekulā, related to Lithuanian kẽkulas (“lump, cluster”), Latvian cekuls (“forelock, cluster”).
From Proto-Albanian *kūpa, from Proto-Indo-European *koupos (“hill”). Cognate to Old Persian kaufa (“mountain”), Old High German hufo (“heap”) and Old English héap (“heap”).
Unknown. Maybe from Proto-Albanian *kapulā, form of *karpudā (hence modern kërpudhë), due to being seen as forest flower and mushroom spirits in folk tales.
