From Proto-Albanian *kla(u)tja, from Proto-Indo-European *kleh₂u- (“nail, pin, hook - instruments, of old use for locking doors”). Cognate to Ancient Greek κλεῖς (kleîs), Latin clāvis, Lithuanian kliaudýti (“to stop, to prevent”).

From Old Albanian kluoj (Buzuku), from Proto-Albanian *klāusnja, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱlows-, from *ḱlew-. Compare English listen, Proto-Slavic *slušati (“to listen”), Ancient Greek κλύω (klúō, “to hear, listen to”).
From Proto-Albanian *klusla, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱleuH- (compare German lauter (“pure”), Lithuanian šlúoti (“to sweep”), Ancient Greek κλύζω (klúzō, “to wash”)).

From Proto-Albanian *klaina, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱloi-n-os (“slanting, askew”) (compare Irish claon, Gothic 𐌷𐌻𐌰𐌹𐌽𐌴 (hlainē)), from *ḱlei- (“to slant, lean”) (compare English lean, Lithuanian šliẽti, Serbo-Croatian slȏj (“layer”)).
From Proto-Albanian *kūla, from Proto-Indo-European *kh₂u-l (“outgrowth; hernia”) (compare Lithuanian dialect kū́la(s), Serbo-Croatian kȉla, Old Norse haull).
From Proto-Albanian *kewira. Cognate to Ancient Greek κοέω (koéō, “to note”), Latin caveō (“to be aware”).

A derivative of an unattested verb *qyej (“to blunt”), from Proto-Albanian *kēnja, from Proto-Indo-European *ken- (“to scratch, to cut”). For the semantic development compare Latin obtũsus (“blunt”) from obtundere (“to beat”). See also qytë.

parole.significato: city, particularly (politics, historical) as a former administrative level
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Albanian *k'iwytéti, from older *kiwitáti, which was borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin cīvitātem, with loss of the -v-. Compare Romanian cetate.
Together with qyrë, derived from an unattested verb *qyej (“to blunt”), from Proto-Albanian *kēnja, from Proto-Indo-European *ken- (“to scratch, to cut”).
From Proto-Albanian *ranka (“gatherings”), close to Lithuanian rankà (“hand”), paranká (“gathering”), renkù, riñkti (“to gather”), Proto-Slavic *rǫka (“hand”).

Suppletive aorist of bie; from Proto-Albanian *rauša, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃rew-s-e-ti, from *h₃rew- (“run, hurry”) (compare Latin ruō (“to rush; collapse”), Ancient Greek ὀρούω (oroúō, “to hurry”), Czech ruch (“movement”)).

From Proto-Albanian *rina, a noun derived from the Proto-Indo-European verb *h₃rinéHti whence Albanian rij (“to make humid”), from the root *h₃reyH- (“move, flow, boil”). It is likely morphologically identical with Illyrian ῥινός (rhinós, “mist”). Further related to Sanskrit रिणाति (riṇā́ti, “to mak
From Proto-Albanian *raida, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂rey- (“reason, count”). Cognate with Latin rātiō (“reason, judgment”), Old Norse ráða, English read.
From Proto-Albanian *(a)rẽndV-, from Pre-Proto-Albanian *aréntu-, from Proto-Indo-European *HrenHtu- (“running”).

Continues an umlauticized Proto-Albanian *raupā, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁reyp- (“to tear, to break”). Cognate to Old Norse rauf (“pit”), Lithuanian raupiù, raũpti (“to hollow out”). Also possibly an ultimate doublet of rrip.

parole.significato: to keep away, give a direction
parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *rašta, from Proto-Indo-European *ros-, *res-, *erH- (“to be still, rest”). Compare Gothic 𐍂𐌰𐍃𐍄𐌰 (rasta, “mile”), Old English ræst (“rest, quiet”).

From Proto-Albanian *rinja, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃rinéHti (“move”), present of *h₃er- (“to move, stir, rise, spring”). Related to re (“cloud(s)”), Proto-Slavic *rinǫti (“push, shove”), Aeolic Greek ὀρῑ́νω (orī́nō, “to move”).
Inherited from Proto-Albanian *rika, based on an onomatopoeic verb, close to Lithuanian ri̇̀kti (“to cry”).
From Proto-Albanian *rauba, from Proto-Indo-European *Hrowb-, *Hrewb-, variant of *Hrewp- (“to break”). Related to Gothic 𐍂𐌰𐌿𐍀𐌾𐌰𐌽 (raupjan, “to reap”) and Old High German roufen (“id”).
From Proto-Albanian *srauga, related to Lithuanian srauga (“id”), srúoga (“skin, hank; tuft, hairlock”).
From Proto-Albanian *wragska, from Proto-Indo-European *wr̥h₁ǵ-sḱé-ti, from *wreh₁ǵ-.

A pluralized form of rangë, from Proto-Albanian *ranka (“gatherings”), with -ull suffix, close to Lithuanian rankà (“hand”), paranká (“gathering”), renkù, riñkti (“to gather”), Proto-Slavic *rǫka (“hand”).
From Proto-Albanian *rapa, denominative of *repa (“to peel, strip off”) (modern rrjep), in reference to a tree's outer bark sheds. More at rrjep.
Pluralized form, from Proto-Albanian *raka, close to Latvian rakt (“to dig”), Lithuanian ràkti (“to hollow out, to pick”).
From Proto-Albanian *wragšta, from the verbal stem rrah (“to beat. strike”). Alternatively a prefixed form of asht (“bone”).
From Proto-Albanian *raθ, diminutive of Proto-Indo-European *Hrot-h₂-ó- (“wheel”), from *Hreth₂- (“to run”). The origin of -th is unclear
From Proto-Albanian *raibā, close to Latvian raibs (“multicolored, variegated”), Lithuanian ràibas (“id”).
From Proto-Albanian *raiba (“multicolored”), attested in rrebe.
From Proto-Albanian *wragā, related to Ancient Greek ῥαγή (rhagḗ, “split, cleft”), ῥήγνυμι (rhḗgnumi, “to break, to split”).
From Proto-Albanian *arn-enja, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂res-. Cognate to Ancient Greek ἀρνέομαι (arnéomai, “to deny, refuse”).
From Proto-Albanian *raika, related to Lithuanian reikà (“need”), reikti (“to be necessary”), riekti (“to cut, to plow the fallow land”). Possibly related to rrok.

From Proto-Albanian *ratsa, from *rat(i)tsa, from pre-Albanian *róth₂iḱom, diminutive of Proto-Indo-European *Hrot-h₂-ó- (“wheel”), from *Hret- (“to roll”) (compare Lithuanian rãtas, German Rad). Plural formation of rrath.
From Proto-Albanian *wribā, from Proto-Indo-European *werb- (“to turn, to bend”). Close to Lithuanian virbas (“rod, birch-rod, twig”), Proto-Slavic *vьrba (“pussy-willow”).
Plurale tantum; from Proto-Albanian *wrimi, from Proto-Indo-European *wr̥mis (“worm”) (compare English worm, Ancient Greek ῥόμος (rhómos, “woodworm”), Romanian vierme).
From Proto-Albanian *repa, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rep- (compare Ancient Greek ἐρέπτομαι (eréptomai), Latin rapere, Lithuanian aprépti).

Plurale tantum; plural of *rodhë, from Proto-Albanian *wrādzā, from Proto-Indo-European *wreh₂ǵʰ- (“thorn”) (compare Ancient Greek ῥᾱχός (rhākhós, “thornbush; wattled fence”), Lithuanian rǎžas (“dry stalk, stubble; prong”), Middle Irish fraig (“needle”)).

Disputed. *Possibly from Proto-Albanian *rēg-n-, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃reǵ-. Compare Ancient Greek ὀρέγω (orégō, “to extend, stretch”). * Topalli supports Mann's proposal of a borrowing from Latin remaneo (“to remain”) and rejects Meyer and Orel's etymologies because they ignore the Gheg form
Inherited from Proto-Albanian *wrāgnja, related to Ancient Greek ῥήγνυμι (rhḗgnumi, “to break, to tear”).
From Proto-Albanian *ruj́ā, from Proto-Indo-European *rou̯ǵ-ah₂- < *rou̯ǵ-. Cognate to Latin rūga.
From Proto-Albanian *wrubna. Cognate to Lithuanian virbas (“branch, shoot”), Ancient Greek ράμνος (rámnos, “thorny bush”).
From Proto-Albanian *wrunjā, femininized form from Proto-Indo-European *wr̥h₁nós, oblique of *wr̥h₁ḗn (“lamb”) (compare Greek αρνί (arní), Persian بره (barre)).

* From Proto-Albanian *rāguša, from Proto-Indo-European *sr̥h₂gós (“berry”), oblique of *sróh₂gs (compare Ancient Greek ῥώξ (rhṓx, “grape”), Latin frāgum (“strawberry”)). * From Proto-Albanian *rušša-, from Ancient Greek ῥώξ (rhṓx).

From Proto-Albanian *raṷīnja, *raudinja, from Proto-Indo-European *HrewdH-. Compare Sanskrit रोदिति (róditi, “to weep”), Latin rūdō (“to shout, cry”), Lithuanian raudà (“weeping”), Proto-Slavic *rydati (“to weep”).
From Proto-Albanian *srūmā, from Proto-Indo-European *srow-m-eh₂, from *srew- (“to flow”). Doublet of rrymë; see there for cognates.

From Proto-Albanian *srūmā, from Proto-Indo-European *srow-m-eh₂, from *srew- (“to flow”). Compare English stream, German Strom (“current, stream”), Icelandic straumur (“current, stream, torrent, flood”), Ancient Greek ῥεῦμα (rheûma, “stream, flow”). Doublet of rrym.

parole.significato: a long, narrow strip of land
parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *wrūpina, from *wrīpa (“belt”).

Uncertain. Three possible theories: * from Proto-Albanian *wretšönj-, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱens-, forming a doublet of them, * from Early Proto-Albanian *wrefenj-, from Ancient Greek φαίνω (phaínō), * from Proto-Albanian *refenj-, from Latin referre through Vulgar Latin
According to Orel, from Proto-Albanian *raimuljā, cognate with Lithuanian ráibas (“multicolored, varied”).
Diminutive of rrënd. Via apocope and final devoicing, from *rrëndë-zë, from Proto-Albanian *r̄ândə-dᶻə.

From Proto-Albanian *wradnjā, from pre-Albanian *wr̥h₂dnih₂-, from Proto-Indo-European *wr̥h₂dnyo-, from *wréh₂ds. Compare Latin rādīx and Ancient Greek ῥάδιξ (rhádix). Ultimately a doublet of radhiqe through the Proto-Indo-European root.
Singularized form of original *rugë, from Proto-Albanian *ruga, from Proto-Indo-European *reu-g- (“to tear, to pull”), close to Lithuanian rúgti (“to become sour”).
From Proto-Albanian *wrunga, from Proto-Indo-European *ṷreng- (“to be bent”). Cognate to Lithuanian rungúoti (“to wind, to bend”).

From Proto-Albanian *rūtja, from Proto-Indo-European *reṷə-. Cognate to Latin ruo (“to rush down, to bring down”), Proto-Slavic *ryti, Lithuanian ráuti (“to tear, to pull”), Egyptian rish (“high leader, boss”).
From Proto-Albanian *raunta, from Proto-Albanian *rauša (“to fall”) (modern rashë). More at rashë.

parole.significato: negates the meaning of the modified verb: not, don't
parole.testo: Short for së (“not”) (not to be confused with adjectival article së and conjunction se (“that (as), when”)). This is in turn from Proto-Albanian *tśe, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷíd (“that (relative)”)

From Proto-Albanian *tswa(n)-ma, a derivative in -mo of the Proto-Indo-European word for dog, otherwise unattested. Compare Sanskrit श्वन् (śvā́), Ancient Greek κύων (kúōn), Old Irish cú and Lithuanian šuõ. For sense development compare Proto-Slavic *govьno (“excrement”) from *gʷṓws (“cow”).
From Proto-Albanian *tšerkā, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷer- (“to make, to build”). Cognate to Sanskrit करोति (karóti, “to build”) and Lithuanian kùrti.
From Proto-Albanian *tśe(i), *tśi from Proto-Indo-European *kʷe-, *kʷ(e)i- (“how, what”). Interrogative and relative pronoun, especially in connection with a preposition.
From Proto-Albanian *śaktā, from Proto-Indo-European *sēk-teh₂-, from Proto-Indo-European *sek- (“to cut”). Cognate to Latin secula (“sickle”), sacena (“pick-axe of the pontifix”).
From Proto-Albanian *ampa, from Proto-Indo-European *ap-. Cognate to Ancient Greek ἅπτω (háptō, “to seize, grasp”), Sanskrit आप्नोति (āpnòti, “to reach”).

A prefixal derivative in -es, also attested in pres (“to cut, carve”), with original meaning 'to cut off, divide, separate in a share'. The origin of the first component, sh-, is unclear, though has been compared to English sell and thus Proto-Indo-European *selh₁- (“to take”). However, Orel later p

From Proto-Albanian *śūh, from Proto-Indo-European *suh₂-s < *sh₂ew- (“to rain”). Compare Ancient Greek ὕει (húei, “it rains”), Hittite [script needed] (ishuwāi, “(s)he pours out, spills”), Tocharian B suwaṃ (“it rains”).

From Proto-Albanian *sūadja, from Proto-Indo-European *sweh₂d- (“sweet”). Compare Latin suavis, Ancient Greek ἡδύς (hēdús), Sanskrit स्वादु (svādu), English sweet. Attributed instead to a Low Latin *suāvilia by Orel.
From Proto-Albanian *iš-gabā, prefixed form of *gabā (whence gabonjë), from Proto-Indo-European *kobuǵos (compare English hawk, Latin capys (“bird of prey”), and Russian ко́бец (kóbec, “falcon”)).
From Proto-Albanian *skaka, from Proto-Indo-European *skek- (“to jump, be agile”). Cognate to Old Norse skaga (“to protrude”), Proto-Slavic *skokъ (“jump”).
From Proto-Albanian *kall-, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kel- (“bend”). Cognate to Latin calco (“to spur”) and Lithuanian atsikalti (“to lean against (upon)”).

parole.significato: to bring down, drag, roll, charm (of fairies)
parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *skala, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kelH- (“to cut, split, chop”). Cognate to Ancient Greek σκάλλω (skállō, “to chop”), Lithuanian skeliù (“to split”) and Old Norse skilja (“id”).
From Proto-Albanian *iš-gardā, etymologically connected with gardh (“fence”). Connected to Romanian zgardă.
From Proto-Albanian *skatja. Cognate to Latin scateō (“to stream, to flow out”), Lithuanian skantù, skàsti (“to spring, to jump”), and perhaps to Ancient Greek σκάξω (skáxō, “to be lame”).
From Proto-Albanian *̥kalim-, from Proto-Indo-European *kel- (“to bend”). Albanian formation with -m(ë).

From kep. Beside shqep, an Albanian formation with the intensive prefix sh-, from Proto-Albanian *skaipa. Compare Old Norse skífa (“to split”), Old Frisian skīvia (“to divide”) and perhaps English shape.

A parallel form is shkrep, continuing Proto-Albanian *krepa (“body”), cognate to Sanskrit कृप् (ḱṛp, “shape, beautiful appareance”), Latin corpus (“body”), Old High German hrēf (“belly”). Similar sense development in Germanic (compare Gothic galeiks (“like”), from leik (“body”)).
Inherited from Proto-Albanian *skalatjā, derived from shkel.
From Proto-Albanian *is-kametjā, a derivative of kmesë.
From Proto-Albanian *skrabā, from Proto-Indo-European *skrobʰ- (compare Latin scrobis (“pit”), Old English screpan (“to scratch”), Latvian skrabt (“to scratch, plane”), Polish scrobać).

parole.significato: to flash, tone, to strike (till sparks fly off), an idea comes to one’s mind
parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *krep-, from Proto-Indo-European *ker-p-, *krep- (“to crack, crash”), an onomatopoeic root. Cognate to Latin crepo (“to resound, ring, tone”). A formation with the prefix sh-.
From Proto-Albanian *skalbā. Cognate to Old Norse skalpr (“ship”), skelpa (“grimace”) and Middle High German scholpe (“mussel”).

From Proto-Albanian *sākska, from Proto-Indo-European *sekʷ- (“to see”) Compare English see, Greek ἕπομαι (épomai). Ultimately a doublet of shikoj via this root. Aorist pashë may be from Proto-Indo-European *spéḱyeti (“to look at”) (compare English spy, Latin specere). However, Orel rejects this ety
From Proto-Albanian *sjāra, related to Hittite [Term?] (/⁠isḫii̯a⁠/, “to bind”), Sanskrit स्यति (syáti, “to bind”), Lithuanian sejú, sjẽti (“id”).

From Proto-Albanian *śēś-, from Proto-Indo-European *seh1i- (“to sift, riddle”). Cognate to Ancient Greek σᾶσις (sâsis, “sieve”). The sh- comes from ś- by regressive assimiliation, with the second -ś- of the next syllable. A loanword from the Greek cannot be excluded.
From Proto-Albanian *sjāutā, from Proto-Indo-European *sau̯i̯eto, with a metathesis.
Prefixed form of *pat, from Proto-Albanian *pata, cognate to Greek πίπτω (pípto, “to fall”), Sanskrit पतति (pátati, “to fly, to sour”). Alternatively from shpatull (“shoulder”).

Gheg variant of Tosk shpih, from Proto-Albanian *dis- and *pīska, from Proto-Indo-European *pih₁-sḱe/o-, from *peh₁-i- (“to taunt”) (compare Old English fēon (“to hate”), Sanskrit पीयति (pī́yati, “to blame, abuse”)).
Continues Proto-Albanian *peikska.
A prefixed form with sh-. From Proto-Albanian *pēri-, from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“to bear, lead across, penetrate”). Cognate to Ancient Greek πείρω (peírō, “to get through, pierce”).
From Proto-Albanian *pāra. Cognate to Ancient Greek περάω (peráō, “to penetrate”), Sanskrit पिपर्ति (piparti, “bring over, save”).
Inherited from Proto-Albanian *sprēujā. Cognate to Middle High German spræjen (“to be scattered”), from Proto-Germanic *sprēwjan.
From Proto-Albanian *eś-pulā, from Proto-Indo-European *pl̥h₂-eh₂ < *pleh₂- (“to spread out”). Compare Ancient Greek παλάμη (palámē, “palm”), Latin palma.
From Proto-Albanian *skera, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (compare Latvian skara (“curly fur”), Polish skóra (“hide”)).

From dialectal shkjerr, from Proto-Albanian *skera, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker(H)- (compare English shear, Ancient Greek κείρω (keírō, “to shear; ravage, destroy”), Lithuanian ski̇̀rti (“to cut, divide”)).
From shkjerrë, variant of shtjerrë. From Proto-Albanian *(ś-)kerā, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)Ker(H)- (“to spring, leap”). Compare Old Norse skirja (“young cow”). More at shtjerrë.

parole.significato: to turn off, switch off, deactivate
parole.testo: Loss of /b/ in Standard Albanian shqim and Gheg Albanian shkym. From Old Albanian shqymb, from Proto-Albanian *skūmba. Cognate to Gothic *𐍃𐌺𐌹𐌿𐌱𐌰𐌽 (*skiuban, “cast, shove”) and 𐌰𐍆𐍃𐌺𐌹𐌿𐌱𐌰𐌽 (afskiuban, “cast away, shove off”), Lithuanian skumbù and skùbti (“to hurry up”) and Proto-Slavic *skuti. See shq

From Proto-Albanian *əśkʲípe, from Pre-Proto-Albanian *əśkʲípii̯ā, from Proto-Indo-European *eǵʰs-kép-ii̯eh₂-, with a semantic change from "that which chops (with a beak)" to "eagle". Connected to qep (“beak”), kep (“to hew; peck”), and potentially to pjek (“to hit, touch”), all from the root Proto-

parole.significato: sense (ability to perceive reality through the organs)
parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *skeitsā, from Proto-Indo-European *skey- (“to split, to dissect”). Compare Latin sciō (“to can, know, understand”).

parole.significato: to distinguish, discern; know (someone/something from others, even from far away)
parole.testo: From sh- (out, ex-) + quaj (name, call), verb quaj from Old Albanian kluoj, from Proto-Albanian *klāusnja, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱléwos (“to hear”).

The conservative form is shklyej. Orel further reconstructs Proto-Albanian *skānja, from Proto-Indo-European *sken- (“to split off”) (cf. English skin, Breton scant (“fish scales”)), although this is impossible due to the lack of a required *-l-, and required *ō instead of *ā.

From Proto-Albanian *skūmba. Cognate to Gothic *𐍃𐌺𐌹𐌿𐌱𐌰𐌽 (*skiuban, “cast, shove”) and 𐌰𐍆𐍃𐌺𐌹𐌿𐌱𐌰𐌽 (afskiuban, “cast away, shove off”) (cf. English shove, German schieben), Lithuanian skumbù and skùbti (“to hurry up”), Proto-Slavic *skuti (cf. Bulgarian ску́бя (skúbja, “to pluck, tear”), Macedonian ску
From Proto-Albanian *stagā, from Proto-Indo-European *stogʰ- (compare English stake, Lithuanian stãgaras (“long stalk”), Serbo-Croatian stȏg (“haystack, rick”)).
From Proto-Albanian *stan-, from Proto-Indo-European *steh₂- (“to stand, set, lay”).

parole.significato: wheat or corn whose grain is still milky
parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *stalpa, from *stela corresponding to modern shtjell, from which root also shqile (“rennet, rennet stomach”), also otherwise also connected to gjalpë (“butter”)—Erat leaves the origin open.
From Proto-Albanian *stalba, from Proto-Indo-European *stolb- (compare Old Norse stolpi (“beam, girder”), Lithuanian stũlbas (“post, pole”), Proto-Slavic *stъlbъ (“post, pole”)).

parole.significato: crossbeam, board (used as a door hinge)
parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *stalkā, from Proto-Indo-European *stel- (“stalk, stem”). Cognate to Ancient Greek στέλος (stélos, “beam”), Sanskrit स्थल (sthála, “elevation”), Middle Low German stale (“post”). Also compare Old English stalu (“wooden upright”) (English stalk), Danish stilk.

parole.significato: to wind up, to coil, to clew up
parole.testo: Formed on the model of the original causatives: *śtalei < *stol-eio/e-. From Proto-Albanian *śtal-, from Proto-Indo-European *stel- (“set/put (up)”).
From Proto-Albanian *stanga related to Old Norse stinga (“to put, to stick”), Lithuanian sténgiu, sténgti (“to be able”), stiñgti (“to become hard”) and Latvian stiñgt (“id”).
From Proto-Albanian *stara. Cognate to Ancient Greek στερεός (stereós, “tough, hard”), Old Norse starr (“stiff”), Lithuanian sterti (“to become stiff”).
From Proto-Albanian *śtat-, from Proto-Indo-European *steh₂- (“to stay, stand, put, lay”). Cognate to Latin status (“standing, stan”), Russian стать (statʹ, “structure of the body”).

From Proto-Albanian *staiga (Orel's notation), from Proto-Indo-European *stóygʰos (“way”), from *steygʰ-. Cognate to Ancient Greek στοῖχος (stoîkhos, “line, row”), Gothic 𐍃𐍄𐌰𐌹𐌲𐌰 (staiga, “way”), Latvian staĩgât (“to walk”) or Latvian pastaĩga (“a walk”).
From Proto-Albanian *sterjā, from Proto-Indo-European *ster- (“barren”) (compare English steer, Greek στείρος (steíros)). Doublet of shtjerrë.

parole.significato: to put in, stick in, insert
parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *sterja, from *sterje/o, from Proto-Indo-European *sterh₃-. Compare English strew.
From Proto-Albanian *śter-, from Proto-Indo-European *sterh₃- (“to spread, scatter, bring down”).

parole.significato: to wind up, develop, sling, loosen
parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *śtel-, from Proto-Indo-European *stel- (“to set, lay, put, place”). Cognate to Ancient Greek στέλλω (stéllō, “to arrange, set, lay”).
From Proto-Albanian *stāga, related to shtagë.

From Proto-Albanian *stānja, from Proto-Indo-European *stnéh₂ti, nasal present of Proto-Indo-European *steh₂- (“to stand”). Cognate to Latin stō, Old High German stān, Lithuanian stóju and Proto-Slavic *stati.
From Proto-Albanian *strapa, cognate to Middle High German straf (“tight”), Lithuanian parstrapi̇̀nti (“to drag oneself back”).
From Proto-Albanian *stragā, cognate to Proto-Germanic. Compare Middle High German strac (“tight”), Old English strec (“hard, strong”).
From Proto-Albanian *streka, from Proto-Indo-European *ster- (“unclean liquid, manure”). Compare Latin stercus (“excrement”), Breton stroñk, Welsh trwnc (“id”).
From Proto-Albanian *straupa, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)rowpos. Compare Serbo-Croatian strup (“scab”), Lithuanian raupai̇̃ (“smallpox”). Possibly a singularized plural of shtrap.

parole.significato: to stretch, stretch out, spread, extend, sprawl
parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *strinja, from Proto-Indo-European *sterh₃-, *streh₃- (“to spread, scatter, bring down”). Related to Latin sternō and Ancient Greek στόρνυμι (stórnumi).
Deverbative formation with the suffix -kë, from the aorist stem Proto-Albanian *štrov-kə of shtroj.
From Proto-Albanian *śt(a)rē-, from Proto-Indo-European *sterh₃- (“to spread, scatter, floar”). Cognate to Old Church Slavonic прострѣти (prostrěti, “to spread”).

parole.significato: narrow runway near gateway of a pen or hold where sheep, goats, or cattle are milked
parole.testo: Uncertain; possibly: * from shtrij (“to spread, stretch”) + unproductive suffix -ungë, compare ballungë, shtëllungë, * from Proto-Albanian *strungā, from Proto-Indo-European *strn̥gʰ-éh₂, from *strengʰ- (“to twist together”), * or dissimilated from Proto-Albanian *satrunkā, from Proto-Indo-European

parole.significato: kind of sand stone (made of volcano ashes used in construction), pumice, tuff
parole.testo: Unknown. Maybe from Proto-Albanian *štuop-se, from Proto-Indo-European *st(y)oy-. Compare Old English stān (“stone”).

parole.significato: column or blanket of smoke or vapour
parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *stula- or *stulwa + -ung, close to Russian столб (stolb), Lithuanian stul̃bas, Latvian stulbs, Old Norse stolpi (“pillar”). Related to shtyllë.
From archaic and dialectal shtynj, from Proto-Albanian *stūdnja, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)tewd- (“push, thrust”) (compare German stoßen, Latin studeō).
From Proto-Albanian *ś(t)ripenī̆, from Proto-Indo-European *serp- (“to creep, crawl”). Originally the plural of gjarpër.
From Proto-Albanian *uka, from Proto-Indo-European *u̯ek (“to bend”). Cognate to Sanskrit वच्यते (vacyáte, “to fly up”).

Possibly from Proto-Albanian *kśul(V)n, from a regional Proto-Indo-European *kséw-lo-, based on comparison to Ancient Greek ξύλον (xúlon, “timber, beam”) and Proto-Slavic *šulo (“wooden post, pole”). Most support a Proto-Albanian origin, whereas Orel, on the other hand, considers a South Slavic orig

From Proto-Albanian *śur-(nā), from Proto-Indo-European *seHur (“to piss, make water”). Cognate to Ancient Greek οὐρέω (ouréō, “to piss”) and Hittite [Term?] (/⁠sēẖur⁠/, “urine”). The hardening of the inlaut may have expressive reasons. A further connection to Proto-Germanic *sūraz (“sour”) and Lith
From an earlier shërbenj (third person singular shërben), from Proto-Albanian *śerbi̯ɔnit, borrowed from Vulgar Latin *serbiō, from Latin serviō.

parole.significato: how; in what way; in what state
parole.testo: Varying reconstructions. Orel descends it from Proto-Albanian *tšei, Matzinger from Proto-Albanian *čī. Ultimately from instrumental Proto-Indo-European *kʷí-h₁. Compare Latin qui (“how, why”), Old English hwȳ, hwī (“why”). An interrogative and relative pronoun, especially in connection with a prepo
From Proto-Albanian *čīlā-, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷih₁-tl-éh₂, from *kʷyeh₁- (“to rest; rest, peace”). Compare English while, Latin tranquillus, Sanskrit चिर (cirá).
From Proto-Albanian *tˢjiwéte, from Pre-Albanian (post-Proto-Indo-European) *ḱyey wétes, dative-locative compound, literally ‘this year’. Same type of construction as sot, sonte. More at vit, vjet.

From Proto-Albanian *tšela, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷél-e-ti, from *kʷel- (“to turn, twist”). Cognate to Ancient Greek πέλω (pélō, “to be in motion”), Tocharian A köllāš (“bring”), preterit śël, Old Norse hvel (“wheel”). Somehow, the archaic form has generated Arbëresh Albanian qellënj with an ap
From earlier *kanj, from Proto-Albanian *kanja. Compare Latvian atkan (“again”).

Syncope of Old Albanian sonëte, from the contraction of the syntagma *só nate, from Proto-Albanian *ti̯ā́ náta, from Pre-Proto-Albanian *tei̯i̯ā́ náta(i̯)i, from Proto-Indo-European *tes(m)i̯áh₂i nékʷti. Same type of construction as sot, sivjet. More at natë.

From Proto-Albanian *tˢjānaktāi, from Pre-Albanian (post-Proto-Indo-European *ḱyeh₂ nékʷtey, dative-locative compound, literally ‘this night’. Cognate with Lithuanian šią̃nakt (“tonight”) and Latvian šonakt (“tonight”).

From Proto-Albanian *tšārnā, from pre-Albanian *kʷērsneh₂, from Proto-Indo-European *kr̥snós (“black”) (compare Lithuanian kir̃snas, Russian чёрный (čórnyj), Pashto [script needed] (kī́n, “left”)). Compare also Romanian cioară; Aromanian cioarã, tsoarã; Friulian çore; Tarantino ciola: Neapolitan and

From a contraction of the syntagma *só diti "on this day", from Proto-Albanian *ti̯ā́ dī́ti, from Proto-Indo-European *tes(m)i̯áh₂i dih₂ti. Same type of construction as sonte, sivjet. See also ditë, which is related to the second component.
From Proto-Albanian *praka, from Proto-Indo-European *pro-ko. Compare Latin procerēs (“protruding beams”), Breton a-raok (“forward”).
From Proto-Albanian *dis-kekja, prefixed form of Proto-Albanian *kekja. Related to Lithuanian kékos (“swing”), Latvian ķekut (“to swing”).
From Proto-Albanian *dis-tapa. Cognate to Old Norse Þefja (“to stamp, ram”).
From Proto-Albanian *tšukā. Cognate to Sanskrit सूच (śûka, “awn of grain, spike of insect”), Avestan 𐬯𐬏𐬐𐬁 (sūkā, “needle”).
From Proto-Albanian *tšula, a zero grade of sjell. Compare Armenian սլանամ (slanam, “to rush on, to dart”), Russian слать (slatʹ, “to send”).
From Proto-Albanian *tˢumba, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱumbʰ- (compare English hump, Latin incumbere (“to lie down”), Ancient Greek κύμβη (kúmbē, “bowl; boat”)).
From Proto-Albanian *tsupa, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱupos (compare English hip, Ancient Greek κύβος (kúbos, “vertebra, hollow before the hip (in cattle)”)).
From Proto-Albanian *tsurma, from Proto-Indo-European *k̑r̥mo-. Compare Lithuanian širmas (“grey”).
From archaic and dialectal shutë, from Proto-Albanian *tšuktā, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱuk- (compare Lithuanian šùkos (“comb; heckle”) (pl.)). Compare Romanian ciută.
From Proto-Albanian *asī, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃ókʷih₁ (dual), from singular *h₃okʷ- (compare Lithuanian aki̇̀s, Ancient Greek ὄσσε (ósse, “eyes”), English eye).
From Proto-Albanian *talna, related to Lithuanian ti̇̀lti (“to become silent”), Old Irish tuilid (“to sleep”), Proto-Slavic *toliti (“to persuade, to make quiet”).
From Proto-Albanian *talā. Cognate to Ancient Greek τῆλις (têlis, “fenugreek”), Lithuanian atólas (“grass stubble”).
From amë, with a prefix t-, continuing Proto-Albanian *at-.
From amë, with a prefix t- (same as in etymology 1), continuing Proto-Albanian *at-.
From Proto-Albanian *tangā (“thick forest”), close to Lithuanian tankù, Old Norse þéttr (“thick”). Possibly a derivative of tangë, with a semantic innovation.
Inherited from Proto-Albanian *tangā, ultimately from Proto-Slavic *tǫga (“grief”).

The first element is from Proto-Albanian *ta ̊, from Proto-Indo-European *to- (“it”). Cognate to Lithuanian tadà (“then, thereupon”) and Sanskrit तदा (ta-dā́, “then”). The second element is from Proto-Albanian *nu, from Proto-Indo-European *nu. Cognate to English now.
From Proto-Albanian *taurāka, from *taura (“bull”) (modern ter). More at ter.
A o- grade continuing Proto-Albanian *tara, related to tjerr.

parole.significato: now, currently, at present, presently, just now, this moment, from now on; momentarily
parole.testo: Cognate to Albanian tashti (“now”). A combination of t- + ash (resp. t- + ashi; t- + ashti; t- + esh). Second element (-ash; -ashi; -ashti) of dubious origins. According to Orel, from Proto-Albanian *to-su (a locative form of the pronominal stem Proto-Albanian *to), derived from Proto-Indo-European

parole.significato: now, currently, at present, presently, just now, this moment, from now on; momentarily
parole.testo: Compound of tash (moment (now)) + ti (-arily), cognate to Albanian tash (“now”), tashi (“id”), tesh (“id”) and ndashti (“at/in this moment”). From Proto-Albanian *to-su, locative form of pronominal stem Proto-Albanian *to- (resp. Proto-Albanian *ta ̊). From Proto-Indo-European *to- (“it”). Cognate t

With assimilation of occlusives, continues *katëpjetë, an antonym of përpjetë, with katë from Proto-Albanian *kata related to Greek κάτα (káta, “down”). It also occurs in Greek κατα-πΐπτω (kata-pḯpto, “fall down”).

From Proto-Albanian *te-k(u), from Proto-Indo-European *to- (“it”). Governs the nominative determinative, due to its relatively recent use as a preposition and its origin as a shortened form of Albanian *te-k(u).
From Proto-Albanian *tai e, a parallel formation to tëhu.

Inherited from Proto-Albanian *tai ̊, from *te ku (< *tóy- kʷu- (“there where”)), from Proto-Indo-European *to- (“it”). Also occurs as a preposition with the meaning ‘ad, apud, prope, versus’. See also te.
From Proto-Albanian *taura, from Proto-Indo-European *táwros.
From Proto-Albanian *tarsja, from *torseje, from Proto-Indo-European *torséyeti (“to make dry”), from *ters- (“dry”). Cognate to Sanskrit तृष्यति (tṛṣyati), Latin torreo, Old Norse þerra.
From Proto-Albanian *taišā, continuing Proto-Indo-European *tetḱ-. Related to Lithuanian tiesiù, tiēsti (“to make right, to build”) and perhaps Ancient Greek τέκτων (téktōn, “artisan”).
From Proto-Albanian *teuša, from Proto-Indo-European *teus-, related to Latvian tusêt, tust (“to pant”).

From Proto-Albanian *taksjā, from Proto-Indo-European *tetḱ- (“to hew”) (compare Lithuanian tašýti (“to hew”), Latin texere (“to weave”), Sanskrit तक्षति (takșati, “to carpenter, cut”)). Related to tollë.
From *(a)te + -të, from Proto-Albanian *atṓ-tā, from Pre-Proto-Albanian *atˢtṓ-tā, from *h₂oḱtóh₁-t-, a suffixed term deriving from Proto-Indo-European *oḱtṓw, meaning "group of eight".

parole.significato: a small double-edged carpenter’s tool with an axe and a chisel side
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Albanian *ϑat(Vr)-, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱeh₃-(i-) (“to sharpen, whet”). Cognate with Latin catus (“acutus, acute”) and Sanskrit शित (śitá-).
Perhaps from Proto-Albanian *ϑau-, from Proto-Indo-European *seh₂us- (“dry, arid”). Oryol relates the term to Lithuanian saũsas, Marrgu sōr, and Ancient Greek αὖος (aûos).
Masculine doublet of thekë; from Proto-Albanian *tsaka, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱokh₂o- (“branch”) (compare Lithuanian šakà, Serbo-Croatian soha).

Alteration of variant cark, from Proto-Albanian *tsarka, from *ḱorH-ko-, o-grade from Proto-Indo-European *ḱer- (“to bind, plait”). More at thur. The Greek and Aromanian/Romanian loanwords were borrowed from the variant cark.
Feminine of North Gheg thak, from Proto-Albanian *tsaka, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱokh₂o- (“branch”) (compare Lithuanian šakà, Serbo-Croatian soha).
From Proto-Albanian *tsala, cognate to Sanskrit शाल (śalá, “stick, cane”), Old Irish cail (“spear”), Old Norse hali (“point of a pole”).
From older and dialectal thalb, from Proto-Albanian *tsalba, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱel- (“to cover”) (compare Ancient Greek κέλυφος (kéluphos, “shell, pod”), Old English heolstor (“darkness”)).
Perhaps from Proto-Albanian *ćau̯ila/*ćau̯ilā, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱówilos/-eh₂. Compare Ancient Greek κοῖλος (koîlos).
From Proto-Albanian *θēm-, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱens- (“to say, instruct, announce”). Cognate with Latin cēnseō (“to give an opinion, to judge, guess, reckon”). Potentially a doublet of rrëfej.
From Proto-Albanian *tsambrā, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ḱh₂emb- (“bent, crooked”) (compare Ancient Greek σκαμβός (skambós), Old Irish camm, Swedish skimpa (“to hop”)).
From Proto-Albanian *tsaipa, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱoypos (compare Latin cippus (“pole”), Sanskrit शेप (śépa, “tail, penis”)).

parole.significato: to cut, gut, prick, pierce, slaughter
parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *tśōr-, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱeh₃-(i-) (“to sharpen, whet”).
From Proto-Albanian *tser-ākā, derived from ther.

Singularized plural of Old Albanian thas, from Proto-Albanian *tsatja, from Proto-Indo-European *ket-. Compare Serbo-Croatian kòtac (“cattle-shed, weir”), Latin catinus (“bowl”), Old English heaþor (“enclosure, jail”).

From Proto-Albanian *ćūs < *ćūs < *sūs, from Proto-Indo-European *suHs, with influence from Proto-Indo-European *ḱuh₁- (“swollen, fat”), hence the initial Alb. th-. Compare English sow, Ancient Greek ὗς (hûs), Latvian sivēns, and Latin sūs. The plural form, also thi, continues Common Albanian *θȳ, f
From Proto-Albanian *θīniā, remade after the class of fem. ā-stems, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱyeh₁- (“dark(-coloured), grey”). Cognate to Old Church Slavonic синь (sinĭ, “dark blue”).
From Proto-Albanian *tsirwa, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱer- (“dark color”), identical with Lithuanian šiřvas (“grey”).

From Proto-Albanian *tsitsa, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *ḱik- (compare Serbo-Croatian sisa (“teat, tit”), Irish cíoch (“breast”), Old Armenian ծիծ (cic, “breast”)) and/or onomatopoeic. Related to thithkë.
Suffixed form of dialectal thithë, from Proto-Albanian *tsitsā, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱik- (compare Serbo-Croatian sisa (“teat, tit”), Irish cíoch (“breast”)). Related to thith.
From Proto-Albanian *tsitsā, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱik- (compare Serbo-Croatian sisa (“teat, tit”), Irish cíoch (“breast”)). Related to thith.
From Proto-Albanian *ϑel(u)-, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱelH- (“to freeze”). Cognate to Lithuanian šálti (“to freeze”). A formation with -(ë)t(ë).

From Proto-Albanian *tserma, a full grade of the root found in zero grade in surmë (“dark grey”), related to Lithuanian širmas (“gray”). A derivative of thjerë (“lentil”) as “having the color of lentils” is also possible.

Ultimate origin is unknown. Possibly a Mediterranean Wanderwort. Orel reconstructs Proto-Albanian *tserā, which he relates to thërrmoj (“to crumble”) and thërrime (“crumb”). Moreover, Demiraj considers this word akin to Latin cicer (“chickpea”), Old Armenian սիսեռն (siseṙn, “chickpea”) and maybe Anc

From Proto-Albanian *tseksta, compound of *ts- (“not”) and *eksta (“outside, beyond”) (modern jashtë (“out, away”)), i.e. 'within reach, close by'. More at jashtë. For sense development, compare French aise (“ease”), from Latin adjacens (“nearby”).

Inherited from Proto-Albanian *ts-angulā, prefixed diminutive of Proto-Indo-European *h₂éngʷʰis (“snake”) (compare Latin anguis, Lithuanian angi̇̀s, Old High German angar (“kind of maggot”)). Alternatiely, from Proto-Albanian *sengulā, diminutive of Proto-Indo-European *sengʰ- (“ant”) (compare Old P

Apocope of *thuan, from Proto-Albanian *(a)tsāna,from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱ- (“sharp”) (compare Lithuanian ašni̇̀s (“blade edge”), Ancient Greek ἄκανος (ákanos, “pine thistle”), English awn (“bristle of barley”)).

Unclear. There are two competing explanations: * From Proto-Albanian *tsupina (“stick”). Cognate with Ancient Greek σιβύνη (sibúnē, “flute case”), itself of Illyrian origin. This is probably a Wanderwort, having cognates in Caucasian and Middle Eastern languages, such as Old Armenian սուին (suin, “s
From Proto-Albanian *upera (“upper”), etymologically related to Old High German obar and Latin super. Alternatively a variant of shufër.

parole.significato: to plait, braid, interweave, to knit
parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *tsurja, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱr̥H-, zero-grade of *ḱer- (“to tie, plait”) (compare Ancient Greek καῖρος (kaîros, “row of thrums on the loom”), Armenian սարդ (sard, “spider”)).
From Proto-Albanian *tsā(i)nja, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱeh₃i- (“sharpen”) (compare English hone, Persian سان (sân, “whetstone”)).
From Proto-Albanian *tsangila, with *ts- prefix, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁óngʷl̥ (“charcoal, coal”).

Uncertain. Possibly: # A variant of thanukël (“common dogwood”), from thanë (“cornel cherry”) + -ukël (diminutive suffix). # From *thanulk-, from thanë (“cornel cherry”) + ulk (“wolf”). # From Proto-Albanian *tsunu-abōla, akin to Lithuanian šunobelė (“buckthorn”) and Dacian κινούβοιλα (kinoúboila, “

From Proto-Albanian *tsanidā, from Proto-Indo-European *-níd- (“nit”). Compare Serbo-Croatian gnjida, Old High German hniz, Greek κόνιδα (kónida) (κονίς (konís)). Matzinger suggests *ćanidā as the Proto-Albanian form instead.
From Proto-Albanian *ϑer, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱer-.

Inherited from Proto-Albanian *tū, from Proto-Indo-European *túh₂; modern accusative ty is from Proto-Albanian Proto-Albanian *twā from emphatic *twḗm, clitic të is from clitic *te, and ablative teje is from locative *toí + -je from meje (see unë).
According to Orel, from Proto-Albanian *tila, based on the pronominal stem *ti̯o, as in Old Norse þít (“there”). Çabej alternatively suggests an analogous formation to ti, tij.
From Proto-Albanian *terka, from Proto-Indo-European *térkʷ-e-ti, from *terkʷ- (“to twist, turn”). Compare Latin torquere, German drechseln (“to turn wood”), Greek αδράκτι (adrákti, “spindle”)).
From Proto-Albanian *tāga, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)tég-os, from *(s)teg- (“to cover”). Compare Latin tegō (“to cover”), Greek τέγος (tégos, “roof”), Old Irish tech (“house”), and others.
From Proto-Albanian *tāslā, from *tēkslā, from Proto-Indo-European *tetḱ- (“to hew”) (compare Latin tēlum, German Dechsel (“adze”), Russian тесла́ (teslá, “adze”)). Cognate with teshë.
From Proto-Albanian Proto-Albanian *toi + tu.

parole.significato: to thicken, to fatten, to plump up (something)
parole.testo: See Albanian trashë (“thick, fat, massive”) (from Proto-Albanian *trauša, according to Vladimir Orel).
From or related to trashë, ultimately from Proto-Albanian *trauša. Close to Lithuanian trąšùs (“fat, fertile (soil)”).

parole.significato: thick, fat, massive (thicker, wider than usual)
parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *trauša. Close to Lithuanian trąšùs (“fat, fertile (soil)”) (cf. Albanian trashi (“fertile soil”)). May reflect ultimate origin in Proto-Indo-European *treu- (“to destroy”), but this is not certain.
From Proto-Albanian *treje, from Proto-Indo-European *tréyes. Cognate to Latin trēs (“three”) and Sanskrit त्रि (tri, “three”).
From Proto-Albanian *treuδ-, from Proto-Indo-European *trewd- (“to squeeze, crush, press”). Cognate to Latin trūdō (“to push, force, press”) and Gothic 𐌿𐍃𐌸𐍂𐌹𐌿𐍄𐌰𐌽 (usþriutan, “to burden”).
From Proto-Albanian *trem(b)-, from Proto-Indo-European *trem- (“to tripp, patter, tremble”). Cognate to Latin tremo (“to tremble”). A formation with labial "epenthesis" in stem auslaut.

parole.significato: to dissolve, digest, melt down, lose weight
parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *trōtja, etymologically identical with Proto-Slavic *trǫtja (“to spend, waste”).
From Proto-Albanian *trī(-ā), from Proto-Indo-European *tríh₂ (“three”). Cognate to Ancient Greek τρία (tría, “three”) and Latin tria (“three”).

parole.motivo_incerta: Of uncertain origin; Probably; modello unc/uncertain
parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *tri/eK-(ś-), of uncertain origin, probably from Proto-Indo-European *tréyes (“three”). Similar formation with degё. Cognate to Ancient Greek τρέχνος (trékhnos) and τέρχνος (térkhnos, “sprout, (young) shoot”).
From Proto-Albanian *trākā, close to Sanskrit तर्कु (tarkú, “spindle”) and Tocharian A tark (“earring”). Related to tjerr.
Continues a Common Albanian *t(ə)rún, inherited from Proto-Albanian *tʲerúna-, from Proto-Indo-European *terh₂unós (“soft mass”), from the root *terh₂- (“to be soft”).
From Proto-Albanian *trūtja, from Proto-Indo-European *trewH-, *truH-. Cognate to Ancient Greek τρύω (trúō, “to wear out, to exhaust”), Lithuanian trūniú, trūněti (“to rot,to go faul”).

From Proto-Albanian *tulla- (“piece of meat”), from older *túli̯a-, from Pre-Proto-Albanian *tuu̯úli̯a- < *tuu̯əl̥i̯-á- < *tuHəli̯-á-, from Proto-Indo-European *tuh₂ló- (“swollen”) or *tuh₂li̯-ó- (“having swelling”), from Proto-Indo-European *tewh₂- (“to swell”). Cognate to: * Ancient Greek τύλος (t
From Proto-Albanian *tunda, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)tu-n-d- (“push, thrust”) (compare Latin tundō, Sanskrit तुन्दते (tundate)), nasal present of *(s)tewd-. More at shtyj.
From Proto-Albanian *tura, cognate to Old High German dweran (“to run fast”), Old Norse þyrja (“to run”).
From Proto-Albanian *tutja, cognate to Old Norse þeya (“to melt”), Old High German douwen (“id”), with 'being silent' as an intermediary stage of semantic development. Alternatively related to tund.
From Proto-Albanian *tutja, cognate to Old Norse þeya (“to melt”), Old High German douwen (“id”), with 'being silent' as an intermediary stage of semantic development. Alternatively related to tund.
From Proto-Albanian *tu (as in këtu), and the second element tje (as in atje), from Proto-Albanian *te, of unclear origin.
From Proto-Albanian *tūtā, from Proto-Indo-European *tewh₂- (“to swell; crowd; be strong”), also forming a doublet of tul and tëtanë (possibly).
From Proto-Albanian *toi ksu, the second component being equal to Ancient Greek ξύν (xún, “with, at the same time”).
From Proto-Albanian *tam-(ϑ-), probably from Proto-Indo-European *tūm- (“to grow”). Cognate to Latin tama (“kind of bumb, swelling”). A formation with -th enlargement.

A prefixal derivative with tër-, based on *thor, from Proto-Albanian *tsāsra, continuing Proto-Indo-European *ḱes-ro- (“to cut”). Cognate to Sanskrit शस्त (śásta, “cut down, slaughtered”), Ancient Greek κεάζω (keázō, “to split”). Related to ther.

From tërthor + -të, the former a prefixal derivative with tër-, based on *thor, from Proto-Albanian *tsāsra, continuing Proto-Indo-European *ḱes-ro- (“to cut”). Cognate to Sanskrit शस्त (śásta, “cut down, slaughtered”), Ancient Greek κεάζω (keázō, “to split”). Related to ther.

* According to Orel, from Proto-Albanian *twana, from Proto-Indo-European *tewH-, compare Lithuanian tvi̇̀nti (“to rise, swell”), Lithuanian tvãnas (“flood”). * According to Demiraj, from Proto-Albanian *tan-, from Proto-Indo-European *tód (“it”). Cognate to Ancient Greek τόν (tón, “it”).
From Proto-Albanian *wa, from Proto-Indo-European *swom, from Proto-Indo-European *swé. Compare Latin sē.

parole.significato: salted, boiled milk or yogurt stored in a leather or cheesecloth bag
parole.testo: From fuller urdhos, from dialectal urdhë + participial -os ~ ues, from Proto-Albanian *wurdā, from Proto-Indo-European *werh₁- (“boil, cook”) (compare Lithuanian vérdu, Serbo-Croatian váriti).
From archaic and dialectal ulk, from Proto-Albanian *ulka, from Proto-Indo-European *wĺ̥kʷos. Compare Sanskrit वृक (vṛ́ka), Persian گرگ (gorg), Lithuanian vilkas, Russian волк (volk).
From Proto-Albanian *udrjā, derived from Proto-Indo-European *wed- (“water”). Compare Latin unda, Sanskrit उदन् (udan, “water”).

parole.significato: to sit down, put (someone/something) on a seat (or on the ground)
parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *wala, from *wol-o-, o-grade of Proto-Indo-European *wel- (“press together”) (compare Lithuanian valýti (“to clean”), Ancient Greek εἰλέω (eiléō, “press together”)). Variant unj is from *ulnj, from Proto-Albanian *walnja, a causative of the previous.

From an unattested *ulm, from Proto-Albanian *ulg(a)ma, from Proto-Indo-European *welg-. Cognate to Old High German welc (“wet”), Lithuanian vi̇̀lgyti (“to make wet”), Latvian valgums (“wetness”), Proto-Slavic *vьlgъkъ (“wet”).
Diminutive of Proto-Albanian *ulma, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁l̥mos (“mountain elm”) (compare Irish leamh, Latin ulmus), oblique of *h₁élem (compare English elm, Polish ilm).

From an unattested *umë, from Proto-Albanian *wamā, from Proto-Indo-European *wemh₁- (“to vomit”). Cognate with Ancient Greek ἐμέω (eméō, “to spit out”), Latin vomō (“to vomit”), Avestan 𐬬𐬀𐬨 (vam, “to spit”), Sanskrit वमिति (vámiti, “to vomit”).
Based on unë, from Proto-Albanian *wandā. Cognate to Old Armenian գինդ (gind, “ring”), Gothic 𐌱𐌹𐍅𐌹𐌽𐌳𐌰𐌽 (biwindan, “to unwreathe”). The variant ognazë is found in the Çam dialect.
From Proto-Albanian *un-, from Proto-Indo-European *wenh₁- (“to love”). Cognate to English wish, Latin venia (“indulgence, kindness”).

Compound of archaic and dialectal u + -në (particle) (compare Tosk Albanian ti (“you”) vs. Gheg tinë). U is from earlier *udh, from Proto-Albanian *udz, from *uǵ, with vowel from *túh₂ (see ti), from Proto-Indo-European *éǵh₂. Accusative mua (var. mue) is from emphatic *h₁mēm, clitic më is from clit
From Proto-Albanian *wantā, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂wn̥tós (“wounded”). Compare English wound, Old Armenian վանդեմ (vandem, “to drive away, destroy”).

From udhë (“way, road”), from Proto-Albanian *uj́ā-, from Proto-Indo-European *uǵʰéh₂ < *weǵʰ- (“to move, walk”). Cognate to Latin vehō, via, Old English weġ. Connected to erdha. Alternative variant of hurdhë. From Proto-Albanian *wurdā, from an earlier *urdā or *uordā, from Proto-Indo-European *wer- (“to boil, to burn”). Cognate to Old Armenian վառիմ (vaṙim, “to burn”), Lithuanian vi̇̀rti (“to cook, to boil”). Compare also Romanian urdă.
From Proto-Albanian *urelā, cognate to Old Norse úr (“drizzle”), Old Prussian wurs (“pool”) and Ancient Greek ἄν-αυρος (án-auros, “devoid of water”).
Derived from *ur. From Proto-Albanian *wana, a nominal derivative of Proto-Indo-European *wenh₁- (“to want, to desire”). Cognate to English wish, Latin venia (“indulgence, kindness”).
Diminutive of variant uri, from archaic ur, from Proto-Albanian *wara, from Proto-Indo-European *wewer (“squirrel”) (compare Serbo-Croatian vjȅverica, Lithuanian voverė, Latin viverra (“ferret”)).
From Proto-Albanian *warnā, from Proto-Indo-European *uer-(e)neh₂ (“alder, poplar”).

With dialectal devoicing of -dh-, from dialectal urdh, masculinized from dialectal urdhë, from Proto-Albanian *wurdā, from Proto-Indo-European *wr̥dʰo (“sweetbriar”). Compare dialectal Norwegian erre, orr (“bush”), Latin rubus (“bramble”), Persian گل (gol, “flower”)).

First attested in 1555. Uncertain, however, suggested to be: * a -të continuation of a Proto-Albanian *(w)ura- (“clever, experienced”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)wr̥h₃ós (“insightful, observant”). * related to Old High German war (“aware, careful”), from Proto-Albanian *urta, from Proto-Indo-Euro

parole.significato: piece of burning wood used for light or fire
parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *warā, from Proto-Indo-European *werh₁- (“boil, cook”) (compare Lithuanian vérdu, Serbo-Croatian váriti).
Identical to ushtë (“spear; unripe spike”), from Proto-Albanian *ušta, close to Old High German ort (“point”), Old Norse oddr (“point”) and Lithuanian usni̇̀s (“thistle”).

Related to shushunjë (“leech”). Could be a derivative with unique loss of initial sh-. Alternatively, if inherited, from Proto-Albanian *ūdsonja, from *ūd (“water”) + *-es (agent noun) + *-onja (feminine suffix) + *-az (diminutive suffix).
From Proto-Albanian *awa-, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ewo. See vë, cognate with Sanskrit अव (ava, “off, down”).
From Proto-Albanian *u̯ɔλa, from Vulgar Latin *oli̯u, from Latin oleum, from Ancient Greek ἔλαιον (élaion).

Possibly from Proto-Albanian *wai, from Proto-Indo-European *wáy (“woe!, alas!”); similar words are found in several European languages. Cognate to Ancient Greek ὀά (oá, “woe!, alas!”) and Old Armenian վայ (vay, “cry of pain”), Latin vae, Icelandic vei, Dutch wee, English woe. Compare also Romanian
From dialectal vajë + -zë (diminutive suffix), from *varjë, from *varë, contraction of *vëharë, from Proto-Albanian *swesarā, from Proto-Indo-European *swésōr (“sister”).

From Proto-Albanian *walnā, from Proto-Indo-European *wólneh₂- (“roll, undulation”), from *welH- (“to roll, undulate”). Compare Lithuanian vilni̇̀s (“wave”), Bulgarian вълна́ (vălná, “wave”), and Sanskrit ऊर्मि (ūrmi, “wave”).
From Proto-Albanian *wallā, from Proto-Indo-European *wel(H)- (“hot, boiling”). Cognate to Old High German walo (“lukewarm”).

From Proto-Albanian *uang-, from Proto-Indo-European *wen(H)g- (“to be bent, curved”). Cognate to Lithuanian vi̇̀ngis (“bow, crooking”) and Old High German wankon (“to shake, totter, stagger”). See Proto-Germanic *wangaz (“meadow, pasture”) for more cognates.
From Proto-Albanian *wang-, from Proto-Indo-European *wen(H)g- (“to be bent, curved”). Cognate with Lithuanian vi̇̀ngis (“bow, crooking”), Old High German wankōn (“to shake, totter, stagger”).
From Proto-Albanian *werja, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂wer- (“to bind, hang”) (compare Ancient Greek ἀείρω (aeírō, “to heave, hoist up”), Lithuanian vérti (“to weigh”)).
From Proto-Albanian *wɔrfana-, ultimately from Ancient Greek ὀρφανός (orphanós), probably through Latin orphanus. Compare Aromanian oarfãn, archaic Romanian oarfăn.
From Proto-Albanian *ā̆ur(V)n, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁er-, close to Gothic 𐌰𐌿𐍂𐌰𐌷𐌾𐍉𐌼 (aurahjōm, “monuments, tombs”, dat. pl.), Old English ēar (“grave, earth”).
From Proto-Albanian *uar(e)nā, from Proto-Indo-European *wer(H)- (“to cut (off), tear”). Cognate to Sanskrit व्रण (vraṇá, “wound, tearing”) and Avestan 𐬓𐬀𐬭𐬀 (xᵛara, “wound, hurt”).

parole.significato: to die (used only for humans and bees)
parole.testo: A formation in -s of Proto-Albanian *awa-deja, from earlier *dej, continuing Proto-Indo-European *dʰew-. Compare Old Church Slavonic давити (daviti, “suffocate”), Gothic 𐌰𐍆𐌳𐌰𐌿𐌹𐌸𐍃 (afdauiþs, “troubled”), Old Irish díth (“end, death”), Avestan 𐬛𐬎𐬎𐬀𐬌𐬛𐬍 (duuaidī, “we press”), Latin fūnus (“death”) and E
From Proto-Albanian *widewā, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁widʰéwh₂ (compare English widow, Latin vidua).
From Proto-Albanian *waigā, from Proto-Indo-European *ueiH, *ueHi- (“to revolve, spin, plait”). Cognate to Latin vieo (“to bend, plait”).

From Proto-Albanian *webnja, from Proto-Indo-European *webʰ- (“to weave”). Cognate with Sanskrit उनब्द्धि (unábddhi, “to bind, compress”), Old High German weban (“to weave”), Tocharian B wāp- (“to weave”).
From Proto-Albanian *wala, Proto-Indo-European *welH- (“to turn, twist”). From the same root of vjell and vjel.
Alteration of dhemje, from Proto-Albanian *dzōmjā, from *dzō (“ground, dirt”). More at dhe.

From Proto-Albanian *wen-ta, an adjectival formation from earlier *wena, itself a gerund formation from vë. The term has been compared to the Illyrian-derived toponyms Vendum and Avendius (compare Οὐένδων (Ouéndōn)); note also Proto-Celtic *wentā (“place, town”).
From Proto-Albanian *vemj- from Proto-Indo-European *h²eu̯bʰ-n̥i̯-.
From Proto-Albanian *wainā-, from Proto-Indo-European *woy(h₁)neh₂- < *wéyh₁ō (“wine”). Compare Ancient Greek οἶνος (oînos), Latin vīnum, German Wein.
From Proto-Albanian *u̯œrbana-, borrowed from Vulgar Latin ōrbus, from Latin orbus (“deprived”). compare Italian orbo, Dalmatian vuarb, Romanian orb.
From Proto-Albanian *werna, from Proto-Indo-European *wern- (compare Welsh gwern, Armenian գերան (geran, “beam, timber”)). possibly borrowed from Proto-Celtic *wernā
From Proto-Albanian *wer-n-. Compare Celtic verno- (Gall. Verno-dubrum, French verne (alder), Irish fern).
From Proto-Albanian *wardjā, from Proto-Indo-European *u̯orHd-i/o (“frog”). Compare Lithuanian varlė̃, Latvian var̂de, Armenian գորտ (gort)).
From Proto-Albanian *wainā-, from Proto-Indo-European *woy(h₁)neh₂- < *wéyh₁ō (“wine”). Compare Ancient Greek οἶνος (oînos), Latin vīnum, German Wein.
From Proto-Albanian *wesi, from earlier *ōusi, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ṓws- and dual ending *-ih₁. Cognate with Lithuanian ausi̇̀s (“id”), Ancient Greek οὖς (oûs), Latin auris.
From Proto-Albanian *wesja, from Proto-Indo-European *woséyeti, from *wes- (compare English wear, Sanskrit वस्ते (vaste), Tocharian B wäs-, Latin vestis).

Altered with v- from veshje of variant eshkë, from Proto-Albanian *aiškā, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂oyd-sk-eh₂ (compare Old Church Slavonic исто (isto, “kidney”), Old Norse eista (“testicle”)), from *h₂eyd- (“to swell”), whence Ancient Greek οἰδέω (oidéō).
From Proto-Albanian *wáinesta sg, *wainésta pl, from *uainā > verë/venë (“vine-branch, wine”).

Originally from *vemte (*vem suffixed with te), from the original form in Proto-Albanian *wadmi, from athematic Proto-Indo-European *weh₂dʰ- (perhaps *weh₂dʰ-mi). Also cognate to English wade (“to walk through water”), Old Armenian գամ (gam, “to come”), Latin vādō (“to go, walk”).

From Proto-Albanian *swetā, from Proto-Indo-European *swet- (“self; one's own”), from *swé; compare Lithuanian svetỹs (“foreigner”), Russian сват (svat, “matchmaker; father-in-law”), Attic Greek ἔτης (étēs, “relative, friend”), Elean Greek ϝέτας (wétas). Related to u. Closely related to Messapic vei
From variant vitë, from Proto-Albanian *aweitā. More at vito.

parole.significato: stretcher, litter, bier, transition (consisting of beams)
parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *uig-, from Proto-Indo-European *weyk- (“to revolve, turn, twist”). Cognate to Old English wice (“patch”) and Old Norse vik (“bight”).
Enlargement in -më of participle of unattested *vegoj, from Proto-Albanian *věgonja, from Proto-Indo-European *sweh₂gʰ- (“to wail”)

From Proto-Albanian *uitśi-(ā), from Proto-Indo-European *weyḱ- (“house, settlement”). Cognate to Sanskrit विश् (víś, “settlement, community, tribe”), Ancient Greek οἰκία (oikía, “house”), Latin vicus (“village”).

From Proto-Albanian *weta, from Proto-Indo-European *wétos (compare Proto-Slavic *věkъ (“age (period of time)”), Greek έτος (étos), Latin vetus (“old”), Old Church Slavonic ветъхъ (vetŭxŭ, “old, aged, ancient”)).

A diminutive in -th, based on Proto-Albanian *wīja (“twisted, woven”), from *weh₁yos (“twisted”), ultimately from *weh₁y- (“to twist, to twine”). Cognate to Latin vīeō, Sanskrit व्ययति (vyáyati), Lithuanian výti, Proto-Slavic *viti.
From Proto-Albanian *weitā, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éwis (“bird”); compare Ancient Greek ᾱ̓ετός (āetós, “eagle”), Latin avis.

From *viz + -ull, from Proto-Albanian *vidza, from Proto-Indo-European *weyd- (“to know; see”). Cognates include Ancient Greek εἴδω (eídō), Latin videō, Mycenaean Greek 𐀹𐀆 (wi-de), Sanskrit वेत्ति (vétti), Old English witan (English wit).

parole.significato: viç m (plural viça, definite viçi, definite plural viçat) (Standard)
parole.testo: From *vitësh (cf. ablative form of vit (“year”) > vitesh), from Proto-Albanian *wetuša, from *wétos-jo, from Proto-Indo-European *wéteso (compare English wether, Sanskrit वत्स (vatsa), Romanian vițel). Related to Albanian vit (“year”).

From Proto-Albanian *wedza, from Proto-Indo-European *wéǵʰeti (“to bring, carry, transport”). Compare Gothic gawigan (“to steal”), Latin vehere (“to bear, to carry”), Lithuanian vèžti. For sense development, compare Proto-Indo-European *bʰṓr (“thief”), from the root *bʰer- (“to carry”), whence Latin
From Proto-Albanian *vedzula, a diminutive of *wedza (“to steal”) with *-ula.

From Proto-Albanian *swexura, from Proto-Indo-European *sueḱue/or-, *swéḱuros (“father-in-law”). Cognate to Ancient Greek ἑκυρός (hekurós, “father-in-law”), German Schwieger (“mother-in-law”), Old English sweor, Latin socer, Russian свёкор (svjókor), Serbo-Croatian svekar, Sanskrit श्वशुर (śvaśura),

parole.significato: to harvest, reap (cereals, profits), pick (cotton, fruit)
parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *uell-, from Proto-Indo-European *welh₃-(s-) (“to tear, seize upon”). Cognate to |Latin vello (“to pluck, tug”), Latvian veli, Lithuanian vẽlės (“the ghostly figures of the deceased”), Gothic wilwan (“to rob”), and Hittite [Term?] (/⁠hullāi⁠/, “fight, struggle”).
Originally ‘wind, twist’, from Proto-Albanian *welwa, from Proto-Indo-European *welH- 'to turn, roll' (compare Latin volvere, Old English wealwian, Ancient Greek εἰλύω (eilúō) ‘to roll up, wrap’).

From Proto-Albanian *werdza, from Proto-Indo-European *wérǵʰ-e-ti, from *werǵʰ- (“to bind, squeeze”). Cognate with Lithuanian ver̃žti (“to constrain, lace”), Middle High German erwergen (“to scrag, strangle”), Latin urgere (“to press”).
From Proto-Albanian *wera, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂wer-o-, from the root *h₂wer- (“to raise, hang”) (compare Ancient Greek ἀείρω (aeírō, “to heave, hoist up”), Lithuanian vérti (“to weigh”)).
From Proto-Albanian *wetās, from *wétōs, from Proto-Indo-European *wétos (“year”). More at vit.
From older vjetësh, a derivative of vjet. From Proto-Albanian *u̯itəś, from PPA *u̯éteśi, plural of *u̯étad (“year”).
From Proto-Albanian *awa-luga, a prefixal derivative of Proto-Indo-European *lewg- (“to bend”). Cognate to Greek λυγίζω (lygízo), Old Norse lykna (“to bend knees”), Lithuanian lùgnas (“flexible”).
From Proto-Albanian *wáinesta sg, *wainésta pl, from *wainā > verë/venë (“vine-branch, wine”).
From Proto-Albanian *wāgā, from Proto-Indo-European *wegʷ- (“wet”), related to Greek υγρός (ygrós, “wet”), Old Norse vǫkr (“id”).

From Proto-Albanian *wāgla, from Proto-Indo-European *Hou-go-, compare Latin vagus (“roaming, wandering”) and Norwegian våk (“child”). Related to vogërr. According to Krzysztof Tomasz Witczak, it is the source of Doric Greek βάδιος (bádios, “child”). According to Matasović, the etymology vogël is co

parole.significato: pipkin, clay pot used to boil food
parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *wāribā, further origin disputed, a semantic development from original "turning, whirling" to "clay pot" is reasonable, compare vorbull and vorbëtirë and toponyms which unlikely would be named after an object but rather than a whirlpool or other natural phenomenons, thus compare

From Proto-Albanian *awa-rangula from Proto-Indo-European *(s)krengh- (“to turn, bend”). Compare Umbrian 𐌊𐌓𐌄𐌍𐌊𐌀𐌕𐌓𐌖𐌌 (krenkatrum), cringatro (“belt”), Proto-Slavic *krǫgъ (“circle”) (Russian круг (krug)), Old English hrung (“cross-bar, spoke”), hring (“ring”).

Inherited from Proto-Albanian *u̯ərátˢ < older *u̯ərátˢə, from Proto-Indo-European *(h)u̯arn-áti̯a/e-, with the meaning going from "to wound (mortally)" to "to kill". This further continues PIE *(h)u̯arnā- (“wound”) (source of varrë (“wound”)). An initial Pre-Proto-Albanian *u̯r- can be excluded as
Tosk variant of Gheg vnesht, from Proto-Albanian *wáinesta sg, *wainésta pl, from *wainā > verë/venë (“vine-branch, wine”).
From Proto-Albanian *awa-ruga, a prefixal form related to Avestan 𐬭𐬀𐬊𐬖𐬥𐬀 (raoγna, “butter”), Old Norse rjúmi (“cream”).
from vrenjt, formation of vë- and re, alternative from Proto-Albanian *awa-rina. see vdes, vras
From Proto-Albanian *wurga, related to Ancient Greek ὀργάω (orgáō, “to be soaked”), ὀργάς (orgás, “marsh, meadow”).
From Proto-Albanian *swesarā, from Proto-Indo-European *swésōr (“sister”).

From earlier *vëllaz-, from Proto-Albanian *swelaudā, from Proto-Indo-European *swé-lowdʰ-, compound of *swé (“self, one's”) and *h₁lewdʰ- (“grow”), whence respectively vetë (“self”) and lej (“to be born”). Displaced Proto-Indo-European *bʰréh₂tēr (“brother”) Summary of theories Bopp (1855) naively
From Proto-Albanian *u̯eladi̯anía. From vëlla + ëri.
From Proto-Albanian *wenta, derivative of vë (“to put”).

parole.significato: wooden rim of a cart/wagon wheel; one section of such a rim: felly
parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *wengā.

From Proto-Albanian *weratja, from Proto-Indo-European *werh₁- (“to speak”); compare Greek εἴρω (eíro, “to say”), Hittite 𒌑𒂊𒊑𒄿𒊍𒍣 (ú-e-ri-ya-az-zi, “it frightens”), and Russian врать (vratʹ, “to lie; tell tales”).

From Proto-Albanian *werā or *werwā, perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *h₁werH- (“to be wide, spacious”) (or derivative *h₁werH-u-) and thereby cognate to Sanskrit उरु (urú, “wide”), वरस् (váras, “space, width”), and Greek ευρύς (evrýs, “wide”).

From Proto-Albanian *werā or *werwā, perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *h₁werH- (“to be wide, spacious”) (or derivative *h₁wérHus) and thereby cognate to Sanskrit उरु (urú, “wide”), वरस् (váras, “space, width”), and Greek ευρύς (evrýs, “wide”).
Compound of Proto-Albanian *ulnā (“forearm”) and *bōra (“bow”), mirror image of bërryl (“elbow”). More at bërryl. Alternatively, from yll (“star”) + ber (“bow”).
From Proto-Albanian *awi-sta, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éwis (“bird”) and *steh₂- (“to stand”). Originally meaning 'to foretell according to birds, to augur'. Compare Latin augurāre and auspicāre.
From Early Proto-Albanian *dis- > *diš- > *dš- > *tš- > s- before unvoiced phonemes, z- before voiced phonemes. It is mainly connected with the formation of verbs.

From Proto-Albanian *dis-banja, prefixed form of *banja (“to appear”), whence modern bëj (“to do, make; (dial.) appear”). Related to Sanskrit भाति (bhāti, “to shine”), Old Irish bán (“white”). Reanalyzable as z- + bëj.

parole.significato: to descend, get off, climb down
parole.testo: Inherited from Common Albanian *əzbréz (with final devoicing to -s), from Proto-Albanian *əzbredᶻə, from Pre-Proto-Albanian *ezbrédyV, with synocope from older *ezbrédiyV, with i-umlaut from older PPA *ezbrádiyV ("to move out, go away"). The word may be dissected as *ez-brádiyV, with the *ez- prefix
A prefixal formation based on Proto-Albanian *d(e)ranja, cognate to Sanskrit दृणाति (dṛṇắti, “to burst”), Ancient Greek δέρω (dérō, “to skin, to flay”).

parole.significato: ulcer, sore, wound (on a horse's withers)
parole.testo: From zdraj (“to swell, to make swell”), a prefixal derivative from Proto-Albanian *d(e)ranja (compare Sanskrit दृणाति (dṛṇāti, “to burst”) and Ancient Greek δέρω (dérō, “to skin, to flay”)).
Feminine of zi. Reconstructed as Proto-Albanian *dᶻu̯édᶻā (“black”) < *j́u̯ídᶻā < Pre-Proto-Albanian *j́u̯ídi̯ā < *ǵu̯idʰ-i̯éh₂ < Balkan-Indo-European *ǵu̯ei̯dʰ-ih₂/*ǵu̯idʰ-i̯éh₂.
From Proto-Albanian *diš-garbā, from *garbā. More at garbë.
From Proto-Albanian *dis-sadā, prefixed derivative of *sada (whence modern gjedh).
Originally meaning "acting like a fool", from Proto-Albanian *dis-garda (“out of the fence”), from *garda (“fence”), + *-mi (“me”), in reference to the behavior of cattle once out in the field.

parole.significato: to beat up (generally with a stick)
parole.testo: A voiced variant of an earlier *shtap, from Proto-Albanian *štapa, related to the word for 'stick'. Compare Old English stæf, German Stab, Serbo-Croatian stap (“staff”).
Uncertain. Lopuhaä claims from Proto-Albanian *žulai.

From Proto-Albanian *džernja, based on a less frequent form zie, from Proto-Albanian *džera, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰér-e-ti, thematic root present of *gʷʰer-. Cognate to Ancient Greek θέρομαι (théromai, “to become hot, to warm, to burn”), Old Irish fogeir (“(he) warms”). See also ζέω (zéō, “to
From Proto-Albanian *dźerm-, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰer-mós (whence Ancient Greek θερμός (thermós), Old Armenian ջերմ (ǰerm)), from *gʷʰer- (“hot, warm”).
From Proto-Albanian *dźerm-, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰer-mós (whence Ancient Greek θερμός (thermós), Old Armenian ջերմ (ǰerm)), from *gʷʰer- (“hot, warm”).

* From Proto-Albanian *dźāg, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵ(h)(u)eh2-G- (“young animal, nestling”). Cognate to Armenian ձագ (jag, “nestling”), and perhaps Persian زاق (zâq, “young animal”). * From Proto-Albanian *j́u̯āgV-, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰu̯ah₂gʰV-. Compare Armenian ձագ (jag, “nestling”). *

parole.significato: lady in a wealthy family with servants
parole.testo: From *džotnja, from Proto-Albanian *dzwāptnjā, from earlier *w(i)tspátnjā, from Proto-Indo-European *wiḱ-pót-nih₂ (“clan matriarch”), from *wiḱpótis (compare Lithuanian viešpatni (“lady”)), compound of *weyḱ- (“clan, kindred”) (compare Ancient Greek οἰκία (oikía, “house (clan)”), Avestan 𐬬𐬌𐬚 (viθ, “

Uncertain. *From Proto-Albanian *dzwāpt, from *w(i)tspáti, from Proto-Indo-European *wiḱpótis (“clan leader”) (compare Lithuanian viēšpats, Avestan 𐬬𐬍𐬯𐬞𐬀𐬌𐬙𐬌 (vīspaⁱti)), compound of *weyḱ- (“clan, extended family”) (compare Ancient Greek οἰκία (oikía, “house (clan)”), Avestan 𐬬𐬌𐬚 (viθ, “royal court”)) and *pót

From Proto-Albanian *dzulā, a zero-grade derivative of Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰewH- (“to call”). Cognate to Sanskrit हवते (hávate, “to call, invoke”), Avestan 𐬰𐬀𐬎𐬎𐬀𐬌𐬙𐬌 (zauuaⁱti) and Old Church Slavonic зъвати (zŭvati).

A z-prefixed form of varrë, from Proto-Albanian *varsa, from Proto-Indo-European *wers- (“to drag on the ground”). Compare Hittite [Term?] (/⁠u̯arš-⁠/, “pluck, reap”), Ancient Greek ἔρρω (érrhō, “to move slowly, limp; go away, disappear”), Latin verrō (“to drag, to sweep”), Old Norse vǫrr (“stroke”)
From Proto-Albanian *j́u̯anʉh, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰwonos. Compare Messapic den (“voice”) Serbo-Croatian zvono (“bell”), Armenian ձայն (jayn, “voice”).

From Old Albanian zan, from Proto-Albanian *džeina, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰendʰ- (compare English begin, Ancient Greek χανδάνω (khandánō, “to hold, contain”), Sanskrit ज्या (jyā́, “force, power”), जयति (jáyati, “to win, conquer”)).
From Proto-Albanian *džanja, a derivative of zë (“voice”).

From older variant çanj, from Proto-Albanian *štšenja, from Proto-Indo-European *sked-n-ie/o, from *sked- (“to cut, hack”) (compare Ancient Greek σκεδάννυμι (skedánnumi), Avestan 𐬯𐬗𐬌𐬥𐬛𐬀𐬌𐬌𐬈𐬌𐬙𐬌 (scindaiieⁱti)).
From Proto-Albanian *štšala, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kel- (“crooked”) (compare Greek σκολιός (skoliós), German scheel, Latin scelus (“curse”)).

parole.significato: forked shoring pole for a wall or fence
parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *štšentra, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱéntrom (compare Ancient Greek κέντρον (kéntron), Old Armenian սանտր (santr), սանդր (sandr)) with s-mobile, from *ḱent- (“to prick; point”) (compare Latvian sīts (“hunting spear”), Old High German hantag (“pointy”)).
From Proto-Albanian *štšepa, from Proto-Indo-European *sḱep- (“cut, split”) (compare Serbo-Croatian rascijepati, Greek σκάπτω (skápto, “to dig”)).
From Proto-Albanian *štšertja, from *skera (modern shqerr). Çabej lists it same as çart. More at shqerr.
From Proto-Albanian *štšela, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kelH- (“split (apart)”) (compare Lithuanian skélti, Old Norse skilja, Ancient Greek σκάλλω (skállō, “to hoe, stir up”)).
From Proto-Albanian *štšepna, from *štšepa (modern çap). More at çap.

Singularized plural form of *çerdhë, either from ç- + herdhe, from dialectal çuherdhe (cf. çubardhë, çafurde etc.), attested in Gazulli as quherdhe, from Proto-Albanian *škerdā, earlier *skarda, possibly reflected in the first part of the Illyrian proper name Skerdilaidas.
From Proto-Albanian *iš-kera, from *skera. More at shqerr.
